LAZYLAND. Three travellers wandered along the strand Each with a staff in his feeble nand; And they chanted le"-, " We are go-o-o- Ing slow-o-osv- Ly to Lazyland. "They've left off eating and drinking, there; They never do anything, there; They never walk, And they never talk, And they fall asleep without winking, there. "Nobody's in a hurry, there; They're not permitted to worry, there; 'T is a wide, still place, And not a face Shows any symptom of flurry, there. "No bells are runs in the morning, there; They care not at all for adorning, there; All sounds are hushed, And a man who rushed Would be treated with absolute scorning, there.. " They do not take any papers, there; No politicians cut capers, there; They have no • views,' And they tell no news, And they burn no midnight tapers, there. "No lovers are ever permitted, there; Reformers are not admitted, there; They argue not In that peaceful spot, And their clothes all come ready fitted, there. "Electricity has not been heard of, there; And steam has been spoken no word of, there; They stay where they are; And 'a coach or car They have not so much as a third of, there. "Oh. this world is a truly crazy land A worrying, hurrying, mazy land; We cannot stay; We must find the way,— If there is a way,—to Lazyland." —The Century Magazine.

A heart that has been often tendered is tough. All men are created equal; particularly twins. Little Bertie : "Does the sun tan you?" Little Reginald: "No, the father." No language can express the feelings of a deaf mute who.steps on a tack in a dark room. Drying the face by upward movements is said to ,counteract wrinkles; but isn't this notion a new 'wrinkle itself?

"Why 'don't the young men marry?" queried her young sister. "I suppose they are not asked," absently replied the bride of 1883. Virtue is like precious odours. most fragrant when they are incensed and crushed, for prosperity doth best discover vice, but adversity cloth best discover virtue. In the New York 41-r!d s report of a politicar.rnPeting the word "shouts" was so ludicrously misprinted as to make the blunder famous: "The snouts of ten thousand

Democrats rant the air," read the report. A reporter on:the New York Herald recently had occa- sion to quote a verse from a familiar hymn. The proof- reader dutifully underscored the word, and the verse appeared, "Hark, the Herald angels sing." MODNiTY. "What hundred books are best, think you ?",,I said. • Addressing ,one devoted to the pen. Be thought a moment, then he raised his head: "I hardly know—l've written only ten." WHY SEM WAS INDIGNANT.—AIicc : It seems to me that you treat Harry very coldly lately. What has he done?" Louise: "lie asked me i for a: kiss." Alice: "Well,!what of that?" Louise: "What of that? The man that wont't take a kiss without asking for it is a snob." _

A COOL COSTUME.—Mrs. Gazzam : "George, I really must have some money for a new dress." Gazzam : "Dresses are all going out of style." Mrs. Gazzam : "What on earth do you mean?" Gazzam : "Well, I read Fin a fashion article that 'nothing but coralornaments will be worn this season."

" l;will be a sister to you," she said. "No," he replied sadly. "I've got one sister: who wears my neckties, borrows cab fares, loses my hairbrush, puts tidies over the furniture in my room, and expects me to take her to the theatre twice a week. I think I'll go out into the -scoria and forget you." Fond Mother: "Well, my pet, did the great dramatic manager say you would quickly become a star, if you would ',adopt the stage as a profession ?" Ambitious daughter: "Well, not exactly; but I think he intends to engage me for a new domestic drama of some kind. He told me to go home and lean to cook." What seems to grow fairer to me as:life goes by is the love and grace and tenderness of it; not its wit and cleverness and grandeur of knowledge, grand as know- ledge is—but just the laughter of little children, and the friendship of friends, and the cosy talk of the fireside, and the sight of flowers, and the sound of music.

Fork fifty years military men clung to the belief that nothing but an ounce ball would do for an army musket. It is only within five years that they have come to:see that if the ball does not hit it is wasted. If it does:hit it kills no sooner that a bullet from a rekvolver. All the new arms, now call for bullets no larger than ahunter uses.

A swell at the seaside was (surprised when leaning against the railings on the parade to notice that Enearly everybody who passed him :burst out laughing. On looking down at his feet some time after he perceived to his horror that he was standing just over a notice board which read in large print, Stand; for one donkey." . . .

A carpenter bought a guinea-pig for:his little boy, and admonished him in the words of the old joke, Dont you hold that pig up by the tail, or its eyes will drop put." The awe-strickenlboy retired, in possession of his hog. Be had ,not amused ihimself long with the pet beflore he shouted out, "Papa, papa! somebody's been holding this!pig up by the eyes; its tail has dropped out." The first vessel of schooner rig is said to have been built in Gloucester about the year 1713. When she went off the stocks into the water' a bystander cried out, "Oh, how she schoons !" The builder instantly replied, "A schooner let her be;" and from that day vessels thus rigged have gone by that name. The word scoon is popularly used in some parts of New England to denote the act of making stones skip along the surface of the water. The Scottish soon means the same thing. The word appears to have been originally written scooner. The other day a careless mason dropped a brick from . .

the second sto-rey of a building on -Which he was at work. Leaning over the wall and lookingdown he saw A resptCti.hi Cltlzcn 7/it') hlB §0 int jaramed over his eyes. The mason, in tones of apprehension, asked, "Did the brick hit anyone down there?" The citizen, with great difficulty extricating himself from the extinguisher into which his hat had ;been transformed, replied, with 'considerable wrath, "Yes, sir, it did; it hit me." That's right," exclaimed the mason, in tones of undis- guised admiration. 6` Noble man ! I would rather have wasted a thousand bricks than have you tell me a lie about it." IT WAS TUE FERLING.—A coloured man, who was evidently in poor circumstances, called at a Gratoit- avenue hardware store the other day, and asked for a door lock, and while he was looking at a line of them the merchant said, "You can't be afraid of burglars?" "But I ar7' was the reply. "Have you got anything to be Stolen " "No, sah. Halt* got $2O worth of stuff in de house." "Then why do you fear burglars?" "It halal 'cause I 'sped t dey would steal anything, but be- cause I doan' want to be woke up in the night and see a burglar at de foot of de bed, an' hear him say, 'Now, Reuben, you hand over dat bag of gold or put six bullets into ye?'" But you have no gold." "That's list it. He'd think I was lyin' an' shute me." CADBURY'S COCOA IS absolutely pure.—. Advt. A FiNexcnsao Foun.—Little Tommy Mulheron is a bright boy of four years, full of cunning tricks and winning ways, and the pet ot the neighbourhood in which he lives. Mast-r Tommy has developed an early fond- ness for pence and shillings, and, although he seldom asks directly for them, wherever he goes the air is full of hints. There is an old lady living near Tom's home who is very fond of him, but who is extremely careful of her small change, so that none of it ever finds its way into the little financier's pockets. Tom had nearly ex- hausted ingenuity in hinting, and at last, by a fortunate hit, succeeded. He went over there the other morning in a penniless condition and leaned affectionately against the knee of his old friend, who at once possessed herself of one of his chubby hands and began to fondle it " I would give a thousand dollars to have sucha nice little , boy as you for my own," she said, petting him. "How I much is a thousand dollars?" asked Tom with wide open eyes. "It's a great deal of money," said the old lady with a sigh. "Am I worth as much as that if papa would sell me?" inquired the young spectiator. "Yes, dear, and a great deal more," said his friend. "Then," said Tom, with a cherubic smile, "don't you think it is worth a penny just to hold my hand?' WOMAN, why work so hard? " SUNLIGHT SOAP " does that. Try h.—Advt.

div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."
On Wednesday, Lord Tennyson, Poet Laureate, entered upon his eighty-second year; and on the same day Sir Henry Thompson completed his three score years and ten. "Many happy returns of the clay."

When are we out of harm's way? Authentic news is to hand of a young woman in Floridahaving just died in untold agony from the results of a bite of an insect which was concealed in a bunch of flowers she wore at her neck.

The subject, in its revised form, of the essay for which the Cobden Club is offering a;prize of twenty- five pounds for competition is 'The past, present, and future ot technical education, in connection with Agriculture in the United Kingdom."

The "Freeman's Journal" has recently stated that "Times" counsel before the Parnell Commission have at length been paid their fees. This maybe correct as regards the Irish counsel, but the At- tornev-General and Sir Henry James are still await- ing a settlement.

The Marchioness of Lorne has just given another proof of her talent as a sculptor, having, says "Woman," within the last few days completed her statue of the Queen at Kensington Palace. The site is close to the Round Pond, and faces the room in which Her Majesty was born.

Dr. Hannay. the esteemed secretary of the Con- gregational Union, has just returned from a two months' holiday in Switzerland, and he looks all the better for his sojourn by the Lake of Thun. The doctor has not, however, quite recovered his health, and goes this week to Scotland for a month.

The Prince of Wales has accepted the invitation of the Earl of Lonsdale to pay a visit to Lowther Castle, Ponrith, a few weeks hence,for the shooting. Extensive alterations have been made at Lowther Castle during the past winter and spring, and the interior of the castle has also been elaborately deco- rated. Lord Lonsdale is enlarging Lowther Park by the inclusion of several thousands of acres of what has hitherto been farm land.

The disablement of three out of the six heavy guns on board the Inflexible and Hero during the manceuvres off the coast of Cornwall has caused a painful sensation in naval circles, and the attention of Parliament is to be called to the matter. After all the talk there has lately been of the increased efficiency of the Fleet, this disaster, coupled with the breakdown of the turret ship Gorgon, has come as a disagreeable disbandonment.

It is believed that the greatest achievement in the way of telephonic communication is that of the telephone between New York and Chicago. By this medium audible converse is held between two per- sons standing just one thousand miles apart. Poor Europe has not yet come up to much more than one-half this distance. The telephone between Paris and Marseilles covers 562 i miles, which is a long way short of the New York and Chicago; but the Paris and Marseilles stands for all that only second in the list of the long-distance telephones.

Though the House of Lords, on Tuesday night, added a Compensation Clause to the Removal of Gates Bill, this will not, as was at one time repor- ted, lead to the Bill being dropped by the London County Council. It is perceived that the addition of the clause is not likely to have serious practical result, it being necessary that damage should be proved in an ordinary court before compensation is payable. It was demonstrated before the Lord's Committee that no real claim for compensation

A man at Eastbourne has improved upon the brain operation with a corkscrew, so often recom- mended since Sidney Smith's calumnious joke at the expense of Scotchmen. Whether to force humour in or to let it out, the Eastborne experi- mentalist drove four nails into his head. In defence of himself at the police court he assured the magis- trate that he felt better for the operation. The medical evidence, we are assured, was to the effect that the nails had penetrated three inches, had, of course, pierced the brain, and had been withdrawn with difficulty. Yet the man is declared to be fully recovered.

The Queen has always passed the morning at Osborne, in fine weather, in a tent on the lawn, wherein (as at Frogmore) she rpad the papers. wrote her letters, and transacted all her public and private business. This summer, however, her Majesty has frequently installed herself in the pavilion which attracted so much attention at the Windsor Royal Agricultural Show, and which now occupies a charming site in the Osborne grounds, and it is a most notable addition to the place and a great convenience to the Queen. The knoll on which it has been erected commands beautiful views over the Solent and Spithead.

Some division of opinion appears to exist among Scotch Roman Catholics as to the advantage to their Church of free education. At the Catholic Con- ference in Glasgow, for example, Monsignor Munro spoke in a most pessimistic way of the danger to the Catholic schools from the extension of free education in Scotland, which he regarded as a certainty. On the other hand the Catholic Arch- bishop of Glasgow, who presided at the Conference, expressed himself as very well satisfied with the result of the advance already made towards free education in Scotland. Ife had been enabled to in- crease his staff of teachers and to pay them a larger amount of money. On the whole his school was carried on to much better advantage.

A glovemaker in Vienna, who, to judge from a Correspondent's account of him, is a veritable Simon Glover in enthusiasm for his industry and mastery of his craft, has produced a pretty little book on the glove. The theme is treated in a lively manner. The ingenuity of modern advertising anecdote is exemplified in the following sample story :—A baron and a countess, who have been betrothed for some time, are about to start for the races, when the countess says, with a deep sigh, "Ah, I am afraid you don't love me as you used to, Muki !" The baron answers by an indignant "What makes you think so, Katinka ?" The lady bends her head low, and answers, "You used to take ages in buttoning my long gloves, and now you do them in a twinkling."

The strong men are going to have another inn- ings. Sandow, having howled out Samson, has cast MS eyes round the world for new giantsto conquer, and he has found one in Germany. It is perhaps a figure of speech to describe the new German as a giant. He is a modest soul, and is content to stand only two inches above six feet. But he prides him- self as being a man of weight and substance. He turns the scale at twenty-seven stone. He is not fat as much as thick and stout all round. His thumb, for instance, if placed on half-a-crown, com- pletely covers it. Sandow has taken the measure and the weight of the gentleman, and proposes to lift him up by one hand in public, as an addition to his exhibitions of feats of strength. This is dis- tinctly good. It is much more interesting to watch a strcng man tossing giants about than playing with iron weights.

"With reference to your statement that the new Westphalian strong man, • Goliath,' once laid a cow upon its back by the horns, it may interest your readers," writes a correspondent of the "Pall Mall Gazette," "to know that Lord Arthur Cecil, a half- brother of Lord Salisbury, once told me a similar incident in connection :with himself. Lord Arthur, though a short an is of .giant physique and enormous strength. He was one day walking through a field on his farm at Innerleithen, when a young bull rushed at him. Instead of turning tail, Lord Arthur coolly seized the animal by the horns, and pushed him back, wriggling and struggling, inch by inch, till he got him into his stall, where he left him cowering and trembling all over."

"Vanity Fair" is responsible for the following instructive anecdote about the Pelicans :—At the recent glove fight at the Pelican Club, which has since formed the subject of interpellation in the House of Commons, a number of strangers were ad- mitted to the club-house; and at an early hour in the morning, when the" fight" had been over for hours, half the lumberer', sharps, and pugilists in London were assembled round the bar, much to the disgust ot the members. The proprietor was at his wit's end to know how to get rid of them, as he would have been a rash man who would have dared to offer to" chuck " them; but the boxing manager solved the difficulty neatly. He had the lights lowered, and went about crying, " Time ! gentle- men, please—all outside, please ' ; and so used are these people to :the pot-house warning that they quite forgot that they were in a club."

Mr. John Burns is about to return to his dail labour. When he was elected to a seat on the Lon don County Council provision was made by his con- stituents and others, amounting to .E. 2 a week. payable during such period as he should devote his time to the public service. These contributions have now fallen away, and Mr. Burns is cheerfully going back to the engineer's shop in which through many years he earned a weekly wage.

Another imeute in .her Majesty's service ! This time the Artillery. We shall, doubtless, hear in time what it is that has led the men of the 52nd Batteiy of the Royal Horse Artillery to express their dissatisfaction by destroying all the regi- mental property they could lay their hands, or sabres, upon. Meanwhile it is instructive to note that it is another " crack" regiment that has gone wrong, and that the officers are once more pointed to as the source of the mischief.

How is this for high, or rather for long? If all the tobacco smoked in the British empire last year were rolled into a rope an inch in diameter, it would form a snake like roll, which, following the line of the equator, would go thirty times round the earth. The same quantity of tobacco squeezed up and moulded into bricks would serve to build a pyramid equal in size to the tlaird largest in Egypt. Or, taking it another way, if the said tobacco was powdered into snuff, it would supply a sufficient quantity to bury a good-sized town as completely as Herculaneum and Pompeii were buried!

Lord Salisbury was in great spirits at the Man- sion House, on Wednesday night. He ate and drank freely, laughed and chatted gaily with Sir Robert Fowler, who sat opposite him, and seemed to be making the fun of the evening, and altogether pre- sented a marked contrast to the heavy, sombre, melancholy figure with which one is accustomed to identify the Premier. The manner of his speech, too, was good—the humorous parts lightly and felicitously touched, the graver portions weighty and forcible. Only it was not in the least'convinc- ing—it was a mere clever after-dinner speech, that was all.

An order has gone forth from the headquarters of the Salvation Army against smoking. This counter- blast is issued by Mr. Bramwell Booth, on behalf of the " General." It calls on the " soldiers " to con- sider the evils that follow the use of tobacco in every form. They should remember that it is in- jurious to health, uncleanly, a waste of money, a disagreeable infliction upon those about them, and an unnatural habit of self-indulgence for which :there is no justification. This is not all. It he who drinks cannot enlist in the Army of Salvation, so he who smokes most expect no promotion. According to this stringent rescript, he cannot, so long as he smokes, be or remain a sergeant, bandsman, ser- geant-major, secretary, or treasurer; in short, he can hold no office in a corps.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 9, 1890
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 9, 1890
THE BRAVE AUSTRIAN HUSSAR.

The following incident occurred during a general review of the Austrian cavalry. Nearly 30,000 cavalry were in line. A little child, a girl of not more than four years, standing in the front row of spectators, either from fright or some other cause rushed out into the open field, just as a a squadron of hussars came sweeping round from the main body. They made the detour for the purpose of saluting the Empress, whose carriage was drawn up in that part of the parade ground. Down came the flying squadron, charging at a mad gallop— down directly on the child, The mother was paralysed, as were others, for there could be no rescue from the line of spectators. The Empress uttered a cry of horror, for the child's destruction seemed inevitable—and such horrible destruction— the trampling to death by a thousand iron hoofs. Directly under the feet of the horses was the little one—another instant must seal its doom—when a stalwart hussar, who was in the front line, with- out slackenirg speed or loosening hold, threw him- self over by the side of his horse's neck, seized and lifted the child, and placed it safely upon his saddle-brow ; and this he did without changing his place or breaking the correct alignment of the squadron. Ten thousand voices hailed with raptu- rous applause the gallant deed, and others ap- plauded when they knew. Two women were there who could only sob forth their gratitude in broken accents—the mother of the child and the Empress. And a proud and happy moment must it have been for the hussar when his Emperor, taking from his own breast the richly-enamelled cross of the Order of Maria Theresa, hung it upon the breast of his brave and gallant trooper.

div.head: SHIP CANAL MANSLAUGHTER CASE. VAUGHAN LIBERATED.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL MANSLAUGHTER CASE. VAUGHAN LIBERATED.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, Edward William Vaughan (22), engine driver, surrendered to his bail, and was indicted for the manslaughter of Thomas Ellaman, on the 27th April, at Rixton, near Warrington. Mr. &tee and Mr. Steel con- ducted the prosecution, and the prisoner was de- fended by Mr, Cottingham. In stating the case for the prosecution. Mr. Shee said that both these men were employed at the Manchester Ship Canal Works, and they were engaged near to each other pumping water out of the excavations. At this time prisoner had possessed a revolver for about a fortnight, and on the day before this affrayEllaman also purchased a revolver. The prosecution were not in a position to prove that 'there was any ill- feeling or quarrelling between the men on the day of Eilaman's death. During the morningprisoner had frequently visited a Wage-house in the neighbourhood, and later on he was affected by drink. He had his re- volver with him that day,. and was noticed' to be en- gaged in firing at rats in the river. The last time Ella- , man was seen alive was a little time before noon, when he was talking to prisoner. Shortly afterwards somel people heard a shot fired, and undoubtedly that shot killed Ellaman. His body was found later on, and there was no doubt that death was due to a bullet wound, and it was alleged' that that bullet came from therevolver which belonged' to the prisoner. Tie afterwarde=made a statement, in which he admitted that it was his revolver that caused thedeath of the man, adding that it,' was all an accident. Soon after the body had been removed to tht lodgings of the deceased,. pri- soner disappeared, leaving all his clothing- and some ZII behind him. The- prosecution suggested that his conduct was suspicious,and not that of r..t man who had an innocent conscience, tut rather of a man who felt his guilt. On the 23rd' of May he gave him- self up to the police, and from further inquiries it was found that he had thrown the revolver away. At first he was charged' with wilful murder,.and in reply to that charge he said " No, it was not will ; it was an accident. Ellaman shot himself. He asked him (prisoner) to bring up the revolver, and whilst Zia- man was examining it the charge went off. Ellaman called out lam shot,'. and then fell and died on his (prisoner's) shoulder:" Prisoner- added that he vras frightened, and so he walked away.—His Lordship said he had listened with a+great deal' or attention ta Shee's opening, and itseemed that' a difficulty wmild arise. He rather agreed with the person who made the original charge against-this prisoner. ft was a case- of murder or nothing. Mt: Shea had Instt said that therewas nothing in the relations of these men by which it could be suggested that them was malicious feeling, or any motive why this man should have wilfully done any- , thing of this sort. If it was not murder the alternative was that it was an accident, for he had carefully read the depositions and had.oome to the conclusion that they could not find a man guilty of manslaughter on the evi- dence that was to be given that day.—Mr. Shee said that was how the case struck him when he first read the- de- positions. After such an expression from his lortilhip there was only one course open fbr him to adopt, and that was to offer no evidence. Mr. Steel agreed with him.—His Lordship said he thought that was proper.— Mr. Cottingham : The case was investigated before- the coroner and an "open verdict" was returned..—The Judge : I know. When I read the depositions I came to the conclusion that it was murder or nothing.—Mr. Cot- tingham : It is quite possible that Enaman caused' his own death by his awkward handling of the revoNer.— At the direction of hie lordship, the Jury found a 'verdict of "Not guilty," and prisoner was discharged. div.head: , THE UNLUCKY PRESENT.
div.p: , THE UNLUCKY PRESENT.

A Lanarkshire minister (who died within the pre- sent century) was one of those unhappy persons, who, to use the words of a well-known Scottish adage, "can never see green cheese but their een reels." He wa.§ extremely covetous, and that not only of nice articles of rood, but of many other things which do not generally excite the cupidity of the human heart. The following story is in corroboration of this assertion :—Being on a visit one day at the house of one of his parishioners, a poor lonely widow, living in a moorland part of the parish, be became fascinated by the charms 01a little cast-iron pot, which happenacl Ektha dine- to be lying on Ulu hearth, full 91 potatoes for the poor _. wounn'S ainiier, and that of her children. He had hever in his life seen such a nice little pot—it was a perfeot conceit of a thing—ft Was a gein—no pot on earth could match it in symmetry—it was an object altogether perfectly lovely. "Dear sake I minister," said the widow, quite overpowered by the reverend man's commendations of her pot, "if ye like the pot sae weel as a' that, I beg ye'il let me send it to the manse. It's a kind o' orra (superfluous) pot wi' us; for we've a bigger ane, that we use for ordinal, ' and that's rnair convenient every way for us. Sae ye'll just tak a present o't. I'll send it ower the morn wi' Jamie, when he gangs to the schule."

"Oh 1" said the Minister, "loan by no means per- mit you to be at so much trouble. Since you are so good as to, give me the pot, I'll just carry it home with me in my band. I'm so much taken with it, indeed, that I would really prefer carrying it myself." After much altercation between the minister and the widow on this delicate point of politeness, it was agreed that he should carry home the pot himself. Off then he trudged, bearing this chrieus little culinary article, alternately in his hand and under his arm, as seemed most convenient to him. Un- fortunately the day was warm, the way long, and the , minister fat, so that he became heartily tired of , his burthen before he got half-way home. Under these distressing circumstances, it struck him, that, if, instead of carrying the pot awkwardly at one side of his person, he were to carry it on his head, the burden would be greatly lightened; the prin- ciples of natural philosophy, which he had learned at college, informing him, that when a load presses directly and immediately upon any object, it is far less onerous than when it hangs at the remote end of a lever. Accordingly, doffing his hat, which he resolved to carry home in his hand, and having ap- plied his handkerchief to his brow, be clapped the pot, in inverted fashion on his head, where, as the reader may suppose, it figured much like Mambrino's helmet upon the crazed capital of Don Quixote, only a great deal more magnificent in shape and dimensions. There was at first much relief and much comfort in this new mode of carrying the pot; but mark the result. The unfor- tunate minister having taken a by-path, to escape ob- servation, found himself, when still a good way from home, under the necessity of leaping over a ditch which intercepted him in passing from one field to another. He jumped; but surely no jump was ever taken so completely in, or at least into, the dark as this. The concussion given to his person in descend- ing caused the helmet to become a hood; the pot slipped down over his face, and resting with the rim upon his neck, stuck fast there, enclosing his whole head as completely as ever that of a new-born child was enclosed by the filmy bag with which nature, as an indication of future good fortune, sometimes in- vests the noddles of her favourite offspring. What was worst of all, the nose, which had permitted the pot to slip down over it, withstood every desperate attempt, on the part of its proprietor, to make it slip back again; the contracted part, or neck, of the patera, being of such a peculiar formation as to cling fast to the base of the nose, although it had found no difficulty in gliding aleng its hypothenuse. Was ever minister in a worse plight? Was there ever contretemps so unlucky? Did ever any man—did ever any minister, so effectually hood- wink himself, or so thoroughly shut his eyes to the plain light of nature? What was to be done? The place was lonely; the way difficult and dangerous; human relief was re- mote, almost beyond reach. It was impossible even to cry for help • or if a cry could be uttered,, It might reach in deafening reverberation, the ear of the utterer, but it would not travel twelve inches farther in any direction. To add to the distress of the case, the unhappy sufferer soon found great difficulty in breathing. What with the heat occa- sioned by the beating of the sun on the metal, and what with the frequent return of the same heated air to his lungs, he was in the utmost danger of suffocation. Every thing considered, it seenstil likely that, if he did not chance to be relieved Ty some accidental wayfarer, there would soon be death in the pot. The instinctive love of life, however, is omni-pre" valent; and even very stupid people have been found, when put to the push by strong and imminent peril, to exhibit a degree of presence of mind, and exert a degree of energy, far above what might have been expected from them, or what they were ever known to exhibit, or exert, under ordinary circumstances. So it was with the pot-ensconced minister. Pressed by the urgency of his distresses, he fortunately recol- lected that there was a smith's shop at the distance of about a mile across the fields, where, if he could reach it before the period of suffocation, he might possibly find relief. Deprived of his eyesight, he acted only as a man of feeling, and went on as cautiously as he could, with his hat in his hand. Half crawling, half sliding over ridge and furrow, ditch and hedge, somewhat like Satan floundering over chaos, the unhappy ministei travelled with all possible speed, as nearly as he could guess, in the direction of the place of refuge. I leave it to the. reader to conceive the surprise, the mirth, the in- ritite amusement of the smith, and all the hangers- on of the smidtily, when, at length, torn and worn,. faint and exhausted, blind and breathless, the un- fortunate man arrived at the place, and let them knovt (rather by signs than by words) the circum- stances of his can. In the words of an old Scottish, song,

ekit cam the gideman, amt high he shouted, Out, cam the gudewife and low she touted, Ande,' the town neighbouls were gathered about it, And them was he,. E trow." The merriment of the company, however, soon gave way to considerations of humanity. Ludicrous as Was the minister, with such an object where his , head should have been, and with the feet of the pot pointing upwards, like the horns of the Great Enemy, it was, nevertheless, necessary that he, should be speedily restored to his ordinary con- dition, if: it were .5:1 no other reason than that he. might ccntinue to. live. Bp was, accordingly, at his own request, kid, into the smithy, multitudes, flocking around to tender him their kindest offices, or to witness the process of release; and having laid down his heal upon the anvil, the smith lost • no time M seizing; and poising his goodly fore-. hammer. "Will E oome aair on, minister?" ea- - claimed theconsidemte mass of iron, in at the brink, of the pot... "As air as ye like,' was the minister's answer; "better a. ohap, it the chafts than die for, want of breath:" lEms permitted, the man let, fall , a blow, which fortunately broke the pot in pieces, , without hurting the, head. which it enclosed, as the.) cookmaid breaks tide- sbel2 of the lobeter, withcrat, bruising the delicate food within. AJew minute& of the clear, air, and, a glass from the gudewifa's bottle, restored the unSrtunate man of prayer;: but, assuredly, the incident is one which will hang, live in the ot the parishioners of

BY HENRY FRITH.
Author of "The Mystery of Moor Farm," "o,i the Wings of the Wind," " Through Flood, Through Eli e," 4-c., Sze.
CHAPTER XI, I MIGHTY, AfAoNiFidtNT, THREE-TIT/AD BAsHAW. "Dean me, how very extraordinary!" exclaimed Sir Walter Watson. as he sat at breakfast—" dear me! Nothing could have fallen out better. It
seems almost as if Providence had arranged matters for us."
"Don't talk nonsense, Walter," replied his lady and very lady-like wife; "you ought to know better. As if Providence would think of interfering in—"
"My dear, hush! Remember the servants, and just after prayers, too! Really I must—l really must insist-"
"What is the matter F" inquired Lady Watson, interrupting her spouse. "What made you ex- claim just now ? Anything in the Railroad Market ? "

" No, no; certainly not. Dear urn! You re- member our arrangement—jokingly put, of course— respecting Captain—l mean Colonel Deane P " "Oh, yes; about the children. I was quite serious, I assure you. The Deanes are an old family, and you are not of a very ancient one--"
"Look here, Maria, I must say that you are speaking in a very unbecoming manner. My father—"
"Yes, yes; we know all about the late contractor. Sir Edward was a good and a very worthy man, but *carcely—well —not quite the equal of Colonel Deane.

When my dear motler first net him she thought him very provincial indeed. Now what has made you so cross ?" " Cross ! You are enough t 5 vex a saint, Maria. No wonder l'm cross. But listen; here's an announce-

ment in the paper: Mrs. Deane, wife of Colonel Deane, V.C., and all the rest of it, a son and heir! Don't you see, Lily and he are just of an age." "She is two days older," remarked Lady Watson, glincing at the paper her husband handed to her. "To be sure that is no great matter. But it is uso- less speculating on such children." "However, the airangement would be a very good one for both sides. Deane has always been very civil to me, and I must say I think I am not behindhand in courtesy. Yes; it will do—very nicely indeed." "I wonder when Mrs. Deane is corning back?
There have been rumours of shipwreck and acci- dent, but she must have returned, else this an-
nouncement could not have been 'inserted in tho

Times. Shall we call ? " asked Lady Watson. " Yes ; it would be as well to inquire at any rate. Let us arrange to do so to-morrow if you are dis- engaged," replied her submissive husband. And then the meal proceeded without any further special conversation, Sir Walter being buried in the news- . .

paper and Lady Watson sitting gazing from the window waiting until her housekeeper came th say that certain domestic concerns needed her authority. We must not imagine from the glimpse of t:,ir Walter Watson that he was always, as quiet and submissive as he appeared at home. There were few people who did not find out the rough sidt of his tongue. He was a really great man in the neighbourhood of The village inhabited by the workpeople at the "shops "—as the engine factory was called—belonged to him. He hind instituted a church and forbade anyone to go to chapel in pain of his high displeasure, but many went all the same. He had a post-oflice;.a school, a publichouse—only one—a reading mom,- and a recreation room, with all modern amusements laid on for the leisure hours of the tenantry who voted . . .

for him in the election to a man—or nOarly so—for Sir Walter never bribed anyone, nor would. he per- mit any apparent interference with a voter, But it was generally understood that Sir Walter ought. to be supported as a Liberal member, and he was, until he was offended at some Parliamentary. inter- ference, and then he changed his politics and- gained a baronetcy. This gave rise to some little discussion, and when the next general election came, Sir Walter pat up as Conservative, and was duly returned. A petition was lodged, but not a tittle of evidence was forthcoming respecting any act of intimidation- or bribery, and the commissioner returned a "clean bill of health" to the new member. Thus Sir Walter retained his seat and his influence like a modern -Vicar of Bray. From these few particulars it may be gathered that this railway magnate ,was really and truly a, greet man—that is a great man locally, and in a' business sense not physically. Personally, the baronet was short and inclined to stoutness He had a firm-set countenance and a clear head. He was generally well-dressed as became a magnate, and rather prided himself upon his short stature; for he remembered that all " great " men in history. were physically small. But to see him at his greatest you should attend a meeting at which he was chairman. Than he came out in his truest and most dazzling colours: He literally "sat upon" the Board. Not a direetora, not a shareholder, dared to ask any question as, to accounts. or procedure. Sir Walter was quite equal, to any' emergency, and resented inquiry as a, , personal insult. The unfortunate man who ventured within reach of the lion's paw was severely handled., anclesarcastic remarks with angry repartee or retort ' was usually the lot of the enterprising bondholder or shareholder in any concern in which the "many'. headed" chairman held a prominent position. Yet with all this he was a kindly man, veryfand of his son and heir, Edward, who had been destinedfor the Church from infancy, but whose talents layemore, in the engineering line. He was still quite a, lad,. and had Colonel Deane s child been a girl,. Sir Walter would have brought about the match egnally,. for he was fond of the aristocracy, particularlysinece he had b come a Conservative, and had serious; thoughts of signing himself "Watson," like a, peer.. The "'Towers," where he lived, was elegem* fur— nished and appointed. Why it had been called the. 'Towers" nobody—not even the oldest inhabitant. —could tell. Not a turret was visible, and nothing approachingto the outward semblance of a, tower rose within a mile of the house, and that was only a beacon Or landmark for ships. But Sir Walter liked the Towers, and nobody, not even his wife,. bad ameceeded in changing his nomenclature. Sir Walter was now happy. The estatess of alb Deanes and his own. (by purchase) woul.llbe united in,the family. He mild run a line througis the estate and double the value. His son should be a millionaire and ruffle it with the best. Ho should go to, Harrow, or Eton and Oxford, andt enter the Ghurehy He should have the living ina the neigh- bourhood,. for Sir Walter had influence, and the cosy corner waa in the gift of the loi el of 'the manor. Those plans were all made, and when, Sir Walter Watson took 'the trouble to make plans, nobody (except Lady Wataon) ever induced him, trennanake themy or to turn away from his objecta ,'Where is Wailer-?" inquired ha- of his wife. want him."

" Down at those horrid workshops, L suppose," replied her ladyship, whose father-hnd, been in the meat line, and, having accumulatodimuch cash, had get knighted fox-assisting the Queen front her car- riage when she opened a new Peo-gle7a Park, and who had then cut the shop and never come- again. So Lady Watson—once Maria Copping..—was extremely grand and aristocratic. Knew the peerage by heart, and felt extremely uncomfortable when she was , alone in society. At home she peeked at her. ; husband, and. worried him not, a little. "Those. horrid workpeople" were realy,.toogreat a trial kr her nerves. We have been particular in describing the Watsons, because in tho course of .this narrativetwe shall see a good deal of them.,' The Towers was I beautifully situated in a commanding eminencsond 1 the view, when not obscured lty the smoke from the terrible shops, was lovely and of considerable extent, the sea being a beautiful background" to a really charming picture in nature's best style. "I will go down to the works and sea whether the by is there. He ought to be better employed," said Sir Walter. "It is his holiday time, and I am sure the child is not doing any harm," replied Larty Watson, somewhat inconsistently, "though the association with workpeople and railroad stokers 4t the best for him, I allow." This gentle rap. at the patient husband, whose father had been a great railway foreman and con- tractor, and who had actually made his great fortune out of the very line of which his sea was chairman, diknot produce any reply- at the moment, unless some nearly inaudible murmurings concerning "butchers and beggars on horseback," concluding with a word which possibly had reference to some Ilelland capital stock, could be called sik reply. Then Sir Walter left the room, and banged the door behind him. He made his way on foot to the 4 great workshops by a private path. through the I domain which led him across the railway. He was about to cross it when a loud. whistling arreAted

him. He stopped in obedience to the signal, and as the enormous " expres " locomotive went past, without a train, he recognised, perched upon the foot- plate, his son and heir his hand on the whistle, de- lighted at the idea of 4 funking the governor" he said to his friend, _Robert Cooper, the driver of the eng The chairman shook his walking-stick at the lad, and the ogim-driver toucked his bat in acker- ledgment as the entre fia-t7ed on to tibe rexl siLic;n. Sir Walter then crossed the rails, and, skirting the canal, came to a under-path which led him to a gato in a high wall. Inside this wall were the shops, and he entered, scarcely heeding the admonition that stared him in the face as he passed in, " BEWARE 01' THE I}AIINTING IsliGIN131" With the knowledge of the locality, begotten of custom, the great man threaded his way through a labyrinth of superannuated waggons without wheels, and wheels without anything to support except themselves, and seemingly almost incalable of that, for they were locomotive paupers thrust into the rail- way poor-house and forgotten by their connections. Rusty iron was piled in another place—" scrap" it is called—and it will be sold some day at a good price. Beyond were linos of carriages waiting repairs, for there was a carriage "hospital" attached to the " poor-house," and here the " cars " were carefully repairechand overhauled. All kinds of trucks were visible farther on some laden with coal, othEr3 empty; and a whole line of tenders, without engines, i looking very rusty and forsaken; and engines with- out tenders, looking for all the world like birds which had had their tails pulled out. Across more sidings where old locomotives had come to a stop for ever; their race was run. No , more shall that swift-running " Lightning " flash along the rails with her Majesty's mails; no more shall that great-driving-wheel, six feet six inches in diameter, revolve at express speed to carry the news of a battle into the country with the papers. Its day is done; its sun has set. The rust upon the wheels, the open furnace-door, the pipes in front all choked with dust and bits of stone, and the open "manhole," where a venturesome bird had made her nest and reared her young, all told the secret of decay. "Unto ' scrap ' shalt thou return.' Passing these skeletons and the unconnected wheels—the chimneyless pensioners of the locomo- tive department—Sir Walter Watson made his way to the erecting shop, where some new engines are being built, and here he finds a perfectly new loco- motive, all brave in brass and paint, and clean as rubbing and oil can make: her. This is his pet vanity. We are all mortal; and Sir Walter had a weak place. This beautiful piece of machinery was nearly ready to come out. Her name had been put on that morning. She was called "Walter Watson," by way of a delicate compliment; te the chairman; and she was the one thousandth engine the company had rc ade. .
We will leave him to contemplate and examine his namesake, and turn to the railway for a few moments, and take up the threattof the narrative at the signal-box.

Wa must go back to tho evening when Lucy Ray- mond ran away, and bring the talirup to the later date. _ _

When the train had passed on, the mangled re- mains of poor Raymond were collected and carried to the hospital to await a formal inquiry, and Bill Bostley was the bearer of the new-s of Luey's elope- ment to George Collier as already related in the first chapter. He did not mention the death of Jack Raymond, believing thd Collier would be as good as his word, and strangle him. For such a sate Bostley the fireman had no taste.

But of course the terrible intelligence very soon came. to George's ears, and he was geartly troubled. Lucy had played him false. After all that had passed; after all the long summer days they had spent together; after a'l the pleasant winter evenings and homely pastimes Lucy had played him false! He would never forgive her—nor forget her Bill Bostley and George Collier had many a con- versation concerning Lucy RaymontLand her ulti- mate fate in India, for her last letter, written from Portsmouth,. had come to its destination, but never reached her father, for whom it was • intended. George had opened it, knowing he had the right to do so, and being likewise urged thereto by curious gossips, who were as anxious from the rum love of scandal as he was for love of Lucy Layton. One evening-George and his friend Bill were sitting chatting together in the room rented,by the. fernier in the village. A bond of sympathy new-united the young men. There appeared a tie between them since Lucy's elopement, and they could now speak of her without bitterness. Well, well," said George after a .pause in the conversation, during which both smoked audibly. "Perhaps it's all for the best; but I Idon't believe anybody ever loved Lucy as I did. "Wait a minute," said Collier; "I'm not quite ready. I must be in at ten, and rve only an hour. But we'll go across." In a few minutes the pair quitted the houses an& made for the inn which had for its sign the head of a girl, and was called the "Village Maid." The evening was rather dark, and the road, shel, tered by trees, was gloomy. As they proceeded, their conversation turned upon the never-failing' theme that had served them when no other topic would have drawn forth an answer—Lucy. They met a few people, and exchanged a "Good night " with some women and children, and not( and then a man alone, and not quite able to taker

care of himself. "A tidy lass" was Collier's comment upon a woman carrying a child whom they passed near the inn. "Rather late for her to be trampin' it just now. Couldn't take her in, I suppose, eh ? Good night," he cried to her. * She made no answer, but when the men had got on a little she halted, and after a moment's consi- deration, sat down in the gloom under the trees. People passed and re-passed, but no notice was taken of her, and there she remained for nearly an hour until Collier passed on his way to the signal - box, and then she rose and followed him, but she was evidently weary. "Not a penny," she muttered. "Not a penny to get a night's lodging or a bit to eat. He'll never refuse me a little. And yet he can be cruel, and he may be harsh. But I must try, or die!" She." hushed" the child kindly enough as sho transferred the burthen to her right arm, and P*ro- ceeded on, her way. Collier, unconscious that he was being followed. went on leisurely, and entered the signal-box in the cutting to relieve his mate, Dick. So good- night, and I'll relieve you early as you like. Good- night !" "Good-night" replied Collier, half sulkily. Beer Is ragin', is it ?"-; Well, then, I hadn't any worth epeakin' about. Only spirits. What's that?" He listened intently, but the sound, whatever it was, was not immediately repeated, and he was too busy to attend to- anything but his diaries for some minutes. At length, what appeared to him to be a tap at the door, zoused Lim, and he turned towards ' it. The door slovrly,:.opened and a ferule form came into the full blazt of the gas-light. The staple trades of Warring-

proposed to be included within the limits of the borough consented, the extension would be granted, tut not otherwise." That was the opinion expressed by the Association of Municipal Corporations. It was casually ',stated by the Chairman of the Committee that he Thought there would be no difficulty in including Arpley Meadows and other parts of the extension, as soon as they were built apon. It was believed that there would be little difficulty, in the course of a few years, in get- ting an extension of the borough on the southern side, by an application to the Local Government Board for a Provisional Order; and as regarded the present exten- sion, it might have been more advantageous to the Corporation to have proceeded by Provisional Order than by the Bill, if the purchase of the Water Works had not necessitated an application direct to Parliament. The ratable value of the borough would, by the extension, be increased by £7,500, which was more than half of the ratable value of that part of the township it was in- tended to include within the borough. When the Bill was before the Commons it was deemed advisable, in order to meet an objection made by one of the G ernment departments, to alter the clauses as to the div°v n of the borough into wards, so as to leave isle whole question to the Commissioner who shou the ap - pointed. During the transit of the Bill, horrever, from one House to the other, and although the Commons Committee had approved of the alterations, the Home Office interposed and threatened to stop it unless the number of Councillors and Aldermen, also the number of wards, were fixed by the Bill; and the promoters were required to state by a certain hour on the same day what those numbers should be. It was not considered desirable to increase the number of the Council, and, as the number of wards had necessarily to be either five or nine, in order to allow of an equal dis- tribution of the Aldermen among the Councillors (the law requiring the proportion of one Alderman for every three Councillors), the number of wards was increased to nine. When the Commissioner was sent down it would be open to the Council to represent to him in what manner the borough should be divided. The altera- tion of the wards would provide for a more equitable representation and reinovethe inequality which had so long existed. (Hear, hear.) Ttespecting the purchase of the Water Works, the Committee reported that it was proved to them that the purchase would be advantage- ous to the borough—(hear, hear)—and they passed the clauses, allowing a suspension of the sinking fund for five years, and, in addition, 55 years for the repayment 'of money borrowed under the Act. That arrangement would be found exceedingly advantageous to the borough—(hear„ bear)—and it was believed that the purchase would not create any charge upon the rates. On the contrary, it was reasonable to suppose that by careful and judicious management the undertaking would in a very short time be a source ot revenue to the borough. The Committee approved also of the agreed clauses between the Corporation and the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Limited, and the other company, by which, it wouldbe remembered, the com- panies would pay to the Corporation the sum of £3,000 by three annual instalments, in addition to a wayleave of 3d. per lineal yard, for the right of continuing their supply of water from the river. The Committee ap- proved, furtheraof clauses authorizing (1) the purchase of lands for the extension of the hospital; (2) the in- crease of the library rate fronfld. to lid. ; (3) the bor- rowing of money for the extension of the baths ; and (4) the repeal of section 37 of the,Act of 1877, which would enable the Corporation to redeem the gas annuities at market price. The Bill went before the Committee of the Lords on the-31st July as an unopposed Bill, and the only alterations made in it were those agreed to by the Corporation, which provided fez a differential rating in the added area for five years and to certain lands belong- ing to the Bon. Leopold Powys for an additional five years if they remained unbuilt &Ton during that period. The arrangement with the lion. Leopold Powys was a very mall matter as affecting the Corporation. and was agreed to in order to save the costs of an opposed Bill. In all other particulars the Bill was agreed to by the Committee, although the Local 'Government Board had strongly reported against the paoposed suspension of the sinking fund; bat the position of the Bill as to that matter was fully explained to the Examiner of Private Bills, and the diliinulty was fully overcome before going into Committee. Looking to the fact that the period suggested bytheLocal Government Board for the repay- ment of moneys borrowed under the Bill should not ex- ceed 3-years, and that no suspension should be allowed, he thought the Corporation had been particularly succes- ful in getting6o-years, during the first five of which, as he had ,explained.the sinking fund would be suspanded. (Hear, hear.) Altogether, he considered that the Bill as passed was a very satisfactory one, and he trusted it would be found tl,'N aluable Act, znd that the many mat- ters with which it dealt would prove of great advantage and utilityto the borough. (Applause.) Alderman Surma-. seconded the proposition.

----------- - - _ _ Councillor BotroN said that so far as he, as a member of the General 'Purposes Committee, was concerned, he was not satisfied with the manner in which the Bill had beem carried out. That was the first opportunity he had had of expressing an opiniab, for eep to the present he had been ,entirely in the dark in tile matter. In the minutes there was i. resolution which read "That the minutes of the Parliamentary Sub-Cestamittee of the 3rd, 9th, and 24th :July be approved." What were those pro- ceedings.? Who knew anything about them, and there was hardiva member of the General Purposes Committee who umderstoed them. Then with reference to the divi- sion of the town into wards, he thougbt that before two or three rnembers,,a la. Committee entirely changed the representation of the town without any- expression from, or any resolution of, tha main Committee—if they did that sort .*thing it was liable to get into a scandal. He failed to see what authority they had to intake an altera- tion without taking the Council into their oonfidence. It had not been straightfotward. With 'reference to the Ship Canal arrazgements, he wanted .to know what authority the Sub-Corrunittee had to deal...with the Ship Canal Company without ,going before the, General Pur- poses Committee'? He would admit that the Ship Canal Company were an actute let. They askedlor a bit, and they got it. They askeet fox more, and they.got it. Then they asked for everything,.and they got that. (Laugh- ter.) The only thing they-ad not eet—well,-he did not know what it was:: they get everything they,osked for. (Laughter.) If suffidient care and diplomacy kad been exercised, the Council would have obtained Whetter Bill than the one they bad. He roved that the resolution reading "That the number of Aldermen and‘Councillors remain as at present, and that the number of wards be increased from five to nine, ,E 0 as to provide lee. each ward being represented by three Councillors and one Alderman," be not confirmed. The MAYOR: This is actually:pa Act of Partiamerrt at this moment. Councillor I3or,reev : What I propose is that this resolu- tion respecting the increase of •tile, wards be not ap- proved. The Mayon: They have all beer confirmed by the General Purposes Committee.

Councillor Borrox : Have they? Not to my know- ledge. Councillor Slum GREEN: These minutes were read over and Councillor Bolton was present; he sat opposite to me on the occasion. Councillor BOLTON: If they were read over they were read over in such a manner that nobody heard them. (Laughter.) The MAYOR: I don't think the Chairmen of the Com- mittees are ever to be found trying to dupe the members. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Dr. Cstomiseconded the amendment. He said that be was perfectly agreeable to a re-arrangement of seats throughout the through, but he thought the members of the Council ought to know how thatre- arrangement would take place. COURCiBOT HENRY ROBERTS: So you will. Councillor CANICELL, continuing, said that that was necessary, so that each member of the Council might know how he stood. He thought the Council had been handled rather sharply with respect to the Bill. The MAYOR: YOU will have every opportunity to put your views before the Commissioner. Councillor Dr. CANNELL : I am like Councillor Bolton, rather doubtful. The MAYOR: The Town Clerk advises me that I cannot accept such a resolution. Councillor BOLTON But you must accept it. (Laugh- ter.) The MAYOR: I must be guided by the Town Clerk. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BOLTON: I refuse to accept these minutes. Councillor PIERPOINT remarked that Councillor Bolton had been wasting the time of the Council. (Hear, hear.) First of all, he was a member of the General Purposes Committee, and he ought to be somewhat loyal to that Committee. For a considerable time it had been well understood that the present arrangement of the voting power of the constituency was not as well equalised ag it might be consequently, when the Borough Bill was being applied for, it was considered a favourable oppor- tunity for bringing forward the other matter. (Hear, hear.) It was not the Council who were going to deter- mine the division of the wards. A Commissioner would be sent down by the Local Government Board, and he would be perfectly willing to hear the evidence of Coun- cillor Bolton, Dr. *Cannel!, or anybody else. (Hear, bear.) There was not a single resolution which the Parliamen- tary Committee had brought forward which had not been submitted to the General Purposes Committee and been adopted in proper course. Alderman BURGESS said that Councillor Bolton, in reality, approved of everything which was done by the Parliamentary Committee. If he disapproved of any- thing Councillor Bolton was not a man who would not make himself sufficiently offensive to the Committee in showing his disapproval. If Councillor Bolton wished to take a position in that Council Chamber he must do his duty outside' and he did not do that. CouncillorßoLrox (warmly) : In what manner? Alderman BURGESS: You have grossly neglected your duties, and then you go and make charges. Councillor BOLTON: I rise to a point of order and ask for that to be withdrawn.

The MAYOR: lam advised by the Town Clerk that the words of Alderman Burgess are fair in debate. There is nothing to be withdrawn. Councillor BOLTON: All I can say is that Alderman Burgess does his duty in such a manner that he dictates to the whole Council. . . .

Councillor HENRY ROBERTS said that as he understood it that amendment could not be received. It was ultra eires. Consequently, there was nothing upon which they had to vote. He moved that the resolution with regard to the payment of two guineas a day to members of the Council when away on Corporation business be not adopted. Any member of the Corporation who went away on Corporation business should do'so ma creditable 'manner and have his expenses paid—the expenses he was out of pocket—but that a specific sum should be allowed out of which any member could make a profit he entirely objected to. Matters should remain as they were, and members going away on the business of the town should be paid their actual out of pocket expenses, whether they were Ins. a day or £lO. Councillor JEERING seconded this amendment. Councillor FLEMING said he understord the two guineas a day were for distant journeys. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR said it was understood the two guineas per day were for long distances. He, however, agreed that the resolution should be withdrawn for further consider- ation. The minutes were then adopted, and the meeting ter- minated.

div.head: BOY DROWNED NEAR BARNSLEY.
div.p: A BOY DROWNED NEAR BARNSLEY.
EXCMNG SCENE.

At two o'clock on Thursday afternoon, a drowning accident, resulting in the death of one and the narrow escape of two other children, occurred at Stainborough, near Barnsley. Edward Brown Hannell, aged ten; Margaret Jane Flannel!, his sister; and Mary Eliza ?akin were all playing near the end of a culvert at Stainborough Mill datnwhen the boy pushed against the girls, and they all fell into the water. A woman named ratkin, residing near, rushed to the place and succeeded in sescuing the two girls, but the boy was drowned.

div.head: ATTEMPTED MURDER OF A SWEETHEART. A DEVOTED LOVER.
div.p: ATTEMPTED MURDER OF A SWEETHEART. A DEVOTED LOVER.

A•aharge of attempted murder and attempted suicide at 1d Bailey, on Tuesday had a singular termination. The ,prosecutrix, a young woman named Mary Ann Capper, made the acquaintance of the accused, William Stock, seven or eight years :ago, and some months ago, when she, her sister, brotheand father were compelled to go to the workhouse by destitution, the prisoner, who 11716 only earning £1 per week, and was allowing his motherlbs. of it, took them ,out of the union, and sup- ported thein wut of the remaining, 10s. On the 21st May the girl left to go to her married brother's, and the prisoner, ,Trket ing her two days after, begged her to return, stating he would put .up the banns next day. She refused, whereupon he cut .her throat and his own with a razor. The girl, in cross-esramination, said she would marry the prisoner if hewas released. The jury recommended the prisoner to mercy, and Justice Grantham said he would only sentence the prisoner to one week's imprisonment, the result loelng that he would be at once discharged. He had hardly.ever heard of such devotion as the prisoner had shown, and the alder- men and sheriffs, believing that the girl would herself recompense him for his devotion to her, would hand her the sum of £1.0., to assist in providing a home for them both.

div.head: ST. ALBA.N'S (R.C.) CHURCH, 'WARRING-
div.p: ST. ALBA.N'S (R.C.) CHURCH, 'WARRING-
TON.

St. Alban's (R.C.) Church, Bewsey-street. was re- opened on Sunday, after the erection of a handsome I second, or Lady, altar and the re-seating of the body of the building. Special services were held during the day, and were attended by large congregations. The musical portions of the services were under the , direction of Mr. J. B.CaldwelL it fact which will be sufficient to indicate the excellent character of the performances. The morning preacher was the Right Rev. Abbot Snow, M.A. (president of the Benedictine Order in England). In the course of his sermon, he re- marked that there was a blessedness in belonging to an old church such as that. At the same altar where the present congregation offered their prayers their fathers and fathers' fathers had done so. How many acts of charity and good work had been done within those walls? A confraternity had been established. One, as the Catholic Philanthropic Society, had been in active work since 1823. Hence they naturally took a pride in their church. They had established another church, as an offsbot, and whatever success was attained in the new church, the congregation in the old one took a pride is, even as a mother took a pride in her child. Before the division St. Alban's had only two priests and one set of schools. Now they had three priests and two sets of schools, and just as large a con- gregation. Having arrived at that position, it became necessary that they should turn their attention to the kceratim of On cllgrch, rd hç74 thlnictiii to (ion- to find that they had thrown themselves ao hartlly into the work. In the evening the Very Rev. Canon Woods,O.S.B. (Hereford), was the preacher. He selected as his text the words "Lord, I have loved the habitation of Thy house, and the place where Thine honour dwelleth," Psalms xxvi. 8. Referring to St. Alban's Church, he said it was not a splendid building. It had no grand archi- tectural features about it, and yet it was a dear place to the brethren who worshipped there. It had many dear recollections and associations. He therefore felt certain ' the congregation would be delighted to give what they could on an occasion like the present. Their priests had been obliged to incur considerable expense in reseating the church, and he was sure his hearers would be only too ready to help them to wipe off the debt.

div.head: EAELESTOWN -MURDER.-
div.p: THE EAELESTOWN -MURDER.-

The alleged terrible murder at Earlestown under circumstances detailed in our last issue has eon- tinued to excite a deep interest in the locality of Earlestown, where the deceased man, Thomas Kay, and the prisoner in custody, Thomas Mercer, who is charged with causing Kay's death, are both well- known. Since his arrest Mercer has been confined in the Earlestown police station, and it is stated that be has manifested a remakable indifference as to the seriousness of the charge against him. There has been an opinion expressed in many quarters that Mercer has not been altogether in his right senses for a considerable time past, and that, while under some mental derangement occasioned by a temporary fit of temper, he committed the terrible injuries to Kay's head from which the latter died aye days later.

div.head: INQUEST AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: INQUEST AT WARRINGTON.

On Saturday afternoon, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner for South-West Lancashire, held a court at the White Hart Hotel, Sankey-st., Warrington, to enquire into the death of Thomas Kay (44), a labourer, of no fixed abode, which was caused by fearful injuries inflicted upon him with an axe, by Thomas Mercer. another labourer, who is in custody on the capital charge. Superintendent Weir, of the Lancashire county 'police, and Inspector Spinks, of the Warrington borough force, watched the inquiry on behalf of the police. Mercer, who was pre- sent, looked 'very unconcerned. John Hatton, grocer and provision dealer, 27, Fair- clough-st., Earlestown, said he had known the deceased man Kay for eight years. He was a labourer or "knock- about." and had no fixed place of abode. On Wednesday, the 23rd of July, he went to witness's shop, and bor- rowed the axe produced. There were then no stains on it. Thomas Singleton, carter. High-st., Newton. deposed that on Saturday, the 26th ult., he was engaged carting bricks from the old Sankey paper mill at Earlestown. He arrived at the mill at about a quarter to eleven in the forenoon, and saw the deceased sitting astride a plank chipping mortar off some bricks. He also saw the pri-' soner there, sitting on some bricks near to the deceased. They appeared to be talking together. As witness was filling his cart he heard someone shout "Oh." That caused him to look, and he saw the prisoner standing be- hind the deceased with an axe in his hand. Prisoner struck the deceased very heavily on the bead with the axe. Witness went for assistance, and on returningwith some other people he saw the deceased running away in the direction of "Vitriol Mountain," which consists of a heap of refuse. Kay was lying across the plank in an unconscious state, bleeding from the head. Thomas Newton, 12 Vitriol-square, Earlestown, a labourer in the employ of Mr. Kellett, builder, said that on Saturday, the 26th ult., he was engaged in pulling down the old paper mill. Kay was working there. He was using the double•headed axe produced, which was the property of his master, and the second axe produced was lying on the ground at the feet of the prisoner. The men were talking together. Dr. Valentine, Earlestown, deposed to being called to the deceased after the occurrence. On examiningshis head witness found five gaping wounds of a contused and lacerated character. One, on the top of the head, was two or three inches in length. The wounds could not have been self-inflicted, but could have been caused by the axe produced. Witness ordered that the deceased, who was unconscious, should be removed to the War- rington Infirmary. The axe with which the blows were inflicted was handed round to the jurymen. The head was spotted with blood, and at the sharp edge were some hairs. Replying to jurors, the doctor said that the wounds could not all have been produced by a fall on the bricks. Two of them might have been so produced, but he thought the others must have been inflicted by three separate blows. Witness Singleton, recalled, said that the blow he wit- nessed was dealt with the sharp edge of the axe. John O'Neill, slater, 15 Duke-st., Earlestown, said that on hearing of the occurrence on the Saturday in question he went towards the works, and found prisoner lying in the grass near to the "Vitriol Mountain," about 150- yards from where the affair took place. Witness handed prisoner over to the police. By the jury: Frisoner seemed to be hiding in the grass. He thought prisoner had had some drink. • _

---S-e-riet-i..ong-worth, Newton, said that on Monday,. the 28th, prisoner was taken before Mr. Pearson at New- ton Town Hall, and charged with doing grievous bodily harm to Kay. After being remanded he remarked—" I only hit him on the head with the hatchet once, and then threw it at him." On the 31st ult. Constable Hughes charged prisoner with killing deceased, and he replied—" Did he die this afternoon." There NM no appearance of a struggle having taken place. , Emily Dobson, nurse at the Warrington Infirmary, said that the deceased was unconscious from the time of admission to the time of his death on the 31st ult. Dr. Bowden, resident surgeon at the Infirmary, de— ' tailed the result of a post-mortem examination of the deceased. There were five wounds on the head. One was behind the left ear, and was sin. long, the second, liin. long, was on the left parietal bone, and the third was on the right occipital bone, and was liin. long. The other two wounds led down to a compound fracture of the One, about 2in. long, was over the left temple bone and the other, which was 24in. lone over the left parietal bone. Death was attributable to these injuries. He thought that the wounds were all caused by separate acts of violence. Either of the two large wounds was sufficient to cause death.

Constable Hughes, Newton, said that on the 26th ult. he found the axe produced near where deceased had. been working. There was blood and hair on it, the blood being wet ; there was also blood on the bricks and at the side of the plank, where it fin med a pool. Witness also found the hat produced, and there were cuts in it. Witness afterwards charred prisoner, who had a spot of blood on his cheek when arrested, wilh unlawfully wounding Kay, and he replied "It was his own fault hit him. I was only going to ask Kellett for a job this morning, and he said A d— thing like you ask for a job, that's been knocking about so long.'" When charged with wilful murder prisoner replied "Did he die this afternoon ?" This was all the evidence taken, and the jury, after a short consultation, brought in a verdict of " Wilful murder." and prisoner was committed to take his trial at the nbxt Liverpool Assizes. During the progress of the inquiry, it was stated that William Moses, a foreman joiner, of Earlestown, had been warned to attend and give evidence, but he declined to leave Earlestown to come to Warrington because there was no one on the station platform to pay his fare, Constables Hughes proved that he warned Moses to attend as a witness, and that he said he would do so. The Coroner thereupon caused the name of the witness to be called three times, and, no answer being received, he intimated that he should impose a fine of forty hogs. On the conclusion of thC iDquest Mercer was removea in custody. POLICE COURT PROCEEDINGS.

On Tuesday morning, the prisoner Mercer was again- brought before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, at the Earlestown Police Station. Small crowds of persons congregated in the vicinity of the Police Station, in. the hope of catching a glimpse of Mercer, but they were subjected to a disap- pointment. The prisoner was not professionally repre- sented, and it was understood that another -remand would be applied for. Police-Sergeant Longworth, who conducted the proceedings, said: This prisoner, Thomas Mercer, who has already been before you, is now charged with the wilful murder of one Thomas Kay, by striking him on the head with a hatchet, on the 26th of last month. On Saturday last there was a Coroner's in- quiry, and the verdict of the jury was one of wilful murder against prisoner. This morning I propose to call' some evidence before you, and then ask you to remand the prisoner until Friday, when the case will most likely be completed. Thomas Singleton, carter, was then. called, and he repeated his evidence as to hearing a cry of "Oh," and to seeing the prisoner strike Kay on the head with a hatchet. —Mr. Gillespie asked the pri- soner if he had any questions to ask the witness.—The Prisoner Well, I can tell a different tale.—Mr. pie i Well, I think you had bytter keen that for your trial. We are not trying you now.—The Prisoner I had the axe in my bard, and Mr. Kellett had been grumbling that the bricks were not half chipped.—Mr. Giltost; You had better keep that until your trial.— The magistrate thought there was sufficient evidence to justify a remand, and the prisoner was accordingly re- manded until Friday.

Ticsamprovement.Bill fon:Warring- Waningt°B' ton has passed bath Houses ,of Par- Bill liament and allthat is nowreqpired !fir the Royal assent. The Mayor was, there- re useful:y occupied at thcL Council, meet- ing, on Tu.aeday,,. in explaining what was being obtained umier the bill. Theee-,was nothing new Ito report beyond the stateraentAhat the agree- l'iltent between the-Companies using the river water land the Cbrporation becomes:Rust of the measure. There wasasome doubt for a. time am to whether Parliament would sanction sueh am agreement; but now that. the matter is satisfactorily settled, the ratep!i.yers will be the geiners to the extent of tho -24€100,whieh are to bes paid in, three instal- ments This sum will goJar, towards inset- ing the,. costa incurred in prometbag the bill; and, with a five years' suspension of the Sink- ing Fund in connection with the purchase of the Water Works, it is lust possible that, after all the talk about ratea„ the bill will not add to themats,much as one penny in the pound. It is disappointing, to be sure, that there is to be no extonsion, on the south side of the borough; and we agree with Councillar Bouroorin thinking that tho,Ship Canal Company have got the better of the Corporation. He summed the matter up in a neat epigram when he said.:--" The Ship Canal Com- pany were an astute lot. They asked for a bit, and they got it. They asked far more, and they got it. Then they asked for everything, and they got- that." Unfortunat3ly CouncillorßoaroN, althougl? a member of the General Purposes Committee, is a, day after the fair with his protest as to the way in which some of tha business has been done. Howis it,.by-the-by,thair nothing was heard at the Comkeil of the agreements which was entered into withAlle ,Ship Canal Company for the inclusion of Arley, or of the reason,why the agreement was repudiated by the Compassy ? Was the agreement approved by the General Purposes. Committee, and, if se, why does it not appear on the minutes as. part of its proceedings ? R.should never ha forgot- ten that Committees and Sub-Committees act as representatives of the.yatepayers ; and tiaat the ratepayeruhave a rsglkt to know what their repro- rentatives have beam doing on their behaif. It may sometimes happen that a Sub-Oastunittee is compellsd'to take immediate action, as in the case of the decision to provide in the Rill for- nine wards instead of five as heretofore ; but there- can be no objection to such a course when a sufficient reason is given and when the matter is made public. As, a matter of fact, the Bill from the first contem- plated a redistribution of seats, and provided for the -division of the wards being made by a, Com- missioner from the Local Government Board ;but some of the members of the Council do not appear to have read the Bill which they have promoted, and therefore knew nothing about this particular improvement. When, the change is made, there will be tie adtlitioß t the number of Cm /0,41 m ;

the addition j to the number of wards. Eacli ward will return three Councillors, and as each Councillor is elected for three years, this means that every ward wiff return one Councillor only every November. In other words, the plan th the bill is a redistribution of seats on the basis of equal electoral districts. At present, South-West Wit, with 544 voters, returns as many nrunbers a.a North-West Ward, with 2,615 voters. This .1a obviously unequal and unfair, and it is an inequalitl which will be rectified when North-West Ward cut up into two, if not three, wards. Referring to other powers of the bill, the Mayor summarised them as authorizing (1) the purchase of lands for the extension of the hospital ; (2) the increaoe of the library rate from id. to 11d. ; (3) the borrow: ing of money for the extension of the baths; afl (4) the repeal of section 37 of the Act of IS7'' which would, enable the Corporation to redeem the 'gas annuities, at market price. Ther.4 are limper" tant provisions„ and there can be neo doubt that the bill—speaking of it as a whole—rill prove to )0 of great benefit to the borough.
