- - "TOUCH AND GO:"
Judgment has been given in the Bell-Cox appeal Case; but is there anybody the better for it—al- Ways excepting the lawyers?

Turkey ought to be taken to task as to the atro- cities and misgovernment of Armenia. The Porte is ' pledged under the Berlin treaty, and should be held to its pledges. There are two sides to. a bargain.

Parliament has done nothing this session-, and it has taken a long time to do it. According to Present arrangements the new Session of Parlia- pleat will open on Thursday, the 20th of Novem- ber, when the policy of "masterly inactivity" will be resumed. --- • Mecca, the birthplace of Mahommed, is just now ill a very bad way, ravaged as it is by; cholera. The latest report is that as many as 180 persons are dying daily. The shrine of the prophet may be in- teresting ; but the pilgrimages to it mean over- -crowding, and overcrowding means dirt, and dirt means disease. Salvation will be found, not in the ahrine, but in sanitation. •

• Excursionists during the recent holidays have made Lymm liiely. Not a few of them have put that enemy in the mouth which steals away the brains; and two of them—one on Saturday and another on MOnday— floundered into the canal. Overheated as they were with whisky, an extra,dose Of Water was perhaps about the best thing they could take.

Mr. Robert Pierpoint is hard on the Prime ltinister. Speaking at the Primrose demonstra- lion at Appleton,on Saturday,he intimated that the man to his taste was "one that can rule and dare • not lie." Now everybody, knows what "a Salis- bury" means; and as for ruling,was it not Bismarck who said Lord Salisbury was "a lath painted to look like iron ?"

Addressing the same meeting, the Hon. Alan • de Tatton Egerton,M.P., had a gooddeal to say as to the failure of the Government to pass the Irish , land Purchase Bill. He made it out that it was ()Wing to the opposition and obstruction of the lvicked people who call themselves Liberals; but he forgot to mention how such Tories as Mr. McCartney,- Mr. Siniih Baty, and Colonel Waring , crowded the notice paper with amendments. The fact is nobody really likes the bill except the Irish Secretary.

As bearing upon the question of obstruction, the following item from the "Daily News" is worthy of note :—" With reference to the observations of the First Lord of Treasury, on Tuesday night, upon the opposition on the Police Bill, it is instructive to note that at the commencement of Tuesday's Proceedings only twenty of the fifty-one amend- .rnents attached to the English Police Bill stoOd in the names of members of the Opposition, thirty-one being placed on the paper by supporters of the Government."

-- "Tommy Burn" is responsible for a good deal of folly in diving from Runcorn Bridge. He had to less than seven imitators on Monday last, who all leaped into the river and got out again more or leas free from injury. On Tuesday one man threw himself from the bridge and was picked up semi-conscious. The performance will continue, /Ve suppose, until some foolish fellow loses his life, and then there will be an interval.

It was expected that the London postmen dis- Missed for taking part in the strike would be re- instated after a time. But there are no signs of this as vet. On the contrary, those who happened to be Volunteers have been expelled from that ser- vice ; and it is stated they are being refused licenses as cabmen. If this be so, it is not merely Punishment; it is persecution. The public ought to stand l3y the men, and see that they have fair Play.

Despite certain sanguine expectations, the Long- ford Manure Works lost money last year, and, as things go, they are likely to lose more during the current year. It was not deemed prudent to give information on the subject at Tuesday's meeting of the Warrington Town Council ; but the present 'difficulty lies, we believe, in an accumulation of • ,stock with falling prices. The difficulty must be faced ;it is no use shirking it, or the loss may be increased.

Warrington has had £5OO left it for art purposes, and it seems to be thought that wonders may be done with it in the way of purchasing works of art. Photof.,rray hs of celebrated pictures are deemed to ,bo good .pnough for the National Gallery of zogiand ; but they are not good enough for the local gallery nf Warrington! Perhaps if Messrs. Pildes, Woods, and Brewtnall are appealed to, they supply us with original works—something nice for ninepence.

It must be very pleasant for frequenters of the Warrington plunge bath to learn that it is fed, in Part, by the overflow from the shower bath. There can be no wonder that the water of the plunge bath has looked at times like a decoction of water and—something else. "Something too much of this." There will be an end of this sort of "economy" when the Corporation become owners of the Water Works.

-- The Cheshire County Council is being invited to inquire into the pollution of the river Croco, and to take proceedings under the Rivers Pollu- tion Prevention Act. Whilst about it, the Council should investigate the condition of the Weaver. It used to be the delight of anglers; but within the last twelve months the river has been so vilely Polluted as to destroy the fish. There is a remedy for this against someone, and that remedy should be applied. One of the questions which will occupy the at- tention of the electors at the forthcoming election of Commissioners at Runcorn is the provision of a Pleasure ground. It was decided at the monthly Meeting, on Thursday, to appoint a Committee to consider the matter. The inhabitants will do well to support tha proposal. Children must have • aonaewhere to play, and, as a town grows, the difficulty is to find places for them. Breathing Spaces in large towns will come to be regarded as a necessity when, with fuller knowledge, the people realise their important bearing upon the health of the community.

Mr. Coningsby Disraeli is either bad to please, or he does not know what he is talking about. In the course of a speech at Manchester, on Satur- day, he said :—" If Home Rule was to be, as Mr. O'Brien would seem to declare it to be, carried on when obtained, unmitigated by the power of l'eligion and morality wielded by the Church, then the fate he destined Ireland to was infinitely Worse than that contained in the formula Home Rule means Rome Rule." Reasoning of this kind is, to use one of Coningsby's choice phrases, "ar- rant humbug." If this flickering light in the darkness of Toryism thinks the State should be governed by the Church, why does he not "go in" for making a Prime Minister of the Archbishop of Canterbury

The House of Lords ought to be improved off • the face of the earth; they don't do much; but When they do anything it is mischief. They have been meddling with the Directors' Liability Bill k 130 as to render directors less liable than they ought to be. The bill will probably pass as they have mutilated it, for it is too late to risk its loss a fight over it with the Commons. But there Will Co a struggle in the Commons about the compensation claus6 which the Lords have inserted in the Removal of Gates Bill. These obstructions IPon the Duke of Bedford's London estate have been a nuisance for years. The nuisance is to be l'emoved ; and the Lords are making provision for ewnpensation, although the Duke has not even a!ilced for anything of the kind. What compensa- ..;don are the inhabitants to have for having for so ''Dng endured the nuisance?
veAr Liverpool sanitary inspector named Robert John gusson was remanded at the Huddersfield Police ; Zurt) on Monday, on the charge of having attempted to Cr his wife by firing a revolver at her.
LOCAL NEWS.
RUNCORN COUNTY COL/RT. His Honour Judge Ffoulkes held a sitting of this Court on Tuesday. There were no cases of public interest.

ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHAPEL, RUNCORN. The Rev. J. Pulford Williams, pastor of this place of worship, preached on Sunday for the first time since his induction and his discourses were listened to by large congregations.

Sr. EDWARD'S LEAGUE Or THE CROSS, RUNCORN. The members of this League took part in the monstre demonstration at Bidston Hill, on Bank Holiday. They were accompanied by their Brass Band, and displayed their handsome banner in the procession. SUMMER SALE now on at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-at., Warrington.—.Advt. PROMOTION FROM WIDNES GAS WORKS. Mr. Timothy Duxbury, assistant manager of the Widnes Gas and Water Works, has been appointed man- ager of the Gas Works of the Middleton Corporation. Mr. Duxbury is the third assistant who has been promoted daring the past five years, a fact which redounds to the credit of the manager, Mr. Carr, and to the assistants themselves.

A PROFESSIONAL TRAMP AT Rmiconw. Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, an old woman named Margaret Mannion was charged with having been drunk in High-st. on the previous , day. The pri- soner said she was "betwixt and between." She was 88 years of age, and was tramping to her son, after leav- ing Prescot Workhouse. She pleaded hard to be set at liberty.—Superintendent Large said the prisoner had been tramping and thieving in the county .or 20 years. She was nothing but a professional tramp.--The woman was fined ss. and costs. • mem CARTS for children.—Garland, Ironmonger, Warring- ton and Earlestown.—Advt. •

ODDFELLOWS DEMONSTRATION AT HALTON. On Monday the members of the Rising Sun Lodge No. 628, G. U.O. met at the Castle Hotel, Halton, their head- quarters, arid headed by the banner of the lodge, and accompanied by the band of the Runcorn Rifle Volun- teers, under the conductorship of Mr. James Wdsds, marched in processional order to Runcorn, to visit the mother lodge. This was the bi-annual procession, and the members turned up in large numbers, the regalia adding to the effect of the procession. In the evening the Volunteer Band played for dancing 311 the green at Halton, and a pleasant time was spent. BATHS, all kinds.—J. S. Garlands, Ironmonger, 51, ,Bridge Street, Warrington. Branch—Earlestown.—Advt.
BANK HOLIDAY AT RUNCORN.

Brilliant sut;;;; NT:e7a-t-lTe-r-fi;;ot7r-ed-liank Holiday, and the exodus of pleasure seekers from Runcorn was very heavy and in excess of previous years, probably because the holiday was more generally observed. About 800 passengers were booked to Liverpool, 750 to Frodsham, 150 to Helsby, and there were. numerous sojpurners to the Welsh Coast, Chestkr, and other places. The cab proprietors also did a brisk trade, and when an alarm of a fire arrived from Frodsbam not a horse could be ob- tained to carry the fire engine there. Happily the con- flagration was confined to a stack of hay, and the flames were quickly extinguished.. _ _

- - MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN RUNCORN. In connection with the Runcorn branch of the Mersey Missions to seamen, the anniversary sermons were held on Sunday, and were attended with the customary suc- cess. In the morning the Rev. C M. Woosnam chap- I lain to the missions, who has sacrificed a comfortable living of £7OO a year, in order to devote his life to labour amongst the sailors, preached an eloquent ser- mon in the Parish Church. In the afternoon and evening, the services were held in the Public Hall, Mr. Woosnam being again the preacher. Large con- gregations assembled on each occasion, and the col- lections realised a satisfactory sum. Sumstra SALE now on at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankepst., Warrington.—Advt. INQUEST AT WESTON POINT. Mr. R. Dobson, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at Weston Point, on Saturday morning, on the body of a young man named Morse, who was found drowned at Weston Point on Thursday afternoon. John Johnson, an able seaman, deposed that on the previous Saturday afternoon, the deceased, and four other young men, and witness went for a sail in a yawl, from New Ferry. Be- tweenEastham and Ellesmere Port one of the party took the tiller against the wish of the witness, and directly afterwards the boat was struck by a squalL The tiller was displaced and the boat capsized. Witness and four other young men were picked up by a boat from the lightship, but the deceased was nowhere to be seen. A verdict of " Accidentally drowned" was returned.
ACCIDENT OR BRONCHITIS?

Mr. W. T. Flu—si:an-ci,--hercie—p-titi-coroner, on Wednes- day held an inquest at the Police Court on the body of John Conlan, 59 years of age, who was a dock labourer in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company. About nine months ago, whilst the deceased and two other men were engaged in unloading a waggon of coal into a vessel, a block of coal rolled off the wagon and struck the deceased on the back of the head, and he was seriously wounded. lie also sustained an injury to the spine, and never recovered sufficiently to return to his work. About six weeks aero he caught a bad cold, and bronchitis set in, and on Saturday last he died. Dr. O'Keeffe informed the jury that the immediate cause of death was bronchitis, and a verdict accordingly was returned. WARRINGTON INFIRMARY. '

The Hon. Treasurer begs to acknowledge with thanks the sum of .E 1 Is. 10d., being the flower service collection at St. Cross, Appleton Thorn. SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT ROCK SAVAGE. ()n Wednesday a terrible fatal accident occurred at the farm of Mr. Stokes, Rock Savage. A. boy named Robert Bradley, ten years of age, was play- ing about the place, when he became entangled in the chopping machine, and his brains were dashed out. He died immediately. An inquest will be held to-day. LORD TOLLEMACHE'S JUBILEE.

Lord and Lady Tollemache celebrated the jubilee of his lordship's accession to his estates on Thurs- day, at Helmingham, in Suffolk. They were pre- sented by the tenants with a beautifully illuminated address of congratulation and thanks, which Lord Tollemache very feelingly acknowledged! Subse- quently his lordship gave a large dinner, over which the lion. Stanhope Tollemache presided. DEATH ON THE ROADSIDE. On Monday afternoon' Charles Shorne, aged forty- three, residing at 12, Dalton-st., Manchester, along with his wife, went to see the Ship Canal Works at Rixton. After having gone over the works, on their way back to Glazebrook Station, at 7.30 p.m., Shorne was taken ill, and lay down at the roadside, where he expired. Police-Constable Scholfield and a man named llarding, had the body removed to the Red Lion Inn CRITCHLEY, High Cla.,s Tailor. Bold-at. Warrington.—Advt. DOG MUZZLING IN LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE. The Mayor of Manchester, introduced by Mr. J. W. Maclure, M.P., had on Wednesday an interview with Mr. Chaplin, President of the IBoard of Agri- culture, on the subject of the dog-muzzling order in operation in Lancashire and Cheshire. The Mayor urged the department to relax the order, and to adopt in lieu of it a system of registration of dogs with a collar and number. Mr. Chaplin, in reply, gave some hope that he might at an early date be able to relax the existing order.

SUMMER SALE now on at 3..& W. DurrOx's Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. FATAL ACCIDENT AT LEIGH. About half-past three on Monday afternoon a fatal accident occurred at the level crossings belonging to the Plank-lane colliery, near Leigh. A. man named George Mansfield,about 60 years of age, was engaged in his usual Occupation in looking after the points, whilst shunting operations were going on, when he got trapped between the wagon which the engine had pushed off the road, aim the engine, he being almost cut in two. Deceased had been employed at the colliery for some years, and the accident caused quite a sensatioa amongst his fellow-work- men. SUMMER SALE now on at J. & W. Dur Tores Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. SALVATION/STS AT HUTTON. _

- - - - Over 3,000 members of the Salvation Army held a demonstration at Huyton, on Monday, trains bringing contingents from Earlestown, Warrington, St. Helens, Widnes, Runcorn, and Bootle,, in addi- tion to the Liverpool and Birkenhead divisions arriving throughout the morning, and marched in procession to fields belonging to Thornton Leigh, where a grand review of senior and Junior troops was held, under the command of Captain and Mrs. Hoggard. A special programme was gone through. which included ex-prisoner and ex-drunkard de- monstrations, special campaigns, and representative gatherings, concluding at half-past eight o'clock with a musical festival.—The Church of England Temperance Society (Huyton Quarry branch), also held their annual outdoor demonstration in a field near the church, and a variety of sports were in- dulged in. ELECTRO PLATED GOODS.—Garland's oldest established Ironmonger. Warrington.—Adot. END OF A MINERS STRIKE.

'The surface bands employed at Messrs. Cross, Tetley, and Co's. Limited, extensive collieries, situ- ated at-Bamfurlong alid Abram, near Wigan, who lately struck work in consequence of not getting an increase of wages, resumed operations this morning, the directors having met on ' Wednesday and con- ceded the men's terms. Some hundreds of hands were affected, Mid it is understood that in making their demand the men have had the united support of the miners connected with the collieries named. SUMMER SALE now on at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-et., WarriagtoiY.---Advt. ALLEGED HIGHWAY ROBBERY AT BIIRTONWOOD. At, the Leigh Police Court, on Monday, John Con- cannon, a young fellow, was charged with robbing William Henry Roberts, carpenter, Elm-terrace, BUttenwood, near Earlestown, on the Ist inst. Complainant said he was returning home from Earlestown about 1030 on Friday evening, and on the way a man snatched his watch from his pocket. The guard broke. It was quite dark at the time. The watch now produced was his.—P.C. Rutter said lie apprehended prisoner on Saturday evening in Mr. 1 Green's pawnshop, King-st., Leigh. He was offer- ing the watch in pledge.—Prisoner asked what time complainant said the watch was taken from him.— The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. Marsh) : You can ask that question at Warrington.—Complainant: About a quarter to eleven.—Prisoner, who then said he could bring witnesses to prove that he was in the- Pear Tree Inn at eleven o'clock the same night, was remanded to Warrington. SUMMER SALE now on at 3, & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-it.. Warrington.—Advt. LANCASHLRE AND YORKSHIRE RAILWAY CO.

The half-yearly meeting of the Lancashire & York- shire Railway Co. was held at Manchester, on Wed- nesday. Mr. Armytage the chairman of the Com- pany, saki that although the receipts of the Company had increased by £68,225, the expenses had also grown to the amount of £87,861. This latter fact ,waS accounted for mainly by the increase in the cost of coal and materials, and the extra wages to the Company's servants consequent on the present high price of labour, In .the locomotive depart- ment alone the increased cost was £53,395, and it was £21,197 in the traffic' department. Coal cost more by £31,525 than in the corresponding half- year. There was an increase in the number of pas- sengers by more than a million, chiefly third class. In regard to railway rates and charges, the inquiry into which had recently been concluded, he hoped they would be placed by the Board of Trade in no worse position than at present. The report of the Directors was adopted without much discussion.
MR. WILLIAM O'BRIEN AND MR. CONINGSBY
DISI1ABLI;

Speaking at Cheadle, Cheshire, on the 28th ult., Mr. Coningby Disraeli, Conservative candidate for the Altriucham division, criticised Mr, O'Brien's speech at Manchester, and described the Irish members as false patriots. Mr. W. O'Brien, having had his attention directed to the speech, has sent the following reply 4—" Housti of Commons, July 31,1890.—Dear sir,—l cannot see anything in the observations of Mr. Coningsby Disraeli except platitudes a little unworthy of his uncle's nephew, but quite up to the average Tory candidate's level. To my three arguments at Manchester he replies by shirking the first—the collapsp of' Farnellism and Crime' ;'.by admitting the secohd—that Home Rule can never again be said to mean Home Rule; and as good as admitting the third—that Mr. Balfour has acknowledged the fear of separation to be .a groundless fear. The rest of Mr. Comngsby Disraeli's speech—the rhetoric—may be safely left to the robust sense of the British workman to estimate.— Sincerely yours, WILLIAM O'BRIEN." accounts included an item of £1 12s. 9d. for painting and papering the overseer's office, and which at a pre- vious meeting Mr. Meadowcroft had argued was an ex- pense that ought to be borne by the overseers, and not by the Commissioners. From inquiries he had made of Mr. W. Handley and Mr. W. Whittaker, who were the overseers at the time, he found that it was arranged that the overseers should take the offices-at £3s,per annum, and that this should be a quit rent. Mr. Sutton and Mr. Linaker said the same thing. When Mr. Meadowcroft took upon himself to refer the matter back to the Com- mittee, he ought, having special knowledge on the sub- ject, to have aided the Committee in coming to a correct decision, but possibly it was inconvenient for him to attend, and possibly he preferred to have his speeches reported in the newspapers, and by this means address a larger audience than the Committee. The allegation Mr. Meadoweroft made that he (Mr. Imison) was an interested party, was not a proper observation to make. The only interest he had was in seeing that the Commissioners-and the Overseers honourably fulfilled their obligations. In his opinion a good deal of time had been wasted in discussing whether the ratepayers should pay El 12s. 9d. out of the left hand pocket or the right hand pocket —Mr. Meadowcroft, in reply. said he would not begin by imputing motives, and remarked that Mr. Imison's extraordinary oration had occupied three times the time he occupied on the last occasion. . He was teld by the secretary that Mr. Imison had sanctioned this work and he said that this was un- fortunate, inasmuch as he was an overseer and chairman of the Finance Committee, and personally interested. Ile did not mean anything offensive by that observation, and only a very sensitive disposition. could have inter- preted it in that sense. Notwithstanding what Mr. Handley and others had told Mr. Ellison as to the arrangement,' there was nothing in theagreement about a quit rent, and there was nothing said about the Com- missioners papering and painting the rooms; and he argued that all the Commissioners undertook to do was to make certain structsual alterations. As to poksing as a speech maker, was a person's mouth to be closed by an observation of that kind ? It seemed to him an extra- ' ordinary position to take up, and so long as he saw any- thing in the minutes or anywhere else, he should exercise his right to inquire what it was and endeavour to get to the bottom of it. The minutes were then passed.

IMPROVEMENT or WATERLOO BRIDGE. The Waterloo Bridge Committee recommended that the tender of Messrs. Morrison and Sons,of Wavertree, for the further improvement of Waterloo Bridge,be accepted, in place of Messrs. Do.vener and Cos., withdrawn. It was further recommended that the weighing machine near to the Waterloo Hotel be offered for sale by tender. —Mr. Pritchard said the Committee had had much trouble with this matter, inasmuch as two tenders had been withdrawn. MeSsrs. Morrisoft had had great ex- perience in stone and iron work, at the Committee had every confidence that the work would be carried out in a creditable manner.—Mr. Fisher seconded the motion. —Mr. Hankinson said the Committee had been in ex- istence four years, and it was getting time the bridge was completed. He hoped this work would be carried out with expedition.—ln answer to questions, Mr. Prit- chard said the tender was below the estimate. A sug- gestion by Mr. Mesclowcroft to exhibit the plans of the bridge in the reading room, so that the public could see what was contemplated, met with considerable opposi- tion, and Was not persevered with. The minutes were passed. THE ATTENDANCE OF MEMBERS. In accordance with a notice of motion by Mr. Pritch- ard, the Secretary had prepared a table showing the attendance of members during the past year, from which the following figures are extracted : No. of Attend- Percent- MeMbers, meetings ances. age. W. Hankinson 92 72 78.2 S. Taylor E. Imison J. W. Lightburn H. J. Chico • 94 58 61'6 W. Fisher J. Pritchard F. Wiswall B4 46 5443 W. Mellor H. White 95 50 52.6 J. Meadowcroft J. Dobson BB 36 40.8 E. Timmins W. Whittaker P. Speakman lO7 32 29.9 W. R. Wass P. Smith 9B 11 W 2 It. Morris - 8-2 Mr. Grice and Mr. Dobson pointed out that their at- tendance had been greatly reduced by illness.—Mr. Lightburn said the list did not include the meetings of the Committee for the purchase of the nightsoil plant, &c., which were about 20 in number.
PROPOSND'PLEAMME _GROUND.

Mr. Imison moved that a Committee be appointed, con- sisting of Messrs. Hankinson, Wiswall, Mellor Pritchard, Grice, and Imison, to consider the question of providing a pleasure ground, to make inquiries upon what terms suitable land could be leased, &c., and to report, to the Board at an early date.—Mr. Imison said the necessity of a pleasure ground would be obvious to anybody who cast his eyes around. At one time there was almost a pleasure ground in every quarter of the town, but now, in consequence of building operations, they had "grown fine by degrees and beautifully less." It was a reflection on the town that there was no provision made for the recreation of the masses of the people. It might be said that the present time was , inopportune, but if they were to wait places wonld be more difficult to get, and if it is ever intended to provide a pleasure ground they could not begin too early. When the new road was made Newtown would really be the centre of the town, and it might be possible at the present time to:acquire what was required. However, an election was at hand, and the ratepayers would have an opportunity of expressing an opinion on the subject, and if they returned members pledged to something of this kind it would help the Board in coining to a decision. —Mr. Lightburn seconded the motion, and said he hoped the. Committee would not lose sight of the natural plea- sure ground, Runcorn Hill and the neighbourhood.—Mr. Hankinson supported the motion, and mentioned the annoyance caused by boys playing football ard other games in the streets.—The motion was then carried un- , animously.
THE CONING ELECTION.
Mr. J. W. Lightburn was appointed returning officer at the election on September 4th, and the lists of owners prepared by the Assistant Overseer (Mr. Sutton) were adopted. .
RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Mr. Jas. Pritchard, the Rev. Canon Wood, the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. J. J. Howitt, S. Taylor, and G. Moss (clerk).
PROPOSED EXHIBITION.

On the reading of the minutes of the last meeting, Dr. McDougall asked what was done with the sewing articles of the school.—The Clerk said the teachers sold them to the best advantage.—Dr. McDougall said in another part of the country he had seen an interesting exhibition of scholars work, and he suggested that such a scheme ought to be carried out with advantage in Run- corn. The Chairman and other members agreed in this viGw.—Dr. McDougall moved that arrangements be made for holding an exhibition of the needlework of the scholars of the Board Schools next year, and that the managers of denominational schools be asked to co- operate.
SCHOOL. ATTENDANCE.
It was reported that he attendance at the various schools during the past month had been 83.2 per cent. against 82 last year.
"A 4 ART SCHOOL PROPOSED.

Mr. T. H. Cooke, of Northwich, applied for the use of a room at the Board Schools for the purpose of holding an art class in Runcorn.—Mr. Howitt said Mr. Cooke had been eminently successful at Northwich, and he moved that he be allowed a room free of charge.—Dr. McDougall was in favour of introducing such teaching but suggested that the letter be referred to the School Management Committee. The Vicar said he was not aware that it was customary to grant a room free, but if it were done in this case, the University Scheme Com- mittee would have a strong claim to a similar privilege. —Mr. Howitt said the school was built for edu- cational purposes, and the public ought to be granted these privileges, and he should be glad to allow the Ex- tension Scheme Committee a room free.—After further discussion, it was'resolved that Mr. Cook be allowed the use of a room on terms to be arranged with the School Management Committee. There was no other business of public interest.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday. Mr. S. Taylor presided, and there were present Messrs. Once, Hankinson, Dobson, Imison, Timmins, P. Smith, Mellor, Lightburn, Wiswall, Pritchard, Fisher, Lake (law clerk), Mar- shall (secretary),.and Barker (surveyor.)
HEALTH OF TETE TOWN. -

The Medical Officer reported that the number of deaths during July amounted to 42, of which two were inquests, and of the remaining 40 deaths 11 were due to diarrhcea, 6 to convulsions, 3 to mesenteric disease, 3 to heart dis- ease, 2 each to chronic rheumatism, premature birth, and pneumonia, and one each to pkthisis, apoplexy, liver disease, paralysis, inflammation of the lining membrane of the brain, cancer, atrophy, scarletina, rochnic disease of the brain, kidney disease, and ab- dominal tumour. The 42 deaths showed an average death rate of 28 per 1,000, and exclusive of the inquest cases of 26 and a fraction.—ln answer to questions, Dr. McDougall said there were no definite cases of ty- phoid fever in the town.
HIGHWAY AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEE.

This Cemmittee recommended :—That the sewer at the Sprinch be extended further to a point marked B on the plan, and that the offer of the Manchester Ship Canal Company to do the work at the rate of O. 14s. Od. per lineal yard be accepted. That th.o, offer of Mr. J. J. Ih'aterworth. dated 30th July, 1890, to give land marked A, B, and C on the plan far the purpose of widening the road (known as Crown-st.,) be accepted on condition that the Board make and complete the road from A to C, and that the street making for the remaining seven yards only be charged to him. That the seal of the Board be affixed to the agreement with Major J. C. Orred in respect of the proposed New-road from Heath-road to , Greenway-road, and that notices be served on the ad- joining owners to sewer, metal, &c. their respective por- tions of the road in pnrsuance of Section 150 of the Public Health Act, 18 '5 ; Tat this road, now known as Crown-st. and Grange View he in future named Victoria- road. That tenders be obtained for the supply of 500 tons of macadam. That the following plans be ap- proved :—Mr. George Marshall for the erection of a villa residence in Weston-road on land adjoining Mrs. Thomas Hazlehurst's property.—Mr. John Thomason amended plan of two houses 'in Norman-road.—Mr. William Thomason for erection of eight; cottages in Stanley-st.— Runcorn Property Company for the erection •of seven houses in Crown-st.--Mr. Thomas Mather for the erection of a villa residence in Weston-road, near Mrs. Ken- wri ght's.—Mr. Fisher moved the adoption of the minutes. —Mr. Lightburn seconded the motion,and congratulated the Board and the town generally on the completian of the arrangements for the new road from Mill Brow to Greenway-road. He considered the road was very pro- perly named.—The minutes were passed. TIIE FIRE MINE.

In moving the adoption of the General Purposes Com- mittee, Mr. Grice referred to the fact that no horses were available on Bank Holiday to take the fire engine to Frodsham. Mr. Peck was under contract to supply horses at any time and immediately on his departure from the town the Committee were in communication with Mr. Jackson who had made no definite offer, but it was understood that he would supply the horses until some permanent arrangement was made. On Bank Holi- day all his horses were engaged, and it was impossible to get horses anywhere in the town.—Mr. Hankinson pointed out:that there was no brake to the fire engine, and that very often persons who did not understand how to conple two horses to a cart interfered in the matter. He thought something should be done.—The Secretary said on Tuesday Mr. Jackson declined to make an offer.— The matter was referred to the General Purposes Com- mittee.

FATALITY TO A CHILD AT DITTON. MD.. HUSBAND ON DOCTOR'S CERTIFICATES. . At the Blackburn Arms, Ditton, on Thursday afternoon, Mr. W. T. Husband held an inquest on the body of George Thomas Houghton, aged six months, son of Thomas Houghton, of Woods' Cot- tages, Ditton.—Mrs. Houghton, the mother, stated that about three months ago the deceased fell out of bed, but she did not notice that he was hurt. About six weeks afterwards she observed the child's hip was tender, and that he appeared to be in pain and she took him to Dr.• Richards, who said the baby appeared tn have hip disease. For two weeks he was under the care of Dr. Richards, and then she took him to the Children's Hospital, Liverpool, where two operations were performed on him. On Saturday last the doctor told her he thought the child was dying, and if she liked she could take it home. She did so, and the baby died on Tuesday morning. Drs. McCambridge and Richards refused to give her a certificate, but she afterwards got one from Mr. Burroughs,, of the Childrens' Hospital, to the effect that death was caused by a diseased hip.—By the Coroner: The doctors placed a card over the child's bed in the infirmary "Fallen out of bed."—The Coroner said the certificate given by Dr. Burroughs was so loosely filled in, the date of death for instance being entered as the 2nd instead of the fifth—that he thought it ought not to have been given. There was no reference to the child having fallen out of bed, and the doctors knew perfectly well there Was'a connection between thai illness and the child's illness which ought to have beth taken notice oh It was not for the doctor to decide whether the child fell out of bed or whether the mother threw it out. The mother had said she thought the nurse filled up the certificate, and if so he considered it a very loose and reprehensible way of giving a'certificate from an infirmary, and the sooner such a method was stopped and the better.—After further remarks the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

div.head: SAVAGE ASSAULTS ON TRE POLICE AT RUNCORN. _ _
div.p: SAVAGE ASSAULTS ON TRE POLICE AT RUNCORN. _ _

- - _ Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, before Major Hazlehurst and Dr. Steele, a navvy named William Buckley, who had been a soldier, was charged with being drunk and disorderly and with assaulting P.C. Edwards. P.C. Edwards said about half-past 'five the prisoner was in the middle of Church-st. with his coat off and wanting to fight Geo. Duckett, the fishmonger and lodginghouse keeper. As he was drunk and refused to clear away, the Constable apprehended him, but they had not walked far when he became very rough and they both fell to the ground. The prisoner kicked him savexal tea 01A the back, and his shoulders were quite bfack. Another prisoner named Hoskins also kicked him.-oeorgeo Duckett said the prisoner came to his shop and used bad language to the boy in charge, and threw two herrings into a bucket of dirty water. Witness pushed him intu the road, and he then wanted to fight, but the Conetable came up sad took him into custody. After they had gone a short distance he saw a scuffle and both fell to the ground and he ran to the Constable's assistance. He helped to take Buckley to the Police Station.—Supt. Large said the prisoner was very violent and refused to be searched.— The prisoner alleged that Duckett was the aggressor, and challenged him to fight in his back premises. Then the constable shoved him about and caught hold of him by the throat. He did not know how they fell to the ground but he denied striking the officer.—fle called Henry Hoskins, of Leamington, a well dressed man,who said he was a retired grocer. He heard the dispute between Buckley and Duckett with regard to the herrings, and he told the constable if he lockld one up he ought to lock the two up. Buckley grappled with the policeman and struck him on the face, and they fell together. Witness dragged Buckley off the constable, as he thought he was in duty bound to assist the police. He followed on to the police station, when he was apprehended. He could not say whether the prisoner was drunk or sober.—Superintendent Large Were you drunk or sober? I had not had more than a quart during the day.—What do you do for a living? My wife is independent.—Shedoesn't give you a very good character. lam receiving letters wee* about you.— Witness : My wile is insane, and takes fancies into her head. I had to come down here out of her way.—The Bench said before they decided this case they would hear the charges against Hoskins.—Hoskins was then placed in the dock and charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Church-st., with assaulting P.C. Edwards, and with wilfully damaging the cell to the extent of El. Mr. A. Linaker, solicitor, defended.—P.C. Edwards repeated his evidence, and stated that when he was struggling on the floor with Buckley the prisoner kicked him violently on the face, injuring his nose, cheek, and eye very badly. He was apprehended by P.C. Hamersley and in the office it took about six constables to search him, he was so rough. After he was placed in the cell he created a great noise, and it was found that he had smashed the closet and broken the windows.—By Mr. Linaker: Instead of the prisoner trying to assist him, he attempted to set Buckley at liberty.—Duckett corroborated.—Superinten- (lent Large said when Edwards was searching Buckley in the office, the prisoner Hoskins kicked him on the back. —P.C. Crowder proved the damage to the cell.—For:the defence Buckley was called, and stated the prisoner was sober and that he never kicked the constable either out- side or inside the office.—Harry Hoskins, employed by the Ship Canal Contractor at Old Quay, said the prisoner was his brother, and he left him at the Egerton Arms at half-past five quite sober.—Mr. Linaker ad- dressed the Bench for the defence, which was a:complete denial of the assault.—The Bench having decided to con- vict, Superintendent Large said there had been six serious assaults on the police since the middle of May and the Chief Constable wished the Bench to inflict such punishment as would a,ct as a deterrent—Major Hazle- burst said the magistrates considered the assaults of a gross character. The other cases did not affect the prisoners, but at the same time thepolice had to be taken care of, and they intended to do it.—Buckley was fined ss. and 6osts Bs. Bd. for the drunkenness, and 403. and costs ss. for the assault, a total of £2lBs. Bd., or in de- fault five weeks' imprisonment. —Hoskins was fined ss. and costs 13s. Bd. for drunkenness, £5 and costs ss. for the assault, and for the wilful damage he was ordered to pay £1 and costs 55., altogether £7 85. Bd., or eleven weeks' imprisonment.—Hoskins said he would pay the ' money. Buckley went to gaol.
TOMMY BURNS " AGAIN.

div.head: ALLEGED STRUGGLE WITH I SHARK AT NEW
div.p: ALLEGED STRUGGLE WITH I SHARK AT NEW
BRIGHTON.

The "Liverpool Daily Post " tells the following "fishy" story : An exciting and extraordinary scene. was witnessed off the New Brighton shore on Thursday evening. Several hundred spectators had assembled at the pierhead and on the sands, to see Tommy Burns, the champion bridge jumper and swimmer, leap into the liver from the pier. This feat having been successfully accomplished, interest was centred in his aquatic feats. He had performed several movements, when he was obsaved to make a signal for help ; and immediately afterwards great consternation was caused among the onlookers, who saw that he was holding deadly combat with a monster fish. A boat was imme- diately sent to his assistance ; but in the mean- time a desparate struggle was taking place. Burns showered vigorous blows upon the body of his assailant, and succeeded in keeping it at bay until the arrival of the boat. He was then handed a clasp knife, with which be quickly despatched the dreaded creature by ripping it up. Burns, who was very much exhausted after his extraordinary adventure, was then brought to the shore, together with the fish; and he received quite an ovation from the anxious spectators. The fish was taken to the pier, where it was inspected with great interest by a large number of visitors. It is about sft. 4in. in length, and has a formidable row of teeth. Professor Boston emphatically declares that it is a young shark, although many expressed the opinion that it was a clog-fish. Burns's left arm is severely scored.the result of his desper- ate encounter; and he is to be congmtulated.upon over- coming so powerful an enemy with no worse injuries. ANOTHER ACCOUNT OF THE ADVENTURE. "Truthful Jimmy," writing to a Liverpool contempo- rary, says :—Truth is mighty and will prevail, and, as a spectator of the scene from beginning to end, lam bound, however reluctantly, to deny that any onlooker saw the gallant Tommy holding deadly combat with a monster fish. He performed his usual jump from the New Brighton Pier about half-past eight o'clock, and after disporting himself a while in the water, he could just in the increasing darkness be perceived mov- ing about rather more vigorously than usual. Naturally, a convenient boat was at hand, and Tommy and something indiscernible in the distance were lifted intc it. When they reached the shore the "something "proved to be a big fish, but so far from anyone imagining that Tommy had been attacked by it and killed it, the universal opinion was that it had been purposely obtained for some new species of performance in the water, and much regret, in which my friends and myself shared, was expressed that the darkness had prevented the novel exhibition from being seen. Singu- larly enough, I heard one of Burn's intimate acquaint- ances declare the other day that something was " going to be done for them soon." Perhaps your readers can perform the arithmetical operation known ai "putting two and two together."

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN IT-IttNCORN, &c. BY AN 'OC6.f3IONAL CORRESPONDENT.

-- ' The celebration of the centenary of the Duke's Club, at Runcorn, on Bank Holiday, was an import- ant event in the history of that friendly society, and takes the mind back to the time, 114 years ago, when the Duke of Bridgewater accomplished his vast undertaking, with the help of that great engin- eer,Brindley. The total cost of the canalwas .£220,000, and Smiles, in his life of Brindley, says : "Probably the most remarkable circumstance connected with the money history of the enterprise is this: that, although the canal yielded an income which even- tually reached about .£BO,OOO a year, it was planned and executed by Brindley, at a rate of pay consider- ably less than that of an ordinary mechanic of the present day. The highest wage he received whilst in the employ of the Duke, was 3s. 6d. per day. For I the greater part of the time be only received half-a- crown." That such a genius should be so miserably paid for accomplishing an undertaking which the skilled engineers of the day protested was impos- sible, is a strange comMentary on those times, and leads one to surmise, what rate of wages the labourers at the locks who established the Duke's Club, were paid in the year of its formation, 1790. We can well imagine it was very meagre indeed, and that the members were much in need of the help ef their fellow workmen in the day of trouble. The celebration of the Centenary was in every way a success. The procession was a pretty sight, and acquired greater importance in the eyes of the members by the fact that Mr. Collier, the general manager, and many ether chiefs of the Company.; took part in the demonstration. At the meeting and concert in the evening, the club was shown to be in a most flourishing condition, and the members fitly acknowledged the valuable services of Mr. Simister, as secretary for a period of 33 years, being no less than one-third of the entire existence of the The general public will, no doubt, be more inter- ested in the important announcement made by Mr. Collier in the course of an able speech. Runcorn Bridge is an impassible bar to large tall-was ted skips travelling any higher up the Ship Canal than our busy seaport, and the gentlemen who control the Bridgewater Undertaking intend to take means to attract such vessels from Liverpool as far as Runcorn. Mr. Wiswall, the resident engineer, Mr. Collierinformed the meeting, is at present engaged in designing plans for the construction of a large dock, in connection with the present docks, to ac- comadate these large vessels, and the town may look forward to a period of greater prosperity when the Ship Canal is completed. There is considerable difficulty in obtaining any accurate information as to the proposed Chemical Union, and many doubts are expressed as to the scheme ever being successfully carried out. Within the past few days, however, members of the Com- mittee of promoters have inspected the works at Runcorn and Weston, and also a great many of the Works at Widnes. Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon and Cu., one of the oldest and most extensive manufacturers in the district, are holding aloof from the syndicate. The Committee is said to consist of the following manufacturers: Messrs, J. Brock, J.P., E. K. Mus- pratt J.P., C. E. Barlow, T. Mathieson, R. H. Davies (all of Widnes), C. Wigg (Runcorn), J. H. Dennis ,I (Globe Alkali Works, St. Helens)—Raynor (Kurtz ' and Co. St. Helens), J.. Tennant (Newcastle) ; —Alexander (manager Sir Charles Tennant, Glasgow) —Davidson (Newcastle Chemical Co.) The Vicar of Runcorn (canon Wood) arrived home last week end after a long sojourn on the continent, and he was present at the meeting of the School Board, on Tuesday night. Mrs. Wood, for the bene- fit of whose hada the journey was undertaken, is, the parishioners will be sorry to-learn, but little better for the change of scene. Early in September the ratepayers will be called upon to elect five representatives on the Board of Commissioners, and the members who retire are Mr. Samuel Taylor, the chairman of *the Board, Mr. W. Whittaker. Mr. IV. Fisher, Mr. P. Smith, and Mr. R. Morris. The last named gentleman does not in- tend to again seek re-election, but the remaining four will again seek the honour of a seat on the Board. The election cry will probably be "Pleasure grounds for the people," and it is to be hoped it will be nearer realisation than Baths, to which several of the members are pledged. Whatever becomes of the question of the incor- poration of Widnes at the meeting of Widnes Local Board on Tuesday next, it is to be hoped that the members will: all be in favour of adopting the Technical Education Act. In no town in the king- dom is there a greater need of such instruction than in Widnes, whose industries are of the most scienti- fic and intricate character. It is not to the credit of Englishmen that the great majority of our skilled chemists receive their training in Germany where the importance of technical educa- tion is estimated at its true value. The Techni- cal' Education Act is a step in the right direction, and the intelligent ratepayers would not begrudge the extra penny in the .£, which the adoption of Act would probably cause to be levied. The autho- rities of the science and art school are prepared, whenever such a consummation is arrived at, to hand over their valuable library of scientific works, and their apparatus to the new educational authQ-, rity that would be created.

PIM/MTH Y.M.C.A. The monthly "social "gathering of this associa- tion was held at Bethany House, last evening week, there being a fair attendance of members. Several items of business concerning the association were satisfactorily settled, after which a miscellaneous programme, consisting of songs, readings, recita- tions, &c., contributed by the members, was gone through. GA.RDDRN PARTY &C.

On Tuesday evening, the members of Mrs. Coop's Female Class, with their pusbands and some friends, in all about forty-five persons, met at Bethany House, by the invitation of Mrs. Coop, for a garden party. At six o'clock a substantial tea was par- taken of under the trees. After tea !Mrs. Coop ex- pressed her thankfulness to God for having spared them another year, and she was more especially thankful that not one of the party—which was the same that met last year—had been removed by death. Mrs. Jenks and Mr. James Watson also ad- dressed the gathering. After the speaking, games were indulged in until half-past eight, when the party repaired to the large dining-room, where the meeting took the form of a love feast until ten o'clock, when the gathering dispersed.

div.head: CHOLERA. EPIDEMIC.
div.p: THE CHOLERA. EPIDEMIC.
HUNDREDS OF DEATHS

A Cairo Correspondent telegraphs that there were over 180 deaths from cholera at Mecca on Wednesday. The epidemic appeared at Jeddah on the Ist inst., and the deaths have now reached one hundred daily. A death from cholera has taken place in Madrid.

THE FIGHTING IN CENTRAL AMERICA. DEFEAT OF REVOLUTIONISTS. NEW Yomt, THIIRSDAY.—Advices from Mexico state that 3,000; Guatemalan revolutionists, under Generals Maximo, Cern°, and Alfonso Irunagavay were defeated on the 4th instant by a force of Guatemalan regulars the command of Pedro Banllas, brother of the President. A telegram from La Libertad states that Honduras is giving moral support to Guatemala. General Ezeta's popularity is increasing. He has assured the diplomatic body that he is anxious for peace. It is reported at New York that the Diplomatic Body at Guatemala are using their efforts to promote peace, and that representatives of Great Britain, France, Ger- many, and Spain have accepted the invitation of the United States Minister in Guatemala to offer their media- tion. Further despatches say that General Rafael Ayala, a claimant for the Presidency of San Salvador, has es- tablished his seat of Government at Senzuntepeque, near the Honduras frontier. General Miranda, a guerilla chief, commands the forces supporting General Ayala. If Ile is capturned by the Salvadorians he will be shot. div.head: POLICE AGITATION.
div.p: THE POLICE AGITATION.

A SETTLEMENT. The Watch Committee of the Warrington Town Council have come to a decision with regard to the agitation among the members of the police force of the borough, who recently presented to the Com- mittee a petition asking for a re-arrangement of the hours of duty, the terms of which have already been made public. The Committee conceded the demand for an equivalent of leisure for time spent when off regular duty in attending court to prove cases, and in undertaking special Market and Cemetery duty. The demand for an eight hours' working day, and one day off in a month, was not granted.. The Committee arrived at this decision at a meeting held on Thursday, after considering statements received from other towns as to the regulations there in force. The Mayor presided over the meeting. It is understood that generally speaking the men will be satisfied with the alter- ations made in the existing arrangements.

div.head: EARLESTOWN TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE EARLESTOWN TRAGEDY.
PRISONER COMMITTED FOR TRIAL

Continuing our account from page 3, we have to recor that yesterday the prisoner Thomas Mercer was again brought up at the Newton Town Hall, before Mr. T. J. Gillespie and Mr. T. 11. Pearson, on a charge of wilfully murdering Thomas Kay. It was generally expected that the resumed magisterial inquiry would be held at the Earlestown police station, but the police authorities decided to remove the prisoner to Newton. He was accordingly conveyed to the Newton police station about three o'clock on Friday morning, in order to avoid any excitement or commotion on the part of the public. The proceedings at the Town Hall commenced about half- past eleven. The fact was not generally known, and very few persons, with the exception of witnesses, were present. Superintendent Weir prosecuted, and the prisoner was again undefended. Without any prelimin- ary statement being made, the evidence was taken. The prisoner took very little or no interest in the proceedings, and to every question if he had anything to ask the wit- nesses, he replied "no." The first witness called was John Hatton, grocer and prevision dealer, Earlestown, who repeated his evidence given at the inquest to the effect that on Wednesday, the 23rd ult., he lent deceased the axe produced. There were then no stains upon it. Thomas Singleton, a carter, residing in High-st., • Newton, was next called,and he also repeated his former statements as to hearing a cry of "Oh," and seeing the prisoner strike deceased on the head with an axe. He gave an alarm, and he saw prisoner running away. Thie man Kay was found lying unconscious with severe cuts on his head.

Thomas Newton, a labourer, who also gave evidence at the inquest, corroborated his former statements. John O'Neill, a slater, was the next witness, and he again stated that he saw the prisoner lying in some tall grass and thistles near the old Sankey paper mill. He shook the prisoner and told him to get up. Prisoner I asked "What's to do," and witness replied " I'll show you what's to do." • William Moses, a new witness, was then called. He I said he was a master joiner, and lived in Chemical- at., Earle.stown. He was emPloyed:by Mr. Bella, and was in charge of the workmen in the demolition of the old paper mill. During the time the men had been pull- ing the mill down, he had seen the prisoner about the premises several times, but he had always seemed to evade him and to keep out of his way. The prisoner had never applied to him for any employment. On the forenoon of the day in question, he saw the prisoner running through a passage and out of the gate. He ran from the direction in which the deceased was working. Witness went to the place, and saw deceased lying on a plank with his head "battered in" and bleeding. He stayed with the deceased until the arrival of Dr. Valentine.

Dr. Valentine, of Earlestown, and Dr. E. E. Bowden, resident surgeon at Warrington Infirmary, spoke to the nature of the injuries inflicted on deceased's head; and Police-sergeant Longworth and Police-constable Hughes repeated their evidence as to the apprehension of the prisoner. Superintendent Weir also gave evidence that after the death of Kay he cautioned the prisoner, and said the charge against him would be altered to wilful murder. The prisoner made no reply.—ln reply to the Clerk, Superintendent Weir added that that concluded the case. The prisoner was then formally charged and cautioned by the magistrates, and on being asked if he had any- thing to say, be somewhat indifferently replied "No." He was then committed for trial at the Liverpool Assins, The proceedings terminated at 1.15.

div.head: ANOTHER EARLESTOWN
div.p: ANOTHER EARLESTOWN
TRAGEDY.
SHOCKING DEATH OF A WOMAN.

The Warrington and Earlestown police were yesterday inquiring into the shocking circum- stances under which a woman died on Wednesday, at the hospital connected with the Warrington Workhouse, with a view to the holding of an in- quest that will probably take place this (Saturday) morning, and perhaps with a view also to further proceedings that may take place at a later date. The woman's name was Alice Ann Dashwood, her age was 26, and, unfortunately for her, she WM married, her husband being a collier of Earlestown. On the 17th of last June she was brought to the Workhouse in a cab, from Earles- tomnt and it 15 etateid that at the time was in a most deplorable stabs. gam was literally covered with bruises, which in the opinion of those who must be deemed qualified to understand such matters, had been caused by kicks and blows, and in addition to this the poor woman Was pregnant and weak-minded. It was thought by those who saw her at first that she was quite idiotic, but later experience leads to the belief that her senses had, as a matter of fact, been beaten out of her, and that she was in a maudlin condition purely as the result of the most brutal treatment. Her right eye was blackened, as well as other parts of her body; and it is said that after being admitted to the Workhouse, she shrinked as thongh in fear whenever approached or addressed. She was treated with all possible care when in the institution mentioned, but, though she improved to some extent mentally, she never sufficiently recovered as to be able give the atten- dants a coherent statement as to how she came to be in such a pitiable condition. In fact, she was from the time of admission up to the time of her death on Wednesday in a semi-conscious state, and during that period she suffered agony that is des- cribed as having been painful to witness. Soon after admission she was confined of a child, and at that time she was almost unconscious. It is stated, indeed, that she afterwards had no recollection of the fact that she had given birth to a child, and that she never recognised it or took any interest in it. The baby, up to yesterday, was living, but it is said that the poor little thing is dwindling away, and that very little hope can be entertained of its living. The confinement took place on the 12th of July. Upon the death of the unfortunate woman the Workhouse doctor declined to give a certificate of death, and it is understood that in his opinion her death was attributable to the ill-treat- ment she had received. Information was, therefore, given to the police, and a search was commenced for the woman's husband, who, however, appears to have left the district. Inspector Spinks, of the borough police force, made inquiries in order to bring evidence before the Coroner, the death having occurred in the borough of Warrington, and the Earlestown police were yesterday seeking for the husband of the deceased, with a view to placing him under arrest if the circumstances of the case, after research, render that course advis- able. The police, it should be said, have re- fused any information on the subject to the press, and it is a question whether they will be able to conclusively prove, by evidence, that the injurinfrom which the woman suffered so severely wore caused by the husband. As to the cause of death, that will be ascertained by means of a post-mortem, and the whole matter will no doubt be thoroughly investigated. It is stated that this is not the first time that the deceased, who has several children, has been sent to the Union by the relieving officer. Six months ago her husband was charged before the Warrington magistrates with neglect of his family, and there is still a warrant out against him for the same offence.
MR. H. BROADHURST, M.P., AND AIR. CONINGSBY DISRAELI.

An elector of the Altrincham division having sent a quotation from Mr. Coningsby Disraeli's speech at Cheadle, on the 28th ult., which stated that all working-men who did a good day's work were Con- serTatives, and those who did not do an honest day's work were Radicals, to Mr. Broadhurst, has received the following reply:- 19, Buckingham-street, Strand, W.C. Dear sir,—lt would be somewhat difficult to treat seri- ously within the limits of a letter the stupid nonsense of a harebrained politician. I have no doubt the trade unionists of the division will give a go4d account of them- selves at the poll whenever the election comes,. and Mr. Disraeli may possibly leave Altrinclaam a wiser if a sadder man.—Yours truly, _
BENET BROADHURST.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

ROBBING A COMPANION. James Fitzpatrick ,of Sankey Bridges, was charged at the Warrington Police Court. on Tuesday, with having stolen 17s. from the person of Patrick Donoghue, who lives at Friars-green. The two men are puddlers at the same forge. On Bank Holiday complainant laid down in a field near to Monks, Hall, and Co's. works, and fell asleep. Prisoner was seen to go to him, and take something from his pocket. He pleaded guilty to having stolen 45., but said that was all. He was sent to prison for a month, with hard labour.

A HUSBAND DOES NOT LIKE LATE BAKING. At Warrington Borough Court, yesterday, George Haddock, of Church-st., was charged with having assaulted his wife on the 31st July. Mrs. Haddock said her husband "slatted "her out of bed, and threatened to throw her out of the window. The defendant, who was represented by Mr. A. Browne, denied the assault, but admitted that he threatened to throw her out of the window because she was in the habit of drinking through the day and looking after her baking late at night. The case was dismissed.

div.head: CHARGE OF HIGHWAY RODISERY.
div.p: CHARGE OF HIGHWAY RODISERY.

A Collins Green collier, named John Concannon, was charged on remand at the Warrington Occasional Court, on Wednesday, with stealing from the person of William Henry Roberts a watch and chain, together of the value of £B.—Prosecutor, a joiner, living in Burtonwood, was returning home on the night of the Ist inst. when a man snatched his watch out of his waistcoat pocket and ran off with it.—The next morning the prisoner was appre- hended whilstendeavouring to pledge the watch at Legh. —He nowsta.ted that he had bought the watch from a man whom he met on the road .—Mr. P. Stubs co.nmitted him for trial.

ASSAULTING A WIFE WIT A LOAF. The Warrington magistrates, on Tuesday, had before them a man named Charles Cummings, whose wife charged him with having assaulted her on the 3rd inst. She said that on Sunday night he came home and asked for his supper. She had nothing in the house but bacon and bread and butter, which he said was not good enough for him. He then used bad language, and threw a loaf of bread at her, which caused her eye to be blackened. Prisoner said that his wife aggravated him. They had been married six years, and he did not think he had hit her twice in that time. A fine of 20s. and costs, or a months' hard labour in default of payment, was imposed.

WARRINGTON V. BOOTLE.—The return match between these clubs was played at Warrington on Saturday, before a large number of spectators. Warrington, on winning the toss,began with Crosfield and Podmore to the deliveries of Needham and Hennessey. A poor start was made, as Crosfield was out before a run was scored. Clarke asd Podmore put on 26 runs for the second wicket. Podmore, Armstrong, and Jolley soon retired—five wickets down for 39; when Yonge and Muir got together, the former scored very freely. The total was taken to 83 before Muir was caught. Yonge retired at 104 for 50, without giving a chance. He hit six 4's. Captain Adam hit very freely for his 18, which included two 4's and two 3's. Griffin played very carefully for his 10, as also did Proud and Unsworth. The innings was declared closed at 4.30. Bootle started with Williams and Johnson to the bowling of Jolley and Crosfield, and fared so badly that all were eut for 38. This result was brought about by the splendid bowling of Jolley and good fielding on the part of the home team. Seeing that Warrington were without the aid of J. J. Crosfield, R. Smith, C. G. WARRINGTON 2ND V. BOOTLE 2:ln.—This match was played at Warrington on Bank Holiday, and resulted in a very hollow victory for the home team, who more than atoned for the defeat on Saturday. The visitors won the toss, but made a very feeble effort, only two being able to get into • double figures, Macfarlane playing very nicely for 17, and carrying out his bat. Unsworth took five wickets for 18 runs, and Birtles 3 for 3 runs. They were all out before luncheon, which was partaken of at the Patten Arms Hotel, and which was done full justice to by the hungry players. Warrington started batting at three o'clock, with the captain (Jolley) and Adamson, and these two played so well that the Bolton total was soon passed, Jolley being the first to leave with the total at 87, after a tine exhibition of cricket. With Clarke on the scene, the score increased very rapidly. Adamson was out with the total at 103 for a patiently-played 41. Yonge scored 10 in 3 strokes, and was then stumped. Proud came in and played very quietly while Clarke continued hitting. These two put on 123 runs, when Proud unluckily hit his wicket, and had to retire for 35, having been in a little over an hour for his runs. Voisey was soon out, and Howard helped to put on 42 runs, and was then stumped. Clarke was the next to succumb, being out with the score at 297, after compiling 130, with a magnificent display of good hard hitting; his 130 was compiled as follows-20 4's, three 3's, twelve 2's, and singles.
