div.head: VIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 9, 1890 THE DUKE'S CLUB, RUNCORN.
div.p: VIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 9, 1890 THE DUKE'S CLUB, RUNCORN.
CELEBRATION OF THE CENTENARY.
IMPORTANT SPEECH BY MR. COLLIER.

In any of the affairs of life, the celebration of a centenary is an important event,and the Duke's Club, Runcorn, having attained the mature age of 100 years,the members determined that the anniversary should be celebrated with due pomp and ceremony. At 3 o'clock on Monday, the members assembled on the lawn of Bridgewater House, Bottom Locks, where they formed in processional order. Leading the way was Mr. Henry Orme, the oldest member of the Club, who bore aloft a new banner, on which was inscribed "Duke's Club Centenary." Following was Runcorn Soap Works Brass Band, playing in- spiriting music,immediately in advance of the hand- some banner of the Club, which was carried by four sturdy watermen. Then came Mr. W. Collierozeneral manager of the Bridgewater Undertaking, Man- chester; Mr. Oldfield, secretary, Manchester; Mr. J. Meadowcroft, agent, Runcorn; Mr. W. Grundy. agent, Liverpool; Mr. McQuannell, agent, Preston Brook; Mr. F. Wiswall, engineer, Runcorn; Mr. J. Rawlinson,Captain Johnson (president of club); Mr. T. Simister (secretary), Mr. T. Done (treasurer), Mr. W. Shaw (Seamen's Missionary), Mr. J. Gates. Dr. Mangan and Dr. Robinson, the medical officers, also took part in the procession. The members of the Committee, each carrying a staff of office, acted as marshals, and their names are as follow :—J. Hals- worth, William Haxworth, Royle Garnett, William Pendlebury, John Pendlebury, Henry Crompton, Thomas Pearson, Joseph Cook and W. Gibson. The members were adorned with the regalia of the club, and in the ranks numerous banners fluttered in the breeze, and the sight was altogether a bright and attractive one; and was viewed by hundreds of spectators. The procession wended its way through all the principal streets and thoroughfares of the town,stoppages being made.en route at the residences of Mr. Meadowcroft, Dr. Mangan, Dr. Robinson, and Mr. Samuel Taylor, of llalton-road. Shortly after five o'clock, the procession came to a stand- still at Bethesda Lecture Hall, where a knife and fork tea.had been provided, and of which about 240 partook. When the tables were cleared, a con- cert was given under the presidency of Mr. Meadow- croft, who was supported by a number of the gentlemen previously mentioned, In the course of the evening several speeches were delivered. The Chairman said he should not detain them long by making a speech, nor should he attempt to deliver a lec- ture upon the advantages of sick and benefit societies, because the advantages were so well known to the mem- bers of the Duke's Club. They were met to celebrate the centenary of the club. It was a hundred years since the club was formed, and that in itself spoke well for the management of the Duke's Club. The position of the club, so far as the finances were concerned, was as satisfactory as it was 100 years ago. (Applause.) The club was managed by the members themselves—there was no interference at all by any official connected with the company—and they had conducted affairs in such a manner as to place the club in a most satisfactory posi- tion. (Hear, hear.) Although there was not as large a number of members as there were 100 years ago, that was to be accounted for by the fact that there were so many more clubs in the town, so many different societies to compete with them, and they could scarcely expect it, but they had not suffered in their general position. Dur- ing, the hundred years the club had been in existence, they had paid between £50,000 and £60,000 to the members who had been sick, and who had lost husbands or wives. That was a considerable sum, and yet to-day there was a balance to the credit of the club of between £1,600 and £1,700. (Applause.) The club was, there- fore, in a sound position, but it could be made more prosperous by an increase of members, and he urged the young men connected with the Bridgewater Undertaking to join the club. It was a duty which every young man • owed to himself, and when he was married, it wasa duty ' he owed his wife and family. He hoped that everyone would do their utmost to encourage the young men to join the society. (Applause.) Mr. Collier (who was received with loud applause), • expressed the delight he felt at being present at that celebration, and said he had known the Duke's Club throughout the whole of his connection with the Coin- • pany, but he never previously looked so clear into its affairs, or was so well able to judge of its prosperous and • beneficial character, as he had been on that occasion. Their finances were in a very sound condition. They had in their capital account more money per head of membership than ever they had before. It was true that on one or two occasions there had been £3OO more in the Bank, but there had been more of them to participate in it; and this must be gratifying, because it showed that they were working on a ' sound and self-sustaining basis, and there was no fear that either now, or in the future, that they would ' not be able to pay the sums which they proposed to pay in those emergencies for which they professed to provide. It was a concrete example of an abstract principle, which was well worth employment at all times, that it is everyone's duty to bear each others burdens; and that was practically what they did in the Duke's ' Club. Some got more and some got less,but it was those who had the misfortune to be ill who got the most. This was the true principal of co-operation whether it be for good of business or for the good of social life. They had his sympathy in everything they did of this nature. (Hear, hear.) He was only too glad to see the employes of the Bridgewater Undertaking considering principles and modes of actions which should benefit themselves and their fellow workers in every way. (Applause.) Flourishing as the club was now, he should like the mem- bership to be augumented and to draw within its circle every man who was employed about the Bridgewater , Undertaking; and he hoped the young men would profit by Mr. Meadowcroft's advice. Alluding to the age of the , club, Mr. Collier said the Bridgewater had always been noted for its traditions with the past. The Bridge- water Canal was the pioneer of the great movement for waterways all over the country. The engineer, • Mr. Brindley, was a hard-working man whose sheer • force of intellect, and whose good judgment, enabled • the Duke of Bridgewater to carry to a successful termination this Bridgewater Canal, which had • been the pattern for so many more. This was not all he did by any means, for he either:made, or design- ed, 400 or 500 miles of canal through the country. In . later years canals had been put in the background, ow- . ing in a great measure to the investing public giving ; their attention to railways, but now the Bridgewater • Canal was associated with the great movement of making a ship canal, which was a great stride ahead of any- thing they had at the present time. They hoped it would 5 not only be a benefit to Manchester, but that Runcorn would see an iinmense improvement, and that those who sat there would participate in the increased pros- - perity. At the present time, their engineer, Mr. Wis- wall, upon whom he placed the greatest dependence, and of whose skill they lad some experience—he was almost a second Brindley—(applause)—Mr. Wiswall was engaged in designing a very large extension of the Runcorn Docks which they hoped to see developed in a short time. (Applause). He had no doubt they had ' expected something of the kind. The crowded state of the docks, and the difficulty of conducting business, • must have been as evident to them as it had been to ' the agent, Mr. Meadowcroft, who had had to battle with the difficulty caused by the congested state of the docks. ' The further ships could get inland and the better it was for themselves. That was the principal which ; underlay the making of the Ship Canal, and Runcorn at ' the present time, and probably for all time, would be •the furthest point that vessels with tall masts could reach without meeting with an overhead obstruction. in ' the shape of Runcorn Bridge. The Bridgewater under- taking intended to be the first in the field by making ; docks to receive these ships, and they hoped for a great , increase of business, an increase of prosperity to the 1 town, and a more regularancl extended field of operations for all classes of trade, and for the hands they employed directly. (Loud applause.) Ile thought they would all see that prosperity realised, and when they had such another meeting as that ten years hence, he trusted the Duke's Club would be three times its present size, and , prospering as it had already done in the past. (Ap- plause.)

6 The Chairman said he was sure that Mr. Collier was speaking authoritatively as to the extension which they might shortly expect, and he moved "That we, the members of the Duke's Club,wish every prosperity to the Manchester Ship Canal Company in the large under- taking in which they are engaged." He coupled with the resolution the names of the Chairman and Deputy Chairman (Lord Egerton and Sir Joseph Lee), and asked Mr. Collier to convey it to those gentlemen.—Mr. Elias Davies seconded the proposition, which was carried unanimously.—Mr. Collier said he should have the great- est pleasure in carrying out their request.

him, but he could not tell them how he appreciated the feelings expressed in the address. They must all know that the secretary of the club had sometimes a good deal to try his patience—(hear, hear)—but he was glad that he had the confidence of the members of the Club, and especially of the Committee that he met month after month. He had always striven to do his best for the Club, for the reason that he believed he was thus helping his fellowmen in the struggle of life,—(hear, hear)—and anything he could do in that way he was only too pleased to do. He was much obliged to all concerned for the present, and he sincerely hoped that the future of the Club would be more prosperous than in the past. (Ap- plause.)

_ , Songs were given by Messrs. J. Pownall, J. Gates, D. Billington„ Wilkinson, Hoxworth, Master A. Done, Miss L. Johnson, and Miss K. Done. Mr. Wickenden gave a reading, and Master Eden a recitation. Mr. C. Le Couteur ably accompanied on the piano.

div.head: AN INTERESTING PRESENTATION.
div.p: AN INTERESTING PRESENTATION.

Mr. Done said the Committee had asked him to un- dertake the pleasing duty of presenting this illuminated address to their worthy secretary, Mr. Simister. It needed no words of his to commend to them his excellent character, and he read the address as folloWsi—" Dear Sir,—We, the members of the Duke's Club, Runcorn, avail ourselves of this opportunity, the centenary of our club, to present you with this small token of our appre- ciation of the very able, effective, and courteous manner in which you have, during a period extending over 33 years, fulfilled the duties of Secretary, and we hereby desire to express our opinion that the flourishing state of our club is in no small degree due to the advice and as- sistance you have given to the Executive Committee. We trust that you will be long spared, and that health may be given you to continue in the position you have so worthily filled for so many years." Mr. Done was frequently interrupted by applause.—Mr. Moadowcroft added his testimony to Mr. Simister's good qualities. He spared neither time nor energy in working for the benefit of Club, and he was most courteous and attentive to the members who had occasion to go to him. If ever there was an address deserved Mr. Simister deserved that address. (Applause.)—Dr. Mangan, as one of the medical officers, said Mr. Simister was always most courteons and agreeable.—Mr. Simister, in reply, I remarked that the present was a very great surprise to i

div.head: WIFE MURDER AT LEEDS.
div.p: WIFE MURDER AT LEEDS.

At the West Riding Assizes, Leeds, on Monday, before Mr. Justice Charles, Samuel Harrison, 30, a Polish Jew, who has worked as a slipper maker in the town fer some seven cr eight years, was arraigned for the wilful mur- der of his wife Dora. Toe defence was that the prisoner was insane at the time he committed the deed. The jury found him guilty, and he was Sentenced to death.

div.head: TWO MEN SHOT.-INQUEST.
div.p: TWO MEN SHOT.-INQUEST.

The inquest on the two men who were shot dead at Kingsland a few days ago, was concluded on Saturday. The jury found that "the deceased died from the mortal effects of a pistol shot, fired by Walter Alfred Hargan," which the Coroner entered as a verdict of wilful murder, notwithstanding that two of the jury protested that a verdict of "manslaughter" or "justifiable homicide " ought to have been recorded.
MURDER AND SUICIDE AT SHEFFIELD.

A shocking tragedy occurred on Saturday morning, at Eckington, near Sheffield. A collier named Edward French, who had been living apart from his wife, went to see her on Saturday, and later on screams were heard from the house. The woman's brother went to see what was the matter, and found Mrs. French lying on the floor with her throat cut from ear to ear. She died im- mediately afterwards. French left the house, and after telling two men what hehad done, went and laid himself on the Midland Railway, in front of a passenger train, which passed over him, severing his head from his body.

div.head: SUPPRESSION OF SLAVERY IN ZANZIBAR.
div.p: THE SUPPRESSION OF SLAVERY IN ZANZIBAR.

A mass meeting of Arabs was held in Zanzibar on Sunday, at which, after some discussion, in the course of which a number of those present expressed dissent, it was agreed to accept the Sultan's anti-slavery decree. On Monday, however, a mob collected and tore down a copy of the decree which had been posted up at the Custom House. The Sultan promptly had the notice re- placed, and the ringleaders arrested. 'Me mob then dispersed and quiet was restored. The Sultan, who dis- played great firmness, and is fully master of the situa- tion, is determined to inflict severe punishment upon the guilty parties.

div.head: LORD SALISBURY AND MR. O'BRIEN.
div.p: LORD SALISBURY AND MR. O'BRIEN.

At the Holborn Restaurant, on Wednesday, night Mr. W. O'Brien, M.P., and Mrs. O'Brien were entertained at a banquet in celebration of their marriage. The dinner was intended as a tribute of respect from the Irishmen of London to the hon. member for North-east Cork and his bride.

The Press Association learns that in going to the ban- quet Mr. O'Brien was served with notice that Lord Salis- bury has instructed Messrs. Hayes and Sons, Solicitors, Dublin, to proceed against him in that country to recover Lord Salisbury's costs in O'Brien v. Salisbury, unless Lord Salisbury's claim is satisfied before the 11th of August.

div.head: MANSION HOUSE BANQUET.
div.p: MANSION HOUSE BANQUET.

The Lord Mayor gave his usual banquet toiler Majesty's Ministers on Wednesday night. Lord Salisbury, reply- ing on behalf of the Ministry, said that never during the past five years had the appearance of the world pre- sented so uninteresting a complexion as it did at present. It was uninteresting because it was so eminently pacific, and this was in consequence of all the nations working in the interests of blessed peace. Afric% was another proof of the strong growing hold of peace on the intellect of the world. The arrangements made there had this one solid practical effect—they had removed the possible causes of quarrel from those members of the res- pective nations who, on account of their very adven- turous, gallant, and self devoted life, were too apt to push with undue ferocity the claims of their respective countries against each other. Great Britian had:been avoiding a cause of quarrel between the nations •of Europe and contributing her quota to the glorious:cause of peace. For cther matters, he might say that nothing in the course of their adminis- tration had k ivert more satisfaction to the Government than the steady progress in the direction of financial equilibrium and the growing prosperity which it has been their privilege to restore in Egypt. The Govern- ment would be compromising every chanceof securing to posterity the great advantages they had produced,if they allowed any consideration to induce them to withdraw their hand from the task which events had cast upon them. He thought the Government might claim to have fulfilled the mandate of the nation in regard to Ireland, , which was now more orderly, contented, and prosperous , than when they took it in hand. Re complained of the growing habit of talk in the House of Commons, but trusted that in the end obstruction would be defeated.

div.head: GERMAN EMPEROR'S VISIT TO THE QUEEN.
div.p: THE GERMAN EMPEROR'S VISIT TO THE QUEEN.

In anticipation of the arrival of the German Emperor on Monday, Cowes Roads were crowded with yachts of all tonnage, and as the weather was delightfully fine, all promised well for the reception of the Imperial guest. The Imperial yacht Hohenzollern hove in sight at ten o'clock off Osborne Towers, and the Queen signalled "Welcome." As the Hohenzollern entered Cowes Roads, the guardship, H.M.S. Volage, fired a royal salute. At the same tune all the yachts dressed. The Alberta arrived back at Trinity Pier at a quarter to eleven, and the Royal party from Osborne House drove down to the landing stage to await the arrival of the Emperor. The party included Prince Christian, Prince Henry of Batten- berg, Prince Alfred of Edinburgh, -and the Marquis of Lorne. The Princess of Wales and daughters were con- veyed in the yacht Osborne. The Alberta had previously steamed out to the Emperor's yacht, and his Majesty was welcomed by the Prince of Wales and the Duke of Connaught, in attendance on whom were Admiral Efornby, Captain Tracy, and Captain Markham, and the Imperial Party steamed through the roads to the Queen's private landing stage in one of the royal barges, and as they left the Hohenzollern the guns of the Volage boomed forth another salute; this time answered by the guns of the Irene, the convoy of the Imperial yacht. The Emperor landed precisely at half-past eleven, Mr. R. W. Beale, Imperial Vice-Consul at Portsmouth, awaiting him.

His Majesty had been preceded ashore by his brilliant staff passing from the barge over the deck of the Alberta. His Majesty, the Prince of Wales, and suite were receiv!.d with much cheering by the assembled people in the small crafts, and on the waterside the Emperor, in exchanging greetings with the Princess Christian, remarked "I am delighted to get to England again." The Emperor and Royal party then entered the carriages awaiting them and drove to Osborne house. There a guard of honour of the Rifle Brigade was drawn up. The Emperor was received by the Queen, the Princess of Wales and daughters and the Duchess of Edinburgh, the band first playing die German and then the English National Anthems. The Emperor, who looked exceedingly well, was attired as a British admiral. Luncheon was served at two o'clock. The Emperor's celebrated band played on the terrace from two till four o'clock before the Queen and the Emperor. The Queen was delightod with the performance. Shortly after four o'clock the Emperor, accompanied by Prince Henry of Prussia and General Duplat, in uniform, droveput in an open carriage with grey horses and outriders, and paid a visit to the Duchess of Edinburgh at Osborne Cottage. Subsequently his Majesty went for a long drive, returning to Osborne shortly before seven o'clock. A grand dinner was given at nine o'clock in two large marquee tents, the Queen being presept. On Tuesday the German Emperor was present, on board the Prince of Wales' schooner the Aline, at the Royal Yacht Squadron Regatta, at Cowes, and afterwards dined with the members of the club.

The Emperor ot Germany was out riding, early on Wednesday morning, at Cowes. The weather there con- tinues brilliant. His Imperial Majesty left Cowes on hoard the Alberta, with the Prince of Wales, the Dukes of Edinburgh and Connaught, Prince Christian, and staff, I for Eastney, to inspect tLe Royal Marine Artillery, and witness the new mode of attack. His Imperial Majesty was received by Lord Wolseley and other officers, and partook of luncheon with the Prince of Wales at Moss House, Eastney, afterwards witnessing the operations. On Thursday, the German Emperor, accompanied by the Prince of Wales, the Duke of Connaught, and Prince Henry of Prussia, paid a visit to Portsmouth Dockyard, which he insnected with great interest in every part. Among those who received the Emperor were Lord George Hamilton, Sir Leicester Smyth, Admiral Sir E. Corn- merell, and a number of other high officials. After lunch at Government House, the Emperor witnessed torpedo practice at Whale Island, and returned to Cowes and dined with the Queen in the evening.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

CRICKET. Dr. W. G. Grace has lately been playing in a style worthy of the "champion " cricketer, and the last three matches in which he has engaged have raised his average very considerably. A cricket enthusiast has sent to the " Sportsman " an elaborate " return " showing the num- ber of runs the champion has made in the last quarter of a century and the number of wickets he has captured in first class matches. It seems that the Doctor has played 843 completed innings and scored 36,197 runs, which is an average of more than 42 runs per innings ; and has " taken ' by way of recreation from the sterner business of batting, no fewer than 2,263 wickets. Twice he has scored more than 300 runs ' • seven times more than 200; land 86 times more than 100 in an innings.

At Grimsby. in 1876, when playing against a more than average 22, Mr. Grace went to the wicket on the Monday morning and carried out his bat on the Wednes- day afternoon for 400 runs. The fielders " expected to get him out every day," as was said of a famous old Sheffield cricketer on one occasion when he had taken a lease of the wicket ; but all their efforts were vain, and the future champion was credited with the greatest number of runs ever made in a public match. And now, after he has had all these accumulated thousands of runs to his credit, it is as true of the champion as it was eleven years ago, when Lord Charles Russell said of him: "Looking at his playing, I have never been able to tell whether he is playing a losing or a winning game. I have never seen the slightest lukewarmness or inertness in him in the field. Should anyone want to know how he plays cricket, let them look at him playing one ball. tVhether on the offensive or defensive, Mr. Grace puts every muscle into it, from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. And just as he plays one ball he plays the game."

A Manchester scribe says the " power " in the Austra- lians of which Mr. Murdoch spoke at Leicester is some- what like General Trochu's famous plan for scattering the German hosts—it is undisclosed. They won a victory over Kent, but were beaten by a team representing—in a sense—the Lyric Club. In this encounter Blackham was not engaged, and the colonials suffered some loss on that account; but we do not believe the result would have been in their favour had the famous wicket keeper been 'playing. The Australians held a slight advantage on the first innings; but Ulyett, Stoddart, bnd O'Brien retrieved the position in their second attempt, and a really well-contested struggle ended in a victory for the club by nearly 100 runs. Mold was very destructive in the second innings, and Barrett gave another exhibition of his fine power as a batsman.

A provincial contemporary asserts that Turner, the Australian bowler, has been asking for £4OO a year, guaranteed for four years, as the price of transferring his services to an English county. Both Gloucestershire and Middlesex, it is said, have been competing for the services of Turner and Ferris, but nothing has yet come of the negotiations. The rule which requires a two years' residence as a qualification for a place in a county eleven has doubtless operated well in this instance, for few counties would saddle themselves with a four years' liability for several hundreds a year for the sake of a bowler, '.hose value in two years' time is quite proble- matical.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

The Harrog.ate camp was 473.-Prened as usual last Friday, and by Saturday night things began to look ship-shape, fresh arrivals continuing to pour in from all parts throughout the day. Many of the tents are, as usual, highly decorated with flowers and bunting, that of the president, Mr. M. D. Rucker, taking the palm. As a social institution the Harrogate camp stands high in the cycling world, claiming as it does adherents from +Edin- burgh to London, and almost from Holyhead to Hull. Saturday's racing gained éclat from the presence of F. J. Osmond, who, along with L. Stroud, the Oxonian, occu- pies a tent not inappropriately styled " Maida Vale Stable," after the situation of Paddington track, on which both men have ridden some well deserved vic- torics both in championship and other races.

div.head: ATHLETICS.
div.p: ATHLETICS.

The sports of the li;l7r-i-n—g-iOriotball Club were be- yond all doubt a very great success, and as the officials had made every conceivable arrangement to make them so, the success was in every way deserved. Consider- ing the quantity of rain that fell before the present spell of fine weather set in, the ground was in very good con- dition. It was satisfactory to notice that the duty of signalling the numbers of the starters and the winners was carefully carried out.

The large crowd that lined the enclosure took an evi- dent interest in the various events, but there was a pleasant absence of rowdyism. There was not, either, much shouting, which is apt to become rather annoying when carried too far—both to the bystanders and to the competitors whom it is intended to encourage. Altogether the meeting was a model one.

div.head: DESPERATE ATTEMPT AT WIFE
div.p: DESPERATE ATTEMPT AT WIFE
MURDER

At Bolton Police Court, on Tuesday, James Cunning- ham, a Venetian blindmaker, was remanded on a charge of attempting to murder his wife. On Tuesday after- noon, according to the prosecution, the prisoner, after deliberately sharpening 4 large knife, made a determined attempt to murder the woman in the streets by stabbing her, and was only prevented from doing so by the crowd. The woman lies at the infirmary, and is not yet reported out of danger, having lost a large quantity of blood.

div.head: LORD CROSS AT STAMFORD.
div.p: LORD CROSS AT STAMFORD.

Lord Cross, speaking on Thursday night at Stam- ford, said that a Government must be judged by its administration as well as byits legislation. In their foreign policy the Government had kept in view the peace of Europe. There had been difficulties with other nations, but these troubles had now almost disappeared, and England stood higher in the esti- mation of the world than she had done for genera- tions. She now had the power as well as the will to demand that the peace of t.urope should not be dis- turbed. In India much good had been done by two excellent Viceroys. The north-west frontier had been absolutely defended against all corners. Eng- land was now more prosperous financially than ever before during this generation. In future, under the existing code, there would be real education in primary schools instead of crammivq. Touching upon legislation, he said that the C Act was not directed against honest men, who need not even know there was such an Act. The defences had been improved, and the coaling stations abroad pro- tected. The Land Purchase and Tithes Bills must and would be passed next session.

div.head: -4--- A RADICAL MANIFESTO.
div.p: -4--- A RADICAL MANIFESTO.

On Saturday evening the Metropolitan Radical Federa- tion issued a manifesto, in :which it is stated that "the following preliminary reforms are ripe for adoption. They are essential steps towards the complete emancipa- tion of labour, and, as such, should be urged upon all candidates for any public representative office. Members of trade unions, working-men's clubs, and all wage earners are therefore strongly recommended to submit the subjoined questions to every candidate seeking popu- lar election (whether for the House of Commons, County Council, School Board, or any local body), and to refuse their support to those who will not give satis- factory replies :—Are you in favour of (1) The exten- sion of the franchise, both Parliamentary and municipal, to every adult, and the abolition of all plural voting? (2) The continuous and successive registration of all electors by public officers, and the shortening of the qualifying period of residence to not more than three months? (3) Payment of all public representa- tives (Parliamentary, muxicipal, School Board, or local) and of all necessary election expenses? (4) The second ballot? (5) The abolition of any property qualification for all public offices? Taxation and Land Reforms.—Will you vote for (1) The abolition of all taxes on tea, coffee, cocoa, and fruit? (2) The taxa- tion of all ground rents and values for all public pur- poses, with a view to land nationalisation ? Industrial Reforms. Will you support (1) The extension of the Factory and Workshops Act to all employers of women and children? (2) The registration and inspection of all workshops, and a large increase in the number of in- spectors composed of practical men and women? (3) The reduction of the hours of labour to a maximum of forty-eight hours per week in all national and municipal public departments? (4) An Eight Hours Bill, with trade option, on the lines suggested by the Fabian Society? (5) The direct employment of labour by pub- lic bodies whenever practicable ? (8) The insertion of clauses in all contracts for Government or other public works or supplies providing against sub-contracting, for the payment of trade union rates of wages, and the 1 maintenance of trade union rules? (7) The construc- tion and maintenance of dwelling-houses under the direct control of the municipality ? (8) A reform of the poor law, providing for a more just and generous treatment of the temporarily employed, the children, the aged, and infirm ? (9) A graduatcd and differentiated income tax? Educational Reforms.—Will you vote for (1) The abolition of fees in an public elementary schools and at continuation evening classes? (2) For the restora- tion of all educational endowments, and the provison by that means of technical schools and of a large number of secondary scholarships ?"

div.head: IN THE FRUIT COUNTRY. I
div.p: IN THE FRUIT COUNTRY. I
BY F. T. BIRCHILL.

West, south-west, and south of London stretches the fruit Country; where " the common places of agriculture," wheat, and mangold, wurtzel, oats and turnips have for once yielded up half their terri- tory to its extravagances and whims. The straw- berry plant, brimming over from the garden patches, has usurped the fields, and its trim rows retire only in orderly files left and right from the stony high- ways, melting seemingly in the distance into a mass of close cropped verdure.

It is a pretty rather than a picturesque country; a garden, ruled by strict nineteenth century prin- ciples of profit and loss, yet with its many quaint old world corners and spots of almost idyllic beauty. There are few more charming or romantic villages throughout England than these of the Kentish fruit country, streaks of russet and grey in a setting of emerald green, now wide awake after a long win- ter slumber, and showing at their brightest. Viewing them in the evening just now there are many who would, perhaps, r.refer the quiet stagnation of the hamlets of the Midlands. Yet in the daytime they are quiet enough in all conscience. No voice is heard save from an occasional group of dirty children left behind by mothers busy at work among the fruit, who scramble restlessly among the patched tents and gaudy caravans of their people, or clamour noisely from the roadside gutter for pennies from the passers by. Only a sullen murmur, now in a high now in a low key,is wafted from the surround- ing strawberry fields, where, in the distance, like flies upon a trim green tablecloth, men, women, and elder children are rapidly filling the heavy baskets which will to-night go down the road for the early market. No sound comes from the sckool-house,for the children are in the fields,while the master takes ' a well-earned holiday far away from his charges. He looked anxious, however, as he left, as though in these days of per centages and Government grants a fruit picking holiday was not altogether an unmixed blessing. Not se the blacksmith, who finds trade brisk as he is pleased to tell you, for waggons break down frequently now, and his aid is wanted with ricketty gipsy vans and nondescript spring carts, either of which rarely complete a journey without mishap. "Not that you gets much out of that,'' he says, "for gipsy folk, whether rich or poor, drives a hard bargain," and he throws a glance of good humoured contempt at a trio of these same folk lounging into the taproom of the Rising Sun over the way. Perhaps it is only as afternoon draws into even- ing that one appreciates best the charm of the fruit country. The light becomes richer and more tender as the sun moves from its meridian to the west. A stronger perfume is shed from the honeysuckle, the woodbine, and coloured meadow sweets, while from the disturbed strawberry beds is wafted the sweet scent of the fruit. It hangs, too, in the wake of the market wagons crawling down the road to- wards London, and in comparison with its subtle intoxication the fragrance of new mown hay is for- gotten, and one wonders no longer at the perpetual drowsiness of the waggoners on their lofty seats. But in the villages, as the night draws near, the charm is broken. Gradually the public-howes until their customers overflow into the road. Dept- ford and Spitalfields have come into the country, and every bar-room is packed to its utmost capacity —men and women drinking shoulder to shoulder in an atmosphere as bad as that of any East-end haunt. Barn and outhouse having become for the nonce a home for the "foreigners," as the natives are careful to style their guests, are occupied by a miscellaneous and often disreputable crew; while from each lately deserted encampment, arises with the blue smoke and pungent odour of burning wood, a babel of voices in every known key. A distance away this is not an unpleasing picture; but stray not too closely. Its effect ag a picture is for dis- tance only, and is apt to be lost if one desires a nearer view.

Yet there are other frescoes which admit of a closer examination. One realises here in these evenings, first and for the time, perhaps, for how much of English love of Nature, of sport, and of the open air, are the long twilights responsible. The day is not ended though its labour is done; so the village cricket club is practising in the paddock; the cottage gardens are dotted with bending figures; and a healthy al fresco life is going on all along the street. One is not surprised either to find the religious element at work. A Church Army officer is running a stirring service in an encampment over the hill, and from the platform under the walnut trees the Converted Gipsy harangues a patient crowd of adherents. The curious can buy her story at the gate for a penny, if they wish, telling of her father, " asentleman gipsy " with "a hankering after high society," the consequence of having fallen in love with a Leicestershire squire's daughter," who, after a clandestine engagement, had run away to become the mistress of his caravan, forfeiting thereby all claim to the home of her childhood and her father's house."

Slowly the deeper twilight closes in. It is never quite dark these summer nights in sunny Kent. Even at midnight a pale twilight reigns, and there is a luminous glimmer in the western sky, reflected where the pond lies deep in the willow shade. The gipsy's audience disperses after a hymn. An occa- sional gunshot across the deserted fields tells that the bird scarer is still at his post, though the birds retired an hour ago. About the Rising Sun a noisy crowd still lingers, but in the encampments move- ment has at last subsided, and the quiet of the lanes is broken only by the creaking of a late market waggon, for it is work again by three to- morrow.

Midnight strikes from the church tower, and gradually the night wanes towards the north as a faint, grey light creeps into the .east. The bats have ceased to7flit across the sky, and the night jar is no longer heard. Sowewhere at hand a cock gives warning of the approaching day. Slowly the cold dawn brightens; the meadows arise out of the mist, the birds wake again. At the first gunshots echoing over the silent fields there is a hurried stir among the tattered tents and gaudy vans showing in such clear relief against the clear skv. .A long line of workers—men, women and children—file through the open gate. Another day is born, even as all
" the dslighters of the sun Dance into light, to die into the shade.

div.head: SHIP CANAL DISASTER.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL DISASTER.

At Chester on Saturday Thomas Dunbabbin, the driver of the engine on which three people were killed in the collision on the Ship Canal a few days ago, was before the magistrates on a charge of manslaughter. Evidence was given to the effect that the prisoner was in charge of what is known as a "mail" engine that the drivers of the engines could see each other three- quarters of a mile apart, and that it was the duty of the driver of the Rhymney, if he saw that a " mail " train was coming towards him, to stop his engine or to go back. The magistrates held that there was no prima-facie case against Dunbabbin, and discharged him.

div.head: VERDICT OF THE CORONER'S JURY.
div.p: VERDICT OF THE CORONER'S JURY.

Mr. Churton, Chester, district coroner, resumed the inquest at Ellesmere Port, on Monday morning, respect- ing the death of Robert Ernest Williams (of Chester), James Benstock and Walter Bennett, who were killed by the railway collision on the canal the previous Monday. Further evidence was given by Mr. Jones, superintend- ent of the Ince section of the canal works, G. Francis, Frederick Nixon, and others.—The Coroner, in summing up, said he did not believe a juryman in the room could come to the conclusion that either of the men were responsible for the accident. He deprecated the employ- ment of boys of tender years, but knew that the officials were often deceived by the parents in their ages, because they wanted their lads to earn money. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death, and added the following riders :—We find that the death of these men took place in consequence of a collision between the engine Deal and the truck in front of the engine Rhymney, and we think the accident due (1) to the engine Deal being turned out from Ince with the knowledge that another engine would be despatched later on. (2) The fact of the Rhymne y being turned out insufficiently equipped, not having a rope runner or practical fireman. (3) The fact of the signals not being in use at the time of the accident. Under these circumstances we think that geater caution should have been exercised by the drivers of both engines. We consider that no persons should be allowed to ride on the engines except those in charge.

div.head: ARGENTINE CRISIS.
div.p: THE ARGENTINE CRISIS.

RESIGNATION OF THE PRESIDENT. AUGUST 6, 4.20 P.M.—Dr. Juarez Celman has beencom• pelled to resign the Presidency of the Argentine Repub: tic, and Dr. Pellegrini, the Vice-President, has assume(' the supreme power. It is expected that General Mitre and Senores Eduardo Costa, Gumstiago, and Levalle win enter the new Cabinet. Public confidence is reviving. The premium on gold is now 170. 5.50 P.M.—The Argentine Chambers have not Yee accepted the resignation of President Celman, and corn- plications are apprehended. Great excitements Pre" yails. Penis, AUGUST 6.—A telegram from Buenos Ayres/ despatched at eight o'clock yesterday evening.states tli the Argentine Senate has refused to accept the resignatio of President Celman, who has consequently withdrawn it. It is reported in Parliamentary circle that the new Cabinet will comprise Senores Levalle, Costa, irojoyen, Lastra, and Agote. Another telegram despatched from Buenos Ayres half-past nine this morning states that the Ministent combination which was regarded as probable, has now definitively fallen through. The " Times " Buenos Ayres correspondent telegraPh,: ing on Thursday, describing the effect of Dr. Celman resignation, says a pall seems to have been lifted frcee the city. There are popular rejoicings all over the city Doctors Hopes and Delaville, the leaders of the Vaiett civica, are receiving proofs of esteem and respect on n. sides. The new Ministry is still unformed.

div.p: LIBRARY AND MUSEUM.
NATURAL lIISTORY IN ELEMENTARY SCIIODLS. _ _

The three delegates who represented the Warring- ton Museum Committee at the recent meeting of the Aluseums' Association, held in Liverpool, were Councillor Henry Roberts, Mr. Linnmus Greening, and Mr. Charles Madeley, and in their report which Was adopted by the Town Council on Tuesday even- these gentlemen mention that, Mr. Chard, of Liverpool, read a very interesting account of the admirable system in force at the Liverpool Museum, for circulating Natural History specimens amongst the Elementary schools in the town. It appears that a number of portable cabinets has been pre- pared, each cabinet containing a series of specimens carefully selected, to illustrate the characteristics Of some group of animals, or other branch of natural science. The objects are mounted so as to bear handling by a class of children, and packed into the cabinet in such a way as to withstand the wear and tear of carriage from one school to another. The result after six years experience is declared to be Satisfactory. The cabinets and their contents were exhibited, and were inspected by the delegates with Very great interest. THE DISPOSAL OF THE LATE MR. BEAMONT'S BEQUEST. The Warrington Town Council at its meeting, on Tues- day considered a recommendation of the Art Sub-Com- mittee (Alderman Davies, Councillor Monks, and Mr. Owen) of the Library and Museum Committee,as to what -disposition should be made of the sum of £450, left by the will ot the late Chairman, Mr. Beamont, to be applied t)wards the support and increase of the Art Gallery." The Sub-Committee recommends that Mr. Beamont's be- quest be set aside as a fund to be used for the systematic development of the Art Department of the Museum as an educational instrument. That is to say, that the aim in I ' expending it should be more particularly the provision of I: objects likely to assist directly in the acquisition of a : taste for art by persons as yet uninstructed, rather than Stich as appeal chiefly to a taste already acquired. Look- ing to the actual visitors to the Museum, the Sub-Com- -1 ?Mace feels that in respect of a large majority of them there is greater need for some attempt to direct them in ; an endeavour to learn to appreciate works of art than there is to provide an art exhibition for those who al- , - ready feel the desire for it, and have the cultivation necessary to profit by it. It is admitted that greater Progress can be made towards the proposed end by means of reproductions of acknowledged masterpieces ta:,han by the purchase of original works of art. WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB SPORTS.

Favoured with good weather, and safeguarded by gool management, the annual August Bank Holiday sports in connection with the Warrington Football Club were a marked success, a large number of people paying for admission, and going away well satisfied at the close with the value received for their money. Over .£l4O was taken at the gates. The meeting was the sixth annual one of the club, and a very attractive programme bad, as usual, been arranged. There were a good many competitors from a distance, whose entries were a source of additional attraction, but the Warrington Contingent of athletes acquitted themselves remark- I ably well. A deal of interest was taken in the bicycle ' races, several of the competitors riding pneumatic-tyred machines, for which, however, they were considerably h indicapped. Fair, of Warrington, won his heat in the tAO miles on a pneumatic. By permission of the officers, the band of the Ist Volunteer Battalion (P.W.V.) Crompton (Runcorn) was a good second. There was a struggle for third position betwem Knott and Webster, and victory rested with the former.

Haynes fell after going 100 yards; a second man fell the same distance further on ; and two others dropped out directly afterwards. PRIMROSE LEAGUE DEMONSTRATION AT APPLE TON PARK.

A demonstration in connection with the Warring- ton and Appleton Habitations of the Primrose League was held in the grounds of Appleton Hall on Saturday. There were athletic sports in connection with each habitation; the Walton band played for dancing; tea was provided in a large tent; the St. James' Amateur Christy Minstrels gave an amusing entertainment, and those fond of politics had an opportunity of listening to speeches from Mr. Egerton, M.P., and others. The day's proceedings com- menced about half-past two with amateur athletic sports in connection with the Warrington Habitation, when prizes to the value of £2O were competed for. The races were well-contested throughout. The winners were :- 100 yards handicap: first heat, W. C. Litton; second heat, J. Holmes; third heat, H. Worsley ; fourth heat, J. Cross; fifth heat, dead heat between, R. Bickerstaff and George Ratcliffe, but the competitors " tossed " for posi- tion, Ratcliffe winning. Sixth heat, H. H. Evans. Final, Ist prize, W. C. Litton, tea service and tray; 2nd prize, H. Worsley, case of carvers • 3rd prize, J. Cross, biscuit jar. Two hundred yards handicap: Ist heat, 1, W. C. Litton; 2, R. Bickerstaff. Second heat, 1, J. Holmes; 2, A. Barnes. Third heat, 1, S. Mather; 2, J. Jolley. Final, Ist prize, case of tea spoons, W. C. Litton; 2nd prize, knife box, R. Bickerstaff ; and 3rd prize, case of nut trackers, J. Holmes. Holmes and Mather ran a dead heat for the third prize, which, after tossing, was won by the former.—Eight hun- dred and eighty yards handicap: Ist prize, marble timepiece, F. Hampson ; 2nd prize, cruet, W. Price; 3rd prize, gentleman's dressing case, G. R. Williamson.—Obstacle race: Ist prize, tea pot, A. Foden ; 2nd prize, a hot water jug, T. Locker; and 3rd prize, brushes, &c., H. Green. Mr. J. E. Warren (hon. secretary of the Warrington Football Club), officiated as handicapper and starter; Mr. T. Pemberton as clerk of the course; and Messrs. J. Smethurst, J. Coxon, and S. Reynolds as judges. The same afternoon sports were held in connection with the Appleton Habita- tion, the successful competitors being as follows :-100 yards (men's race), 1, F. Broadey ; 2, Cole; 3, Isaac Hamblett. 100 yards (boys' race), 1, G. Risley ; 2, E. Oakes; 3, I. Vernon. Obstacle race (men's), 1, Davies; 2, J. Smith ; and 3, Vernon. Money prizes were awarded. The Sports Committee consisted of Messrs. Charles Marson, Colin Maclver, Logan-Wright, J. Ellison, F. Timperley, and W. Shaw. Between the hours of four and six o'clock a substantial tea was provided in a largo marquee, and from 1,300 to 1,400 persons partook of it. The caterer was Mr. T. 0. Speakman, of the Saracen's Head Hotel, Wilderspool. Commencing at six o'clock, a political meeting was held in the open air at the rear of the house, the chair being occupied by Mr. Lyon, and among the audience were the Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton, M.P., Mr. Robert Pierpoint, Mrs. Lyon (Ruling Councillor of the Appleton Habitation). Mrs. Reynolds (Ruling Councillor of the Warrington Habitation), Mrs. Logan-Wright, Mr. Logan-Wright, Mr. Charles Marson, Mr. C. H. Wood, Mr. John Hampson, Miss Ireland Black- burn°, Miss Lyon, Miss M. Lyon, Miss F. ALAN DE TATTON EGERTON, M.P., then made a speech in which he referred to various political topics. An address was also given by Mr. R. div.head: LORD AND LADY D UNLO.
div.p: LORD AND LADY D UNLO.

A representative of the " Irish Times " has had an interview with Lady Dunlo at the Shelbourne Hotel, Dublin. In reply to the reporter, she stated that since the trial Lord Dunlo had called on Mr. Wertheimer, and assured him that he did not bear him any and expressed a hoped that Mr. Wertheimer would forgive I him for having dragged him into the recent proceedings. He regretted the whole matter very much, and asked Mr. Wertheimer to make friends with him. Mr. Wertheimer met Lord Dunlo in the same spirit, and Lord Dunlo having expressed a desire to see Lady Dunlo, it was ar- ranged that they should meet at the Café Royal and have luncheon together. Accordingly they met there. and Lord Dunlo expressed his regret that the action had ever been brought, and said that as far the part that he took in it he was really forced into it. The result was that they made up their differences and subsequently dined together, the party including Mr. Augustus Harris. On Saturday night they occupied a box at the Comedy Theatre, and subsequently Mr. Harris entertained them at supper at th 3 Continental. Lady Dunlo added" lam very happy at the result of the trial. I knew that I was going to win. Lord Dunlo is delighted with the verdict. He is coming over here, and will be here on Wednes- day." To the question whether Lord Dunlo approved of her remaining on the stage, Lady Dunlo said he would like her to r,etire from it, but she was unwilling to do so. She would not again appear in music-halls. She understood from Lord Dunlo that Lord Clancarty wanted him to go to South Africa, and Lord Dunlo asked her to accompany him, but she was unwilling to do so, as she believed she would achieve success in her profession, and she had now an engagement with Mr. Harris for two years.

POLITICS AT PENKETIL Sir,—ln the report of Mr. John Atherton's annual trip, it was omitted to be stated that several widows of Liberals—who were left in the cold on the occasion of the Parochial trip to Southport—went to Chester at the expense of Mr. G. Broadhurst. Hitherto it has been the custom to provide for all the widows in Penketh without respect to the political creed of their departed husbands. But Mr. P. Pownall, who had the management of the widows' trip, evidently determined that the widows of Liberals should suffer for the sins of their husbands, and so, but for the kindness of Mr. Broadhurst, they would have been left entirely in the cold this summer. Yours, &c., A LIBERAL.
HINTS ON CYCLING:

_ Sir,—Since the advent of the Safety Bicycle, cycling has increased to an enormous extent, not only among the young but also those of mature age. Perhaps a few hints to the young ridersw ill not be out of place here .While the Safety has many advantages, it still lacks the grace and freedom of the "good old ordinary," and it therefore behoves Safety riders to acquire a style that will not cal forth the ridicule of the non-riding section. 'The style assumed by some of our :Safety riders of riding with the head over the handle bar, and back rounded, is not only unpleasing to the eye but is injurious to the riders them- selves. A great deal of this is due to the saddle and handles being wrongly adjusted. A plumb line drapped from the peak of the saddle should fall from 2-1 to 3 in. behind the crank axle, and the handles- should come well back, so that when the arms are extended they can be reached without having to stoop to them. When pedalling, jerks should be avoided, and a smooth action maintained. The heel should be dropped when the pedal is at the highest point and raised when at its lowest point to help in pulling the crank past the dead centre. The ankle is thus brought into play and a correct and easy style of pedalling obtained.—Yours, "AS ITHERS SEE US."

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

ACTION AGAINST THE COMPANY. Yesterday week, in the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice, Mr. Justice Kay, on the application of Mr. Henderson, who appeared for the plaintiff's in the action of Wig,c,, Brothers and Steele v. the Manchester Ship Canal Company, consented to a settlement, the parties being sui juri.s, on terms arranged between the parties, but which were not disclosed in court. VISIT OF IRONMASTERS. On Wednesday a party of 60 gentlemen, representing the principal pig iron firms in the country, inspected the Manchester Ship Canal. The party were conducted over the entire length of the canal by Mr. C. J. Galloway and Mr. M. Stevens. At the Ferry Hotel, Eastham, in the evening, Mr. J. F. Wilson (Wilson. Pease, and Co.) pro- posed, and Mr. David Cowan (the Carron Company) seconded, a vote of thanks to the directors of the com- pany for allowing the ironmasters the opportunity of inspecting the undertaking. Mr. C. J. Galloway replied on behalf of the directors. Mr. M. Stevens also delivered a short speech, in which he compared the present freight charges between Manchester and Scotland, South Wales, the East Coast, and Snuth Staffordshire, showing the scale on the opening of the canal to be lower than cur- rent rates, and, in consequence, the great importance of the canal to the ironmaster.

div.head: IMPROVEMENT BILL.
div.p: THE IMPROVEMENT BILL.

The Warrington Extension, Water, and Improve- ment Bill has passed the third reading in the House of Lords, and now only awaits the Royal assent, which will, in all probability, be received in the course of the next four or five days. The extension portions of the Bill come into force on the 30•. h of next October, and the Water Works' purchase clauses on the Ist of July in next year.
THE VACANCY ON THE :WARRINGTON

div.head: -TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: -TOWN COUNCIL.

The resignation of Caluncillor Marsh, as a mem- 1 ber of the Warrington Town Council, has caused a vacancy in the representation of the South-east ward. It is not probable, however, that any steps will be taken to fill it up until November. when Mr. Marsh would have retired by effluxion of time. In the meantime, Councillor Percival takes his place on the Watch Committee, and Alderman Wright on the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee. It will be seen from our advertisement columns that Mr. Marsh there addresses the burgesses on the subject -of his resignation.
THE DIVING "CRAZE" FROM RUNCORIS

div.head: BRIDGE.
div.p: BRIDGE.

Diving from Runcorn Bridge is at present epide- mic. Burns has shown the way, and other men, who possess neither his skill norjudgment, attempt to imitate him, and the whole affair has degene- rated into a farce, which may not improbably end in a tragedy. On Saturday, McNamara, a chemical labourer, of Widnes, and a sailor, named J. W. Cun- nah, of Liverpool, had a competition. Almost simul- taneously they dived from the bridge into the Mer- sey, and then swam to the shore, near the Widnes Accident Hospital. Cunnah, who appeared the strongest swimmer, was the first to arrive, and both men were loudly cheered by the thousands of people who had assembled. On Monday McNamara re- peated his feat in good style, and afterwards seven others either dived or dropped into the water below, three of whom received injuries. but not of a serious character. A man named Joseph Ashton, of St. Helens, dropped in most awk- ward fashion, and striking the water with his chest be was partially "winded," and had some diffi- culty in keeping afloat until taken on board a boat. A salt cake worker named Faulkner who lives in Nelson-st., Widnes, accomplished a neat dive, and -then declining the assistance of a boat, swam up and down the river for a considerable distance. A coloured sailor, named William Alexander, dropped in a most awkward fashion, and coming in contact with a piece of floating timber, he received an injury to the face. The nanvs of the whole of the -divers did not transpire. On Tuesday the dive was accomplished by three mien. The third named Hugh Thompson, a Widnes man known as the "fiddler," fell into the water face foremost and the force of the concussion rendered him nearly insensible. He remained under the water a considerable time, and on rising to the sur- face, was with difficulty dragged into a boat which wa,s.in attendance. A vigorous rubbing was ad- tm.nistered with good results, and on landing on Widnes shore, he was able to walk with assistance, although evidently he was much shaken. The railway. company, who have sole control of the Bridge intend to put an end to these foolhardy attempts in .the future, and public opinion will sustain them in such a course. On Wednesday afternoon a flatman named John Nash, of Widnes, made a drop from Runcorn bridge in ,orderto settle a wager. In his ordinary clothes, he sat on the ledge of the footwalk and allawed himself to slide off in- to space. lie maintained an upright position in his des- cent, and struck the water feet first. He was a consider- able time before he again re-appeared on the surface, and the watchers were assured of his safety when they -saw him swimming to the shore. On his arrival, how- ever, it was found that his left knee had been dislocated i and the hip of the same leg was also badly njured. He was carried into the Mersey Hotels and put in a warm bath, but it was subsequently necessary to convey him to the Accident Hospital, where he remains a patient under the care of Dr. McDonnell and Dr. Richards. :eash, who is about 50 years of age, was one of these who suc- cessfully dropped from the bridge on Monday. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone arrived at Hawarden from London on Wednesday. The Glasgow Liberals intend approaching Mr. Gladstone with the view of inducing him to deliver a speech in Glas,gow during his ensuing yisit to the North.

div.p: GREAT STRIKE IN SOUTH WALES. The threatened great strike of railway and dock em- ployes in South Wales began on Thursday morning. It was announced on Wednesday that all efforts at com- promise having failed, arrangements had been made on all hands for the great lockout. The strike affects 100,000 workers, and at least four times that number of individuals. The excitement in Glamorganshire is very great. The men's demands are that 60 hours should constitutea week's work ; eight hours to be paid for as a day's overtime on completion of 60 hours; Sunday duty to be paid for as time and a half ; and a guaranteed week to be given. Last night, terms were arrived at which virtually bring the strike to an end. The mail train due to leave Cardiff for the Rhondda Valley at 3 a.m., on Thursday did not run. The men had previously come to an understanding not to unneces- sarily incommode the public, and to allow the mail to proceed; but telegrams were received shortly before three o'clock from stations along the line intimating that it would be dangerous to run the train, as there were men stationed all along the line among the hills. The train therefore did not proceed. The Taff Vale Railway Com- pany ran the five minutes to eight train from Merthyr as usual, the traffic inspector acting as stoker. The train from Cardiff to Merthyr, however, did not run. The Merthyr train returned to Merthyr from Cardiff at 12.10, and traffic on the line is now stopped. The coal traffic is stopped in several directions, and the mails had in some cases to be sent by carts. A confer- ence of the railway directors was held during Thursday, and the men asked if they would consent to work at the rate of 240 hours a month, but they elected to press the demand they had previously made. There was scarcely any business on 'Change at Cardiff, and already trade and industry have been seriously checked by the strike. A telegram from Cardiff at midnight states that the Direc- tors and the men have had a further conference, and there is every probability of a speedy settlement of the dispute. YESTERDAY'S NEGOTIATIONS. THE STRUGGLE CONTINUED. A Cardiff correspondent, telegraphing at 12.35 yester- day, says :-1 he railway men at their meeting this morn- ing rejected Thursday night's offer by the directors and decided to adhere to their original demands. The meeing which was very crowded, was presided over by Mr. Hilborne, and he was supported by Mr. Harford and the delegates who took part in the interview with Mr. Inskip, at which terms were arranged, subject to reference to

the men. With regard to the dockers' dispute there is no change to report. The men refuse to ship coal brought down by blacklegs, but are working on present supplies. There are few, and little work is doing. After the result of yesterday morning's meeting the struggle was renewed with greaterdetermination. Mr. Harford sent- an intimation by Mr. Vaughan Nash that the overnight proposals had been with- drawn, while the officers sent out strong pickets in every ' direction.
-INCREASING EXCITEMENT AT CARDIFF.

On 'Change --;:t Liverpool, yesterday morning, a tele- gram was received by the president of the Camber of Commerce, received from the secretary of the Sailors' Un'on, threatening to stop all Cardiff vessels from obtain- ing men. He urged those present in the face of such a telegram to go with him to the offices of the railway companies that afternoon, and protest against Trade Unionism—be it seamen, dockers, or railway men. It was decideded by a show of hands to adopt the sug- gestion of the Chamber, amid great excitement. " Blacklegs" have been unearthed by pickets, and in several instances blows have been returned. Thelex- citement increases hourly.

div.head: PLEURO-PNEUIiONIA.
div.p: PLEURO-PNEUIiONIA.

The farm of Mr. W. Parkinson, Collins Green, has been declared to be an infected place, and in consequence. his whole stock of cows, numbering 16, were ordered to be slaughtered. It is stated that the remainder of the cattle, numbering ten, on the farm of Mr. John Kenny, of Kenyon, where a case of pleuro-pneumonia was reported last week, have been slaughtered during the present week.

div.head: TRIPLE MURDER BY A MOTHER.
div.p: TRIPLE MURDER BY A MOTHER.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, before Mr. Justice Vaughan-Williams, Leah Charlton, 23 years of age, was indicted for the wilful murder of her three children, William Robert Charlton, four years old ; Dorothy Bennett Charlton, two years old; and Barbara Bennett Charlton, 11 months old, on the evening of the Bth May, at Toxteth Park, Liverpool. It was stated that the prisoner, who was the wife of a Customs clerk, resided in Garmoyle-road, Toxteth, having come to that city on account of her husband's removal from Southsea to Liverpool. She seemed to feel the change greatly, and deplored the loss of her friends. For some little time she had been in an unsatisfactory condition of health, and suffered from a disease which affected her mind and her nervous system. She got it into her head that her neigh- bours thought she was a spy and wanted to take her life and the lives of her children. On the date in question, . . .

when Mr. Charlton returned home from business, he was horrified to find his wife lying in the lobby with her throat cut. He immediately sent for a doctor and called in some neighbours. They found that prisoner's wind- pipe was almost severed, and for some time her life was despaired of. The house was searched by the police, and they found the children lying in bed. Their threats were cut, and they were dead. Prisoner was asked what she had done, and, taking up a piece of paper, she wrote that she cut her own throat with a razor and afterwards the children's because she was afraid of the mob who were against them. All witnesses, in the course of cross-examination, admitted that prisoner for some time had acted very foolishly. She always seemed to be fond of her children. The medical officers from the Tox- bath Hospital, the gaol at Walton, and Rainhill Asylum were called by the prosecution, and examined by Mr. Swift. They gave it as their decided opinion that prisoner was of unsound mind when she committed the murders.—ln reply to his lordship the jury said there was no need for the counsel for the defence to call his witnesses as they had made up their minds. Their ver- dict was that the prisoner was guilty of the act, but that she being of unsound mind was not responsible for her actions.—His lordship ordered her to be detained during her Majesty's pleasure.

div.head: ALLEGED BIGAMY AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: ALLEGED BIGAMY AT ST. HELENS.

At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, before Alderman J. Harrison and Alderman J. C. Gamble, Patrick Tierney, a collier, formerly of Earlestown, and now of Sutton, was brought up on a charge of bigamy by going through a form of marriage with Louisa Tilley, at Ravenhead Church, his wife Mary then being alive. Mr. T. Garner (Messrs. J. 0. and W. Swift) appeared for the prisoner, and when the case was called lie said he wished to ask for a remand and that the prisoner be admitted to bail, himself in £lO and two sureties of £5 each. He thought the police could not have any objection to a remand. The case was not a serious one, as the prisoner's wife had known of his whereabouts, and lie had not attempted to get out of the way. If the bail was put higher than the figures he had named the probability was that the prisoner would not be able to procure it.—The Magistrate's Clerk (Mr. T. Brewis) stated that he did not think bail would be I objected to if it was satisfactory. It was an important charge.—Mr. Garner said that bigamy was serious in some respects, but in that particular case it was not. The prisoner might have got away if he had liked, and for that reason he (Mr. Garner) asked that the bail should be oh a moderate amount.—The Clerk said they had better hear some evidence.—Peter Caine said he was a collier and lived at 5 Queen-st., Golborne. He had known the prisoner for seven or eight years, and was present at his marriage with Mary Noon, at All Saints' Church, Golborne, on the 3rd January 1889. Witness signed the register, and Mary Noon was now alive.— Louisa Tilley of Elephant-lane, Sutton, said that on Christmas Eve 1889 the prisener came to her mother's house and got lodgings. He began working at the Sut- ton colliery, and represented himself as a single man. She commenced to walk out with him afterwards, and banns were put up at Ravenhead church. They were married there by the Rev. H. S. Bolton.—Mr Garner: You knew before you were married that this man had a wife living? Witness: No.—Mr. Garner: Did not the prisoner wish to tell the circumstances to your mother, and you requested him not to do so—Witness: No.— Mr. Garner: We shall be able to prove this.—Alderman J. C. Gamble: He had no reasog for getting out of the way? Mr. Garner: Except that his lawful wife was en- quiring about him and he thought she must have known about it.—The Bench ultimately refused to admit the prisoner to bail and he was remanded until Thursday. The prisoner was again brought up at the Town Hall, on Thursday. Mr. J. 0. Swift defended and endeavoured to show that the woman Tilley knew the prisoner had a wife living, before she went through the marriage cere- mony with the prisoner. This, he said, would not affect the offence, but it might be urged in mitigation. The prisoner was ultimately committed for trial at the Assizes, and was admitted to bail, himself in £4O and two sureties of £2O each.
