div.head: 11-11 X kMINETZ, SATt RDAY, AUGUST 9, 1890,
div.p: THE 11-11 X kMINETZ, SATt RDAY, AUGUST 9, 1890,
Effi
a I
GENEROUS GIFT TO THE TOWN.

We understand that Mr. Robert Davies, solicitor. has generously given to the town the piece of sculp- tore, by the late Warrington Woods, called " Rachael," which was purchased by Mr. Chorley, the borough treasurer, at the sale in London last week. The purchase price of the picture was .£54.
LOCAL REDISTRIBUTION OF SEATS.

One of the most interesting changes that will be brought about by the local Act of Parliament which the Warrington Corporation have just obtained, is a "redistribution of seats," or, to put it less grandly, a re-arrangement of the wards into which the borough is divided for the purposes of municipal elections. At present the town is divided into five wards—the North-west, the North-east. the South-west, the South-east and Latchford. The four first-named of these wards are each represented in the Town Council by six members. two of them retiring every November ; while Latchford has only three repre- sentatives, one of whom retires annually. It is now expressly provided in the Warrington fmprovement and Extension Act that iti future the town shall be divided into nine wards and not five, and each of the 'nine will have three representatives. A redistribu- tion of Towneouncillors' seats has been advocated for some years back, and indeed had become absolutely necessary if the Town Council was to be of a fairly representative character. No doubt when the town was originally divided into warda an equitable re- gard to population was had in the allotment of members, but time brings changes, and one of these changes has been wrought by the rapid growth of some of the wards and the "Much slower growth of others. For instance, the latest list of burgesses shows that the North-west ward has 2,615 voters as compared witirthe meagre total of 544 in the South- west wards, yet the North-west ward has no more Town Councillors to represent its thousands than the South-westchas for its hundreds. Perhaps the unjustness of the present arrangement strikes us still more forcibly when we see that Latchford with 894 burgesses has only. half the number of represen- tatives that the-South-west ward has for its 544 electors The North-east ward has now 2,597 voters on its list, and the South-East 1,255,and these figures, with those givettfor the other wards, make a total of 7,905 persons entitled to vote at municipal elec- tions. As population is now 1,,.e acknowledged basis Ifor representation, it follows that when the town I comes to be divided into nine wards, each ward I will, or ought toosontain as nearly as can be con- veniently arranged 880 , voters, which is, broadly speaking, the ninth part of 7,905. That is to say, Latchford, as it is at present with 894 electors and three representatives, is very nearly a typical ward, while the South-west ward, which has not even sufficient voters to entitle it to three members in place of its present six, will have to be enlarged so as to include nearly 400 additional names on its bur- gess roll. The North-west ward when partitioned will be almost equal to three of the new wards, and the same may be said of the North-east, especially when we consider that that is a district in which the population is increasing,very rapidly just now. The population of the South-east ward is scarcely sufficient to give it a claim to six seats, but it is certainly entitled to more than three. The final decision as to the area of the nine new wards will rest with the Local Government Board. The Corporation will most probably recommend a plan, and then the central authority will send down a commissioner to Warrington to hear any sugges- tionsor objections that may be made with regard to the proposal, and the final decision will probably be made in, accordance with the commissioner's report.

div.head: Bit PARKER AT WYCLIFFE.
div.p: Bit PARKER AT WYCLIFFE.

Dr. 'Parker. the eminent,- minister of the City Temple,;Loridon,"preached last evening, in Wycliffe Church, in-aid of the funds of Cockhedge Mission. There was a very large congregation, every seat, both in the body of the church and in the gallery, being well filled. Amongst those present were several ministers of different denominations, and in the se ngr eg ation most of the other churches and chapels of the town seemed to be pietty largely re- presented: The Rev. J.Yonge accompanied Dr. Parker in the pulpit,and conthicted the first part of the ser- vice. As his text Dr. Parker selected Hebrews "Wherefore, seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which cloth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us." The preacher gave an eloquent and very forcible exposition of this text, the discourse at times moving some of the auditors to: unusual expressions of sympathy. At the conclusion of his sermon, Dr. Parker made a powerful appeal on behalf of Cockhedge Mission. He was glad. he said, to associate himself with his friend Mr. Yonge in that matter. He had noticed in their little congre- gational publication for August the peculiar word "deficit." He advised them to take the advice of a Welsh deacon, and not think of their deficit till they had paid off their debt. Let them not Latinise their waytout of that difficulty. They wanted .£5O, and there were twelve men in that church, any one of whom could write them a cheque of £5O, but at the same time they wanted the pence of the poor. lie did not wish Christ to be an eternal mendicant in His own church. The collection which was after- wards taken realised about £22.

div.head: COUNTY COUNCIL MEETINGS.
div.p: COUNTY COUNCIL MEETINGS.
CHESHIRE.

The Cheshire County Council held its quarterly meeting, at Chester on Thursday. Protracted discussion tot& plane upon the proceedings of the Main Roads and Rivers Committee, which dealt largely with the amount to be paid by urban authorities for the repair, maintenance, and improvement of these roads. In the result an amendment to the resolution of the Committee was adoptedain accordance with which the amount to be offered by ,the Committee to urban authorities was placedaitSlB,32o for repairs and maintenance and £1,506 ' for improvements. With regard to river pollution it was stated that a scheme proposed by the Cheshire County Council had been accepted by the Lancashire Council. The object sought was not to make the streams sporting streams, but to prevent them from being injurious to the .health of thii district. The County Councils proposed to do this with the minimum amount of disturbance to the trading interests which had grown up on their banks. LANCASHIRE. At a quarterly meeting of the Lancashire County Council, on Thursday, a committee of nine members was appointed to consider the provisions of local taxation, Customs and EICCiSe, with the view of representing to the Council the desirability of appropriating the whole, or any part, of such grant to technical, including agri- cultural and commercial, education. Mr. Guthrie, chairman of the Finance Committee, in presenting the budget, congratulated the Council on the the fact that the sum required this year was £167,908, as against £224,028 last year. Some discussion took place regarding the position of the Parlia- mentary Committee of the County Council as opponents of bills brought forward by various local authorities. and Mr. V. R. Armitage complained strongly of the Local Government Board having thrown unnecessary expense on the Parliamentary Cosnmitteee, by insisting on the insertion of clauses to which the Bootle and Warrington Corporations had already agreed. Alderman Forrest re- plying to Alderman Muspratt, said that if the London ana North-Western and Great Western Railway Companies did not accept the schedule for classification of rates which the Board of Trade had issued, he understood that the latter body would introduce a provisional order based upon that schedule and classification.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.

IMPORTANT MEETING. A specially-convened meeting of the members of this Society was held on Thursday evening, in the Bold-street schoolroom, to consider the society's position, having regard chiefly to an adverse balance. Mr. John White occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance. The propriety of amalgamating the Warrington Musical Society with the Orpheus Orchestral Society was the remedy discussed to relieve the society from its present embarrassing position. It was made clear to the meeting that the society could not go on giving expensive concerts as it has done, nor could it see its way to any longer retaining the services of Dr. Hiles, the conductor, for the same reason—the need of funds. It was thought that the services of Mr. Crossley, the conductor of the Orpheus Society, might be secured for the suggested eplarged society for twelve months gratuitously, and that, by giving concerts on a much diminished scale of expenditure, the society's financial position might be retrieved. It was, of course, seen by all present that it would be unfair to ask the Orpheus 'Society to take any share or responsibility in regard to the debts of the Musical Society. As the settling of the terms upon which the two organisations might amalgamate proved a somewhat delicate question, it was proposed that a committee should be formed to approach the Orpheus Society on the subject,and to negotiate with that body as to the terms and conditions upon which the two societies could' merge their interests. An amendment was pro- posed to the effect that the Musical Society, being unable to pay its way, should winfl' up, and defray its debts out of the assets. / This course, we may mention, would have involved the selling of the organ in the Public Hall, which is the society's property. The amendment, though it found a seconder, met with an' almost united opposition, for, on being put to the meeting, only the proposer and seconder voted in its favour. The original proposal for a committee was after- wards put and-carried. The committee appointed consists of Messrs. W. H. J. Jenkins (secretary), L. Reynolds(treasurer),John White. J. P. Reynolds, W. Parkinson, and John Rylands. The committee will report the Pegult of their negotiations to the annual meeting of the Musical Society, to be held at an early date.

div.head: WARRINGTON BUTCHERS AT
div.p: WARRINGTON BUTCHERS AT
VARIANCE,

THE VERDICT. The action brought by Christian Bower, butcher, of Church-st., Warrington, against John Cross, butcher, of Corporation-st., to recover damages for assault, which was commenced yesterday week in the Nisi Prius Court at the Liverpool Assizes. before Mr. JustiCe Smith and a common jury, was concluded on Saturday morning. Mr. Addison, Q.C., 'M.P.. and Mr. Mulholland (instructed by Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw of Warrington) again appeared for the plaintiff ,and Mr. Bighorn, (LC., and Mr. A. G. Steel (instructed by Mr. Arthur Browne, of Warrington) for the defence. The defence set up was that if the defendant committed the assault, which he denied, he did so to preserve the peace. The case for the plaintiff was gone into' at the first hear- ing, and reported in our last issue. It may be mentioned that the claim for out of pocktt expenses was fixed at £142, made up as follows i—£ss to his brother-in-law for looking after his business since the assault;' Dr: Cannell's bill, £l2 12s.;' Profes4or Hare's, £9 95.; Dr. Glascot's, £4 45.; travelling expenses, £1 Bs. ; extra nourishment £25; expenses at the seaside and elsewhere, £35. On Saturday morning Mr. Bigham addressed the Court for the defence, and called the following witnesses. —Dr. Richmond, of Warrington, stated that in the first instance the injury sustained by the plaintiff might have been serious; but he was oi opinion that there were no .effects remaining. He. differed with Dr. Cannel!, who was the plaintiff's medical attendant, and who had said that • Mr. Bower was ruined for life.— Dr. Bickerton, of Liverpool, gave evidence as a specia- list, and described the tests he had put the plaintiff's sight to. The result of these was that he was of opinion that plaintiff's eye was not affected. Witness had given him spectacles of the same strength, but of different makes, and he had described the effects on his sight as various.—John Cross, the defendant, was then examined, and said he was present at the sale which was held on the 3rd of February in the Eagle and Child yard, when he saw his son, who appeared to be injured. He spoke to the plaintiff about the matter, and said he would serve•him the same. He struck him over some- one's else's shoulder with a stick, which wis produced, and which was a light one.—His Lordship at this point, observed that the case was undefended, except as re- garded damages.—The counsel consulted for a short time, and subsequently Mr. Bigham said he could not deny that his client was liable, and it had been agreed to leave the question of damages to his lordship.—His Lordship said he believed the plaintiff had inflated his ease—he would not say, more than that. However, there was no doubt that plaintiff was at one time in a critical condition, although his sight was no longer affected. He had made out that he bad been put to an. expense of £lOO, and he (the learned judge) gave him another £5O, or £l5O in all.—A verdict for that amount was agreed to with costs.

LOWTON WIFE BEATER COMMITTED.—At the Leigh Police Court,on Monday, Patrick Burke, sinker, Lovvton, was summoned by his wife for assault, on the 13th of June. The Bench sent him to prison for 14 days, and made a separation order for 10s. per. week.

div.head: RAINFORD MURDER.
div.p: THE RAINFORD MURDER.

In the trial at Liverpool Assizes, yesterday week, of John Duckworth Pickavance, and his wife, Mary Jane Pickavance, for the murder of Henry Granger Foster, at Rainford, the following evidence was given in addi- tion to that which appeared in our columns last week :—Dr. James Barr, medical officer of the Kirkdale Prison, said he had daily opportunity of seeing the male prisoner between the 17th and 27th of July. He seemed to him an excitable, irritable, and very passionate Man, but still he could find no evidence of insanity,or delusions, or hallucinations. In every respect he seemed to know the nature and import of the act, and he also seemed to be able to control his actions and to discriminate between right and wrong.—By Mr. M'Keand : It was frequently the case that a man might be temporarily insane. Irres- pective of the crime, he thought it would be almost impossible to get two medical men to certify this man as insane. Certainly he would not at the present time sign a certificate of lunacy.—This closed the case for the pro- secution.—Mr. M'Keand said he would call his witnesses first and then address the jury.—Elizabeth Preston, wife of John Preston,and sister of the male prisoner, said that when he lived next to her she noticedthat he was strange in his manner in many respects. He was always com- plaining about his head. He would come into their house sometimes, stand quite still without saying any- thing, and then go track into his own house. He was strange with them all. He would stare straight at the wall, then go into the house, and picking up some pots would throw them against a wall. Her younger brother had always been very simple. There had been three deaf mutes in the family, and her father had another son who had always been strange, sitting and talking to himself all the night through. The male prisoner was of a religious turn of mind, and went frequently to the Salvation Army.— William Bullock, relieving officer of the Prescot Union, said he had known the prisoner's family all his life, and gave corroborative evidence of the strange behaviour of some of its members. One of the relatives had to be confined in an imbecile ward.—Dr. Egerton Francis Hall, medical officer of the Prescot Union, was called and cor- roborated the facts as to the confinement of a member of the family in an imbecile ward.—Dr. J. Barlow, physician at Prescot, said the prisoner consulted him as to his condi- tion. He complained of pains in his head and of hearing voices. He came to the conclusion the man was not of sound mind.—John Hobbins, watchmaker, said the male prisoner was a particular friend of his. He was always complaining about his head being numbed, and he told him that he was paying about 4s. 6d. a week for medi- cine.—Ellen Carroll, a married woman, spoke of the prisoner complaining about his head, and of his having a strange look.—John Preston, brother-in-law to John Pickavance, said he was a sober, well-conducted young man.—Annie Haigh, living near to the prisoners, said she showed him a story in a paper the day before the murder. He said he would write a story and call it" The Holy Stocking," and then asked his wife for the pen and ink with which to write it.—H. Hackett, shoemaker, said he worked with the prisoner at one time, and then he used frequently to complain of pains in his head. He used to have a revolver, and the first time he slept with him he shot it through the window twice.— After the speeches for the defence and a lengthy sum- ming up by the Judge the jury retired at 9.45 p.m. to consider their verdict. Shortly after half-past twelve on Saturday morning the jury returned into court with a verdict of not guilty against the male prisoner, John Pickavance, on account of insanity, and he was ordered Ito be confined during her Majesty's pleasure. Mrs. Pickavance was acquitted. At a quarter to one o'clock Mrs. Pickavance, in com- pany of her sister and an aunt, left the St. George's Hall by the entrance opposite Lime-st. Station. It was raining at the time, and there was a crowd of between eighty and ninety people gathered on the steps. Mrs. Pickavance and her two relatives entered a cab, and gave directions to drive to Huron. When the cab left the hall the crowd cheered and then a number of men ran after the cab, cheering as it moved along Lime-st. to London-rd. A large force of police were present. The male prisoner was shortly afterwards removed to Kirkdale gaol.

STATEMENT BY A JURYMAN. One of the jurymen who tried Pickavance and his wife for the murder of Mr. Foster, at Rainford, in the course of an interview with a Press representative, stated that the jury were unanimously agreed as to the guilt of the male prisoner, and they were wholly and solely influenced in arriving at the decision to find him " Not guilty," on the ground of insanity, by the evidence of Dr. Wigles- worth, medical officer of the Rainhill Lunatic Asylum, and by the details given by the neighbours of the pre- vious history and conduct of Pickavance. Respecting the guilt of the female prisoner there was a division of opinion among the jury, but ultimately they decided to give her the benefit of the doubt, and found her "not guilty." The juryman added that the action of the Home Secretary in the Maybrick and Crewe cases was not men- tioned or even hinted at, and that the agitations in connection with these cases was not referred to at all.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

THURSDAY.—Beforo his Honour Judge Wynne Ffaulkes. THE CAUSE LIST comprised one default summons, nine adjourned plaints, 46 original plaints, and 50 original judgment summonses. CLAIM AGAINST A CYCLIST.—A claim was made by S. Walton, Cross-lane, Earlestown, cab proprietor, against Henry Millar, Bewsey-rd., Warrington, cab-maker's ap- prentice, for £l2 for damages for injury to horse and harness and waggonette, and by loss of services of horse occasioned by the negligent riding of a tricycle by the defendant on the 26th May last. Mr. H. -J. Longton appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. A. Browne for the defendant. It was stated by Mr. Longton, in his open- ing remarks, that on the day named the plaintiff's I waggonette was proceeding with a party to Frodsham, and on getting to the bottom of the hill at Preston Brook the conveyance was stopped to let some of the passen- gers in. At that time the defendant was seen coming down the hill at a great speed, apparently having lost control of the machine, and when near the waggonette he threw himself off the tricycle which went in amongst the legs of one of the horses causing it to fall and do the damage for which the claim was made.—Two witnesses for the plaintiff having been called, the case was adjourned for a fortnight. ILLEGAL DISTRAINT FOR RENT.—ALLEGATIONS OF PERJURY. Thomas Oliphant, of Bruche Lodge, employed at the rubber works, sued Thomas Holbrook, bailiff, Fennel-st., Warrington, fer £8 odd in lieu of returning goods, alleged to have been illegally distrained, and he also claimed for damages for such distraint. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. T. Swift, barrister, (instructed by Mr. J. W. Knowles, of Widnes) defended. In his opening statement, Mr. Browne said that the plain- tiff formerly lived at 24, Glazebrook-st., Warrington, and had, no doubt, been in arrears for rent. On the 12th June, the day of the alleged illegal distraint, Mr. Oliphant was at work and Mrs. Oliphant in the house. Hearing a noise at the back-door,which was fastened,Mrs. Oliphant went upstairs to see who was there, and as soon as she had got upstairs she heard a terrible thud at the front door, which had been locked, and immediately after a bailiff named Lindley called from .the bottom of the stairs for her to come down. She replied that she would make him pay for that, and demanded the warrant for breaking into the house. Lindley replied that he needed no war- rant ; they could do as they liked. Mr. Holbrook, who was a certificated bailiff, afterwards came in but refused to produce the warrant for the distraint. Witnesses from Glazebrook-st. were then called, and stated that they had seen Lindley. who was accompanied by another bailiff. named Bromley, kick open the front door of Oliphant's house. A lock, which it was stated had been broken on the occasion, was also pro- duced. In cross-examination, the plaintiff admitted that he had no other reason for keeping his doors locked than to prevent the landlord from getting his rent. He had made a practice of it for three or four months. In his address for the defence, Mr. Swift said it was rather peculiar that the law, while providing punishment for the offence of removing goods in order to avoid distraint for debts, did not make any provision for when goods were locked up. The effect was the same: the landlord or creditor was unable to distrain on the goods in pay- ment for his debt or rent. Under the present law there was no doubt the defendant had no right to force open a door or to gain admission to a place by violence, but he denied that any violence was used. The defendant and his two assistants, Lindley and Bromley,were then called, and they denied absolutely that any violence had .been used to open the door. Defendant had himself tried the back door, but finding it ',eked, they went to the front door and Lindley simply turned the handle and walked in. Each of these witnesses swore that the warrant was read over by the defendant to Mrs. Oliphant and, later on, to her husband. In cross-examination, Lindley said they got 2s. 6d. each for these cases of distraint. Robert Lowe, auctioneer, stated that he con- dected the distraint sale, and the furniture realised £4 id., which was, he thought, its full value. In giving judgment, his Honour said that was, in his opinion, a very serious case, because there was not any possibility of reconciling the evidence given on each side. . The course taken by the defendant and his witnesses was net merely to deny one or two things, but to deny everything. There was hardly one single statement made by the plaintiffs witnesses that was not contradicted by the defendant's witnesses. Having referred to the fact that on the plaintiff's side there were independent witnesses, while no witnesses were called from Glazebrook-st. by the defendant, his Honour went on to say that he had to chose between the witnesses for the plaintiff and defen- dant, and it would be monstrous if he were to prefer the evidence of defendant's witnesses to that of at least three independent witnesses on the other side, against whom nothing could be brought. It was very shocking that there should be that act of perjury, for it was nothing more or less, and it would be a serious question to con- sider the position the defendant held in connection with that Court. He must find that there had been a totally illegal distraint, and he did not feel disposed to give the plaintiff a farthing less than the £8 he claimed. A ver- dict for the plaintiff was given accordingly.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
COMING EVENTS.

An organ recital will be given by Mr. Walter Farron, of Sale, to-morrow (Sunday), in the Cairo- st. Chapel, at the conclusion of the usual services. To-morrow (Sunday), anniversary services will be held in connection with Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel, when the Ret. Thomas Champness, of Roch- dale, will preach, and when special music will be rendered by an augmented chair. The morning service will commence at 10.30, as usual, and not at 10 o'clock, as was, owing to a clerical error, inti- mated in a public announcement.

div.head: ASSAULTS ON CHILDREN.
div.p: ASSAULTS ON CHILDREN.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, Martin Burns (60). labourer, was found guilty of having, on the 14th July, at Warrington, criminally aisaulted Lucy Michaels, 13 years of age, and was sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment with hard labour. On Thursday. William Roberts (59), labourer, was found not guilty of having, on the 29th • April, at Warrington, criminally assaulted Emily Bassett; 13 years old. THE LATE Mn. Jan SAVA.GE.

The funeral John took place at the cemetery on Saturday afternoon. The deceased, who was the third son of the late Mr. Wm. Savage, of Church-st., was 26 years of age at the time of his death, vVhich was due to typhoid lever. The ceremony at the graveside was performed by the Rev. Thomas Rigbyoricar of St. Peter's Church, of which the deceased was one of the sidesmen. There was a large attendance. A number of choice wreaths had been forwarded. ACCIDENT TO A WARRINGTON BOY AT CHESTER. An accident happened, on Monday, to a lad named Hesketh Parr, about seven years of age, who lives in Monks-st., Warrington. He had been with his parents to Chester with the picnic from St. Mary's Church, Bank Quay, and when returning from Chester he fell from the top of a 'bus to the ground, alighting on his head, which was badly injured. He was immediately picked up and conveyed home by train. his wounds were dressed at Warrington, and, we understand, he is progressing favourably. PRESENTATION AT LATCHFORD.

Mrs. Herbert Woods, who has recently left Latch- ford, was on her del arture made the recipient of a handsome drawing-room timepiece subscribed for by the members of the Church Workers' Associa- tion and the various officials connected with Christ Church. The following tribute accompanied the timepiece :—" Presented to Mrs. Herbert 'WoOds on the occasion of her leaving Latchford, as a mark of their appreciation of the many services rendered by her and Mr. Herbert Woods, ;during their resi- dence in the Parish."

FORESTERS ANNIVERSARY. The anniversary meeting of the Mount Tlermon Benefit Society of the Ancient Order of Forester, was held on Tuesday at the Dog and Dart Inn, Grappenhall. Abont fifty members and friends were present, and Mr. M. Lomas (sec.) presided. The balance sheet, which was submitted, showed that although the year had been a rather heavy one for the society, there was still a balance of between £1,400 and .£1,500. An excellent dinner vviis after- wards partaken of, and the rest of the evening was pleasantly spent on the bowling green.

div.head: . _ @DDFELLOWS' ANNIVERSARY AT CROFT.
div.p: . _ @DDFELLOWS' ANNIVERSARY AT CROFT.
£5BB

The members of a branch of the Earl of Wilton Lodge, formerly of the Loyal Order of Oddfellows' Friendly Society, but now a separate society, held their anniversary, on Saturday afternoon, at the Joiner's Arms Inn, Croft. Members to the number of about 22 met at the lodge at one ,o'clock, and partook of an excellent dinner provided by Miss Gleave, the hostess. The usual monthly meeting of the Society took place in the evening. The number of members in the society is about 39, and the funds are in a prosperous condition. Dancing was engaged in, and a pleasant evening was spent. THE B/RTII AND DEATH RATE Or WARRINGTON. For the week ending Saturday, August 2nd, 1890. —The mean temperature was 602 Fahrenheit, and therefore 3 degrees higher than the pre- ceding week. The maximum temperature 72 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the let inst, and the minimum temperature, 44 Fahrenheit, on the 2nd inst. The rainfall measured .54in. The general direction of the wind was S.W. During the week, which was the 31st of the current year, 39 births and 15 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 15.6 per thousand, against 156, the average of the previous four weeks, and against 291 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from enteric fever, 1 from dia.rrlicea, 1 from cancer, 2 from premature birth, 3 from brain disease, 1 from lung disease. Two cases of scarlatina were reported under the re- quirements of the Act of Parliament.—JoHN H. GORNALL. Medical Officer of Health.

SUDDEN DEATH .A.T THU VULCAN Wonirs. An extraordinary sudden death occurred at Hades- sown yesterday morning. James Massey, 61 years, was following his employment as driller, at the Vulcan Locomotive Works when he dropped to the floor and immediately expired. The deceased had been off work three weeks, and returned on Wednesday. His medical attendant Dr. Mouncey states that he expired in a faint- ing fit, owing to lack of vitalitt,to restore respirations Deceased retursed to work too soon after illness.

AN UNOPPOSED ELECTION. Yesterday Mr. Abel Thomas, Liberal, was elected un- opposed for East Carrnarthenshire. BARROW ELECTION EXPENSES. The expenses of the three candidates in connection with the recent Parliamentary contest at Barrow, are as follows —Mr. Caine, £295 1.95. lid.; Mr. Wainwright, £5BB 12s. 2d. ; Mr. Duncan, 1V1,P., £484 7s. 9d. BOAT ACCIDENT AIID LOSS OF FOUR LIVES. A fortnight ago, three pitmen and a girl left Sunder- land in a pleasure boat, and have not been seen since. It was hoped that a passing vessel picked them up, but the bodies of two were washed ashore, on Thursday. Doubtless all perished. SERIOUS RAILWAY COLLISION. The Press Association says the traffic on the London and North-Western Railway between the North and ton- don was delayed for some hours yesterday morning by a collision between two goods trains between Harrow and Watford. The mail trains to London were much delayed. , THE NEW CROSS POISONING MYSTERY. IMPORTANT DISCOVERIES.

The Central News states that the police are in posses- sion of information regarding the New Cross tragedy, which practically leaves no doubt that Mrs. Townsend administered poison to Mr. De La Motte and afterwards to herself. The actual purchase of the poison has not been traced to the lady, but evidence will be given at the adjourned inquest that she attempted to purchase poison of a local chemist who refused to supply her. Other startling evidence will be forthcoming.
PEACE IN ARGENTINE..

Yesterday the Argentine Legation in London re- ceived the following official despatch from the Minis- ter of Foreign Affairs of the Argentine Republic :—"Con- gress accepted Dr. Juarez Celman's resignation. Dr. Pellegrini assumed the executive power, appointing the following Ministry; Interior, General Roca ; foreign affairs, Eduardo Costa; finance, Vicente F. Lopez; jus- tice and public instruction' Jose M. Gutierrez; war and marine, General Levalle. Complete order and satisfac- tion in all the republic. Circulate to the legations and publish.—Signed, EDUARDO COSTA." LORD DUNLO IN DUBLIN. - -

Lord Dunlo travelled to Dublin, on Thursday, from London, with Mr. Cave, an English gentleman. Soon after their arrival at the Shelbourne Hotel, accompanied by Mdlle. Delaport and Mr. Cave, Lord and Lady Dunlo drove to Flowth. Lord Dunlo said that he saw in sever- al papers a statement to the effect that he intended to go to South Africa, and he wished to say that he had no intention whatever of doing so. As to Lady Dunlo, her intention was to conclude her engagements. He added, "I am going to stop here till Sunday next, when I shall have to return to England for a few days, but I shall join her ladyship immediately after, wherever she may be." Lord Dunlo further stated that he was sure his father would make him a sufficient allowance.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS,
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS,

The House met at 4.15. MISCELLANEOUS .—Lord HOWTH withdrew his opposition to the Dublin Corporation Bill, which was read a third time. The housing of the working classes bill was read a third time, andthe Reserve Forcesßill was read a second time.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. THE EXETER SOLDLERS.—MP . STANHOPE informed Sir Stafford Northcote that a court was inquiring into the alleged insuborcff nation among the soldiers at Exeter. COINAGE MARKS.—Mr. GOSCHEN informed Mr. Coghill that he proposed to consult certain authorities before finally deciding, but he hoped to be able to meet the wishes of those desiring the clear value of the marks upon silver coins. The public was perfectly familiar with gold coins. DISMISSED POSTMEN. -Mr. SmITH, replying to Mr. Pickersgill, said the Postmaster General had nearly com- pleted his enquiry respecting the reinstatement of the dismissed postmen, and the decision would be short!), made known. . .

... THE RUPEE GRIEVANCE.—Mr. GORST, replying to Mr. Lethbridge, said the Indian Secretary of State in Council had adopted the resolution of the Select Committee on the Grievances of the Uncovenanted Civil Servants, and pensions payable in the United Kingdom would be at the rate of is 9d. per rupee. This would apply all pensions payable during this financial year. BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.—Mr. SMITH moved that the House rise to-morrow, after dealing with the Govern- ment Bill. .Mr. Lea moved to permit the Intoxicating Liquors (Ireland) Bill be taken to-morrow. He pro- tested against the Government's treatment of Ireland.— The amendment was defeated by 120 to 46, and Mr. Smith's motion having been accepted, the House went into committee, . . .

NAVAL DEFENCES —On the vote for the Admiralty Office being prpposed, Captain VERNEY called attention to a report of the Committee on naval defence, and to the serious statements they made, and the important recommendations that they put forward.—Lord G. flammtroic said all the recommendations had been acted on, and were actually in working order at the admiralty. —Mr. DUFF called attention to various points in the re- port of the Royal Commission, and notably to the ques- tion of ordnance, expressinc, the opinion that the navy should be allowed to get their own guns without going to the war office. Lord G. HAMILTON said that neither he nor the Secretary of War were satisfied with the system of the supply of ordnance. He believed the Admiralty would soon have more control over its ordnance.
rLEFT SITTING.]
LYMM..

ANNIVERSARY SERMONS.—The anniversary sermons in connection with the Baptist Sunday school were preached in the chapel, Higher-lane, on Sunday, by Mr. Ernest Hughes, of Manchester. Collections were taken in be- half of the Sabbath school. SUNDAY Scnoot. TREAT.—The annual Sunday school. treat was given to the . children attending the Higher-lane naptist Chapel, on Thursday afternoon. There was a good attendance, and after a substantial feast, the evening was spent in games such as children delight in. • PRIMITIVE METHODIST TEA MEETING.—A tea meeting was held in tbe Primitive Methodist Schoolroom, on Thursday night, in aid of the funds for the erection of a new chapel. There was a good attendance. Mr. Ball, of Statham, was the host who provided the good things. After tea a meeting was held, theßev. W. Evans occupy- ing the chair, when songs and part singing took place, together with readings and recitations. A very pleasant meeting was held. EXCURSIONISTS IN THE CANAL.—On Saturday a number of excursionists from Manchester visited Lymm. One of them, whilst skipping along the canal bank near to the water's edge, over-balanced herself, and ere she could recover her equilibrium, she fell into the water. Her screams soon brought her companions to her rescue. This unexpected immersion acted as a " damper " to the party. The performance was repeated on Monday, when another excursionist fell into the water. LYMM LOCAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this Board took place on Thursday night. There were pre- sent—Mr. Cameron (chairman), Messrs. Rogers, Harri- • .n, Brazendale, Forster, and Gibbon; Mr. Ridgway law clerk), Mr. Mullard (clerk), and Mr. Mort (sur- veyor). The gas report stated that the gas registered 1850 candles during the month.. The mains of the district had been examined by the new gas manager, and the 9in. mains were found defective, having been badly laid. He had also got the five old retorts out, and things were ready for new ones when they arrived. The Law Clerk reported in reference to the obstruction of the highway by' a wooden erection put up by Messrs. Gibson at Massey Brook, that it would be removed in the course of a few days, and he had taken no action in the matter. The gas manager was allowed a week's holiday. This was all the business.

SUICIDE OF AN EXCURSIONIST. At the Fleece Hotel, Lymm, on Wednesday morning, Mr. Worsley, coroner, held an inquest on the body of a man whose identity had not transpired, and who was found hanging to some iron railings at Lymm, on Tues- day morning. Evidence was given to the effect that the deceased was found suspended by his handkerchief by a man named Concannon, who was going to his work along the Long Butts-lane. The jury returned a verdict in the following terms :—" That'the said man, unknown, committed suicide by hanging at tyrkmm." The deceased man was apparently an excursionist who had visited Lymm on • Bank Holiday, and it is supposed he came from the neighbourhood of Manchester. He was about 28 or 30 years of age,sft. Bin. in height,dark complexion, dark hair,clean shaven with the excoptionsf moustache, and had grey eyes. The deceased was dressed in a dark mixture cloth jacket and vest, and black worsted trousers. He also wore a blue-striped shirt, brown stockings, and lace-up boots. The lining of the hat in- dicated that it had been purchased at Hyde.

FLORAL AND HORTICULTURAL SHOW.—The seventh annual show in connection with the Golborne and Low- ton Floral and Horticultural Society was held in Brown's School, Golborne on Saturday. There was a good num- ber of entries, and the exhibits were fully up to the aver- age. Collections of plants had been sent by Captain Seton, Mr. S. S. Brown, and Mr. G. W. Rigg, for decoration. The following received prizes for the neatest front cottage garden in the society's district, 1, C. Spencer ;2, R. Mawson ;3, J. Barrow. Mr. Cotterill, secretary, worked assiduously with the Committee, to make the show a success. ALLGIBD ATTEMPTED ROBBERY.—On Tuesday, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, William Cartwright, a boy of 15, was charged with attempted robbery from the Eccleston-lane-ends Post Office, kept by Alfred Stockley, on the 28th ult. P.C. M'Lean, watching the premises from an unoccupied house opposite, saw Mr. Stockley lock up, and afterwards saw the prisoner shake the door (the fastener being faulty), and go inside, where he was taken into custody. Seine sweets and a halfpenny were found upon him. It was alleged that the boy went there to buy sweets. The Bench considered that there was a doubt in the case, and dismissed the boy.

TO THE BURGESSES OF THE SOUTH-EAST WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—It is With very great regret that I have been compelled to resign from the lown Council, as one of your representatives, but through the uncourteous treatment I have received, I could no longer remain a mem- ber thereof, and I now respectfully ask all Burgesses, and especially my supporters and workers, to accept my best thanks for all past kindnesses and support. To those who are anxious to know the reason of my resignation. I would respectfully call their attention to the proceedings of the Conn. ell of Tuesday last, the sth of August, of which they will find afu 1 report in all the local newspapers of this week. Again thanking, Yours faithfully, R. W. MARSII, 1, Mersey-st. August Bth, 1890.
